answer.text:
This is an (attempted) NMOS common-gate stage.

* Gate is the common terminal: $V_G=V_b$ DC, $v_g=0$ ac.
* Drain is the output terminal: $R_D$ to $V_{DD}$ ac ground.
* Source is the input terminal: AC coupled through $C_1$
  to $V_{in}$.

Put $C_1$ a short for signal, $V_{DD}$ and $V_b$
AC ground, $M_1$ in saturation. Bulk is p-sub = GND.

Source and bulk are both DC tied to GND.

### DC bias

$$V_S =0,\;\; V_G = V_b$$

$$V_{GS}=V_b$$

$$V_{SB}=0$$

so no DC back-gate:

$$V_{TH}=V_{TH0}$$

In saturation:

$$I_D = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}_1
(V_b-V_{TH})^2\big(1+\lambda_n V_{DS}\big)$$

$$V_{DS}=V_D-V_S = V_{DD}-I_D R_D$$

$$V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-I_D R_D$$

For saturation we need

$$V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TH}$$

$$V_{DD}-I_D R_D \ge V_b-V_{TH}$$

This fixes a $g_m, r_o$:

$$g_m = \mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})(1+\lambda V_{DS})$$
$$r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D}$$

So far so good. The problem is AC.

### Small-signal

AC model: gate grounded, bulk grounded, $V_{DD}$ grounded.

But the source is also directly tied to GND:

```
Vin --- C1 ---+--- s M1 d ---+--- RD --- gnd
              |              |
             gnd            Vout
              b M1          g M1 --- gnd
```

Hence the signal node $v_s$ is forced to AC ground:

$$v_s = 0$$

despite the connection of $V_{in}$ through $C_1$.
In other words $V_{in}$ ideal is shorted to ground
for AC by $C_1$. With a source resistance $R_S$ all
of $V_{in}$ drops across $R_S+1/sC_1$. Nothing reaches
the transistor.

At the output node KCL:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}+\frac{v_{out}-v_s}{r_o}
+ g_m(v_g-v_s)+g_{mb}(v_b-v_s)=0$$

With $v_g=0$, $v_b=0$ and $v_s=0$ :

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_D}+\frac1{r_o}\right)=0$$

i.e.

$$v_{out}=0$$

$$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = 0$$

$v_{gs}=v_g-v_s =0$, so the transistor generates
no signal drain current. The small change in $V_{SB}$
is also zero: $v_{bs}=0$, so the $g_{mb}$ generator is
also zero.

Input resistance looking into the source, before the
hard ground, would be the usual CG impedance:

With test $v_x$ at source, drain loaded by $R_D$:

$$R_{in,s} = \frac{R_D+r_o}{1+(g_m+g_{mb})r_o}
\approx \frac1{g_m}$$

But it is shorted by the DC wire to ground:

$$R_{in} = R_{in,s}\parallel 0 = 0$$

Seen from $V_{in}$:

$$Z_{in}= \frac1{sC_1}$$

Output resistance is normal for a grounded-source,
grounded-gate device:

Apply $v_x$ at drain, $v_s=0$, $v_g=0$:

$$i_x = \frac{v_x}{R_D}+\frac{v_x}{r_o}$$

$$R_{out}=R_D \parallel r_o$$

In short: DC current flows, setting a DC $V_{out}$,
but no signal can develop $v_{gs}$. The stage has
zero gain.

This is a flawed common-gate amplifier. To make it work
the source must be free to move for AC while still
getting DC bias. Typically the direct wire to ground
is replaced by a high-impedance tail current source
$I_{SS}$ to ground, or by a resistor $R_S$ to ground.

With an ideal $I_{SS}$, $v_s \approx v_{in}$, and the
familiar CG results are obtained:

$$A_v \approx (g_m+g_{mb})(r_o\parallel R_D)$$
$$R_{in,s}\approx \frac1{g_m+g_{mb}}$$
$$R_{out}=R_D\parallel r_o$$

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies that the source is hard-shorted to ground, so the input cannot produce a source signal and the ideal voltage gain is zero.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
The small signal circuit is 2nd order.

Put $V_{DD}$ to ac ground. Let $V_g$, $V_d$ be the
gate and drain ac voltages. $V_s=0$.

$C_{SB}$ is connected source to bulk. Both are ac ground.
Its ac voltage is identically zero. It stores no signal
energy.

Remain $C_{GS}, C_{GD}, C_{DB}$ with

* G: $\dfrac{V_g-V_{in}}{R_S}+V_g sC_{GS}
      +(V_g-V_d)sC_{GD}=0$
* D: $\dfrac{V_d}{R_D}+V_dsC_{DB}
      +(V_d-V_g)sC_{GD}+g_mV_g=0$
      neglecting $r_o$

i.e.

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\frac1{R_S}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD}) & -sC_{GD} \\
g_m-sC_{GD} & \frac1{R_D}+s(C_{DB}+C_{GD})
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_g\\ V_d\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{in}/R_S\\0\end{bmatrix}$$

The determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}
D(s) &=
\left(\frac1{R_S}+sC_1\right)\left(\frac1{R_D}+sC_2\right)
+sC_{GD}(g_m-sC_{GD}) \\
&=\frac1{R_SR_D}+s\left[\frac{C_1}{R_D}+\frac{C_2}{R_S}+g_mC_{GD}\right]
+s^2\left[C_1C_2-C_{GD}^2\right]
\end{aligned}$$

with $C_1=C_{GS}+C_{GD}$, $C_2=C_{DB}+C_{GD}$.

$$\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{sC_{GD}-g_m}{R_S\,D(s)}$$

$D(s)$ is quadratic in $s$. 

$C_{GS},C_{GD},C_{DB}$ make a capacitive loop
gate-drain-ground-gate, so 3 capacitors give
2 independent states. That is the familiar Miller input
pole and output pole, plus one RHP zero due to $C_{GD}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two poles and justifies them by showing CSB has zero voltage, the remaining capacitors have only two independent states, and the transfer-function denominator is quadratic.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
The small signal model has, in AC,

* $G$ : $R_{S}$ to $V_{in}$, $C_{GS}$ to gnd,
  $C_{GD}$ to $D$
* $D$ : $R_{D}$ to gnd, $C_{DB}$ to gnd,
  $C_{GD}$ to $G$, $g_{m}V_{GS}$ to gnd

$V_{GS}=V_{G}$, $V_{DS}=V_{D}=V_{out}$.
$C_{SB}$ is connected gnd to gnd.

Put $s$ for complex frequency. KCL $G$ and $D$:

$$\frac{V_{G}-V_{in}}{R_{S}}+V_{G}sC_{GS}+ (V_{G}-V_{D})sC_{GD}=0$$

$$\frac{V_{D}}{R_{D}}+(V_{D}-V_{G})sC_{GD}+V_{D}sC_{DB}+g_{m}V_{G}=0$$

i.e.

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\frac1{R_{S}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD}) & -sC_{GD} \\
g_{m}-sC_{GD} & \frac1{R_{D}}+s(C_{GD}+C_{DB})
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_{G}\\V_{D}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{in}/R_{S}\\0\end{bmatrix}$$

The determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta(s)&=\left[\frac1{R_{S}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD})\right]
\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+s(C_{GD}+C_{DB})\right]
+sC_{GD}(g_{m}-sC_{GD})\\
&=\frac1{R_{S}R_{D}}+s\left[\frac{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}{R_{D}}
+\frac{C_{GD}+C_{DB}}{R_{S}}+g_{m}C_{GD}\right] \\
&\quad+s^{2}\left[(C_{GS}+C_{GD})(C_{GD}+C_{DB})-C_{GD}^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}$$

quadratic in $s$.

In particular $V_{C_{GS}}=V_{G}$, $V_{C_{DB}}=V_{D}$,
$V_{C_{GD}}=V_{G}-V_{D}$ are not independent.
There are only 2 independent node voltages.

$C_{SB}$ is shorted out.

Hence the $V_{out}/V_{in}$ denominator is 2nd order.
2 poles, 1 feedforward zero.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly derives a quadratic characteristic determinant and explains that CSB is shorted while the remaining capacitor voltages have only two independent degrees of freedom. The conclusion of two poles is correct.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
The small signal circuit has 2 signal nodes.

Put $V_{in}=0$ for the natural frequencies.

* source is ac ground,
* body is ac ground.

So

* $C_{GS}$ is $G$ to ground,
* $C_{DB}$ is $D$ to ground,
* $C_{GD}$ is $G$ to $D$,
* $C_{SB}$ is ground to ground.

$C_{SB}$ has identically zero ac voltage. It is
shorted out and gives no dynamics.

There remain 3 capacitors. They make the loop

$$ G-C_{GS}-gnd-C_{DB}-D-C_{GD}-G $$

with no resistance in the loop. Hence

$$v_{CGD}=v_{CGS}-v_{CDB}$$

Only 2 capacitor voltages are independent.

With $V_g$, $V_d$ :

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_g-V_{in}}{R_S}+sC_{GS}V_g+sC_{GD}(V_g-V_d)&=0\\
-g_mV_g+\frac{V_d}{R_D}+sC_{DB}V_d+sC_{GD}(V_d-V_g)&=0
\end{aligned}$$

i.e.

$$\begin{bmatrix}
1/R_S+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD}) & -sC_{GD}\\
-(g_m+sC_{GD}) & 1/R_D+s(C_{DB}+C_{GD})
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_g\\V_d\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{in}/R_S\\0\end{bmatrix}$$

The determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta(s) &=
\left[\tfrac1{R_S}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD})\right]
\left[\tfrac1{R_D}+s(C_{DB}+C_{GD})\right]
-sC_{GD}(g_m+sC_{GD})\\
&=\frac1{R_SR_D}
+s\left[\frac{C_{DB}+C_{GD}}{R_S}+\frac{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}{R_D}
-g_mC_{GD}\right]\\
&\quad+s^{2}\left[C_{GS}C_{DB}+C_{GS}C_{GD}+C_{GD}C_{DB}\right]
\end{aligned}$$

and

$$\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=\frac{g_m+sC_{GD}}{R_S\Delta(s)}$$

$\Delta(s)$ is 2nd degree in $s$. Generically 2 finite
poles, with a feedforward zero at $s=-g_m/C_{GD}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two poles, explains that CSB is shorted and only two of the remaining capacitor voltages are independent, and confirms the result with a second-order denominator.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a self biased common-gate stage.

```
 top = drain to RD to VDD
M1 NMOS bottom = source to Vin
 right = gate to VF
```

$V_{F}$ is the tap of the $R_{1},R_{2}$ divider
sensing $V_{out}$:

$$ V_{G}=V_{F}$$

Body is normally gnd, source is $V_{in}\ne 0$,
so there is back gate effect. Put for small
signal

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

$$v_{gs}=v_{g}-v_{s},\;v_{bs}=-v_{s},\;v_{ds}=v_{d}-v_{s}$$

Neglect caps. Assume saturation and unloaded
output.

### 1. Feedback topology

KVL around input:

$$v_{gs}+v_{s}-v_{g}=0$$
$$v_{gs}=V_{F}-V_{in}$$

Input voltage $V_{in}$ and feedback voltage $V_{F}$
are in series to create the error voltage $v_{gs}$.

Feedback network $R_{1},R_{2}$ is in parallel
with the output, i.e. it senses output voltage.

* sampling output voltage : shunt
* mixing in series with input : series

This is series-shunt, voltage-voltage, feedback.

Check sign. Let $V_{in}\uparrow$ :

$$V_{in}\uparrow \to V_{GS}\downarrow \to I_{D}\downarrow
  \to V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}\uparrow
  \to V_{F}\uparrow \to V_{GS}\uparrow$$

opposing the original change.
Let $V_{out}\uparrow$ :

$$V_{out}\uparrow \to V_{F}\uparrow \to I_{D}\uparrow
  \to V_{out}\downarrow$$

Negative feedback.

In fact the FET is a differential device:

* gate to drain : inverting, $\approx -g_{m}R_{D}'$
* source to drain : non-inverting, $\approx +(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{D}'$

Gate is the inverting input, source the
non-inverting input. Output divided to the
inverting input: like a non-inverting op-amp
amplifier.

### 2. DC bias

DC, gate draws no current:

$$V_{G}=V_{out}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}=kV_{out}$$

$$k=\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$$

$$I_{D}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D}}$$

$$I_{D}=\frac12 \mu_{n}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
 (V_{G}-V_{S}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{DS})$$

$V_{S}=V_{in,DC}$, $V_{DS}=V_{out}-V_{in,DC}$,
$V_{TH}=V_{TH0}+\gamma(\sqrt{2\phi_{f}+V_{S}}-
\sqrt{2\phi_{f}})$.

DC feedback stabilizes: $I_{D}\uparrow\to
V_{out}\downarrow\to V_{G}\downarrow\to
V_{GS}\downarrow\to I_{D}\downarrow$.

Saturation $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TH}$ is:

$$V_{out}-V_{S}\ge kV_{out}-V_{S}-V_{TH}$$

$$V_{out}(1-k)\ge -V_{TH}$$

always true for $V_{out}>0$. Once on, device
is in saturation. Need to be on and keep
drain as drain:

$$kV_{out} > V_{in,DC}+V_{TH}$$

which then implies $V_{out}>V_{in,DC}$ since $k<1$.

### 3. Small signal exact

AC gnd $V_{DD}$. $v_{d}=v_{out}$, $v_{s}=v_{in}$,
$v_{g}=v_{F}$.

Gate: no current:

$$\frac{v_{F}-v_{out}}{R_{1}}+\frac{v_{F}}{R_{2}}=0$$

$$v_{F}=k\,v_{out} \tag{1}$$

i.e. the divider loads the output with $R_{1}+R_{2}$.

$$v_{gs}=k v_{out}-v_{in}$$
$$v_{bs}=-v_{in}$$
$$v_{ds}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

$$i_{d}=g_{m}(k v_{out}-v_{in})-g_{mb}v_{in}
 +g_{ds}(v_{out}-v_{in})$$
$$=v_{out}(g_{m}k+g_{ds})-v_{in}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})
\tag{2}$$

KCL drain: currents leaving the node through
$R_{D}$, into the drain, through $R_{1}$ :

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}+i_{d}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{F}}{R_{1}}=0$$

But $(v_{out}-v_{F})/R_{1}=v_{out}/(R_{1}+R_{2})$.
Hence:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}+i_{d}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}=0
\tag{3}$$

Insert (2):

$$v_{out}\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}
 +g_{ds}+g_{m}k\right]=v_{in}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})$$

Let

$$N=g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}$$
$$\frac1{R_{eq}}=\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}+\frac1{r_{o}}$$
$$D=\frac1{R_{eq}}+g_{m}k$$

Then voltage gain:

$$ A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{N}{D}
 =\frac{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}
 {\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}+\frac1{r_{o}}+g_{m}k}
\tag{4}$$

### 4. Loop gain, ideal gain

Break loop at gate, $v_{in}=0$, drive gate with
$v_{t}$. Source grounded so $g_{mb}$ is dead.

$$v_{out}=-g_{m}v_{t}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{1}+R_{2}\parallel r_{o})$$
$$v_{r}=v_{out}k$$

Loop gain:

$$T=-\frac{v_{r}}{v_{t}}=g_{m}k\,R_{eq} \tag{5}$$

$T>0$ = negative feedback.

Write (4) as

$$A_{v}=\frac{N\,R_{eq}}{1+T}
 =\frac{A_{s}}{1+A_{g}\beta}$$

where $\beta=k$, forward source gain
$A_{s}=N R_{eq}$, forward gate gain
magnitude $A_{g}=g_{m}R_{eq}$.

Ignoring $g_{mb},r_{o}$ :

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m}R_{D}'}{1+g_{m}R_{D}'\beta},
 \quad R_{D}'=R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})$$

For $T=g_{m}R_{D}'\beta \gg 1$,

$$A_{v}\approx \frac1{\beta}=\frac{R_{1}+R_{2}}{R_{2}}$$

Positive, set by resistors, desensitized to
$g_{m}$. Including body:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{eq}}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{eq}}
 \to \frac{1+g_{mb}/g_{m}}{\beta}$$

### 5. Input resistance

With $I_{sup}$ the current supplied by $V_{in}$
into the source, KCL at source gives
$I_{sup}=-i_{d}$.

From (2)-(4), $1/R_{in}=I_{sup}/v_{in}$:

$$\frac1{R_{in}}=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})
 -A_{v}(g_{m}k+g_{ds})=A_{v}G_{L}$$

where $G_{L}=1/R_{D}+1/(R_{1}+R_{2})$. Hence:

$$ R_{in}=\frac{1}{A_{v}G_{L}}
 =\frac{R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})}{A_{v}} \tag{6}$$

This is $R_{open}(1+T)$ for a common-gate.
Indeed with no feedback, $k=0$, $R_{1}+R_{2}\to\infty$,
(6) gives $R_{in}=(R_{D}+r_{o})/(1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o})$,
the classic CG $ \approx 1/(g_{m}+g_{mb})$.

Series mixing raises the low CG $R_{in}$.
For large $T$, $A_{v}\approx1/\beta$,

$$R_{in}\approx \beta\,[R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})]$$

still relatively small.

### 6. Output resistance

Set $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$ at output.
Then $v_{g}=k v_{x}$, $v_{s}=0$,
$i_{d}=v_{x}(g_{m}k+g_{ds})$.

$$i_{x}=\frac{v_{x}}{R_{D}}+\frac{v_{x}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}+i_{d}
 =v_{x}D$$

$$ R_{out}=\frac1{D}=\frac{R_{eq}}{1+T} \tag{7}$$

i.e. open-loop $R_{eq}=R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})\parallel r_{o}$
divided by $1+T$. Shunt sampling lowers $R_{out}$.
For large $T$:

$$R_{out}\approx \frac1{g_{m}\beta}
 =\frac{R_{1}+R_{2}}{g_{m}R_{2}}$$

In summary, series-shunt feedback:

* stabilizes gain to $\approx 1/\beta$
* raises $R_{in}$ of CG by $\approx 1+T$
* lowers $R_{out}$ by $\approx 1+T$
* stabilizes DC operating point

Dominant pole is at the output. Resistive feedback
is unconditionally stable at low frequency. At high
frequency the gate node $R_{1}\parallel R_{2}$ vs.
$C_{gs},C_{gd}$ creates a second pole; $R_{1},R_{2}$
must be kept small enough to keep it beyond the
loop unity-gain frequency.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source as the input, the output divider feeding the gate, and the negative-feedback action. Its closed-loop gain is consistent with the golden result, with body-effect and finite-ro refinements.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a common-gate stage with its gate
not ac ground but driven by a fraction of its own
drain voltage.

```
 VDD
  |
  RD   drain = Vout
  |
  +-----+------ Vout
  |     |
  D     R1
 M1     +------ VF = gate
  S     R2
  |     |
 Vin    gnd
 source = Vin
```

Put $V_{F}$ the gate voltage.
For dc, ignoring gate current,

$$V_{F0}=V_{D0}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$$

$$ \frac{V_{DD}-V_{D0}}{R_{D}} = I_{D0}+\frac{V_{D0}}{R_{1}+R_{2}} $$

$$I_{D0}= \frac12 k_{n}(V_{F0}-V_{S0}-V_{TH})^{2}
 \left[1+\lambda (V_{D0}-V_{S0})\right]$$

$V_{S0}$ is the dc component of $V_{in}$.
$V_{GS0}=V_{F0}-V_{S0}$, $V_{DS0}=V_{D0}-V_{S0}$
must be $>V_{GS0}-V_{TH}$ for saturation.

If $I_{D}$ tries to increase, $V_{D0}$ falls,
$V_{F0}$ falls, $V_{GS0}$ falls, opposing the
increase. This is dc negative feedback,
like collector-feedback bias in bipolar.
It stabilizes the Q-point.

For ac it is also negative feedback.
Put source ac ground and go around the
gate-drain-gate loop: $+\delta V_{G}\to
+\delta I_{D}\to -\delta V_{D}\to -\delta V_{F}$.
Hence negative.

Small signal: assume saturation, body to source,
$g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$. Let lower case be ac.

$$v_{s}=v_{in},\;v_{g}=v_{F},\;v_{d}=v_{out}$$

$$i_{d}=g_{m}(v_{g}-v_{s})+g_{ds}(v_{d}-v_{s})$$

Gate draws no current, so $R_{1},R_{2}$ is
a divider:

$$\frac{v_{out}-v_{F}}{R_{1}}=\frac{v_{F}}{R_{2}}$$

i.e.

$$v_{F}= \beta v_{out},\quad 
\beta =\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}} $$

the feedback factor. The divider loads the
output with $R_{1}+R_{2}$ to ground.

KCL at the output node. Current from $R_{D}$,
ac $-v_{out}/R_{D}$, equals current into drain
plus current into $R_{1}$:

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}} = i_{d}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{F}}{R_{1}}$$

$$\frac{v_{out}-v_{F}}{R_{1}}=\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$$

Hence

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=
g_{m}(v_{F}-v_{in})+g_{ds}(v_{out}-v_{in})
+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}+R_{2}} $$

With $v_{F}=\beta v_{out}$:

$$v_{out}\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+g_{ds}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}
+g_{m}\beta\right]=v_{in}(g_{m}+g_{ds})$$

Let

$$\frac1{R_{L}'}=\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}$$
$$\frac1{R_{p}}=\frac1{R_{L}'}+g_{ds}
 =\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}+\frac1{r_{o}}$$

$$D =\frac1{R_{p}}+g_{m}\beta$$

Then the voltage gain, non-inverting, is

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m}+g_{ds}}{D}$$

$$ =\frac{(g_{m}+g_{ds})R_{p}}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{p}} $$

$\approx g_{m}R_{p}/(1+g_{m}\beta R_{p})$.

If $R_{1}+R_{2}\gg R_{D}$ and $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{D}}$$

Without feedback, $\beta=0$, $A_{v0}\approx g_{m}R_{D}$,
the classic common-gate gain. Feedback divides it
by $1+g_{m}\beta R_{D}$.

For large loop gain the gain becomes resistor defined:

$$T = g_{m}\beta R_{p}$$

is the loop gain around gate-drain-gate with
source ac ground: forward $-g_{m}R_{p}$ times
$\beta$. Then

$$A_{v}\approx \frac1{\beta}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

$$T\gg 1:\;A_{v}\to \frac1{\beta}=1+\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}$$

Indeed $v_{gs}=v_{F}-v_{in}=\beta v_{out}-v_{in}\to 0$,
so $v_{out}\approx v_{in}/\beta$. This is the
desensitivity benefit of feedback: gain no longer
depends on $g_{m}R_{D}$.

Input resistance at the source. Test current into
source is $-i_{d}$:

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{-i_{d}}$$

$$-i_{d}=(g_{m}+g_{ds})v_{in}-(g_{m}\beta+g_{ds})v_{out}$$

Using $v_{out}=A_{v}v_{in}$ gives

$$-i_{d}=v_{in}A_{v}\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{1}+R_{2}}\right]$$

i.e.

$$R_{in}= \frac{1}{A_{v}}\,R_{L}' $$

$$ =\frac{D\,R_{L}'}{g_{m}+g_{ds}}
 =\frac{1+R_{L}'(g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta)}{g_{m}+g_{ds}} $$

If $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$R_{in}\approx \frac1{g_{m}}+ \beta R_{L}'$$

Classic CG with gate grounded has $1/g_{m}$.
Feedback raises it by $\beta R_{L}'\approx \beta R_{D}$.
In the limit $T\gg1$, $R_{in}\to \beta R_{L}'$.

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$
at output. Still $v_{F}=\beta v_{x}$,
$i_{d}=g_{m}\beta v_{x}+g_{ds}v_{x}$.
KCL:

$$i_{x}= \frac{v_{x}}{R_{D}}+i_{d}+\frac{v_{x}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}=\frac1{D}$$

$$ =\frac{R_{p}}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{p}} $$

i.e. $R_{p}=R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})\parallel r_{o}$
divided by $1+T$. Voltage sampling reduces $R_{out}$.
If $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}\approx \frac{R_{L}'}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{L}'}
 =R_{L}'\parallel \frac1{g_{m}\beta}$$

Summary with $r_{o}\to\infty$, $R_{L}'\approx R_{D}$:

* open, $\beta=0$: $A_{v0}=g_{m}R_{D}$,
  $R_{in0}=1/g_{m}$, $R_{out0}=R_{D}$.
* closed: $A_{v}=A_{v0}/(1+T)$,
  $R_{in}=R_{in0}(1+T)$ with $T=g_{m}\beta R_{D}$
  to first order, $R_{out}=R_{D}/(1+T)$.

With body effect, body to ac ground, replace
$g_{m}+g_{ds}$ in the numerator of $A_{v}$ by
$g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}$. $R_{out}$ and $T$ are
unchanged to first order because source is grounded
for that calculation.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source input, output-divider feedback to the gate, and negative feedback. Its closed-loop gain is consistent with the expected result, including divider loading and finite output resistance; extra resistance and body-effect discussion is not required.

answer.text:
This is a 1-transistor op-amp in non-inverting
feedback.

Put $V_{S}=V_{in}$, $V_{D}=V_{out}$, $V_{G}=V_{F}$.

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$$

$$I_{D}\approx f(V_{GS})=f(V_{G}-V_{S})$$

so to first order

$$v_{out} = -g_{m}R_{D}\,(v_{g}-v_{s})
 =+g_{m}R_{D}\,(v_{s}-v_{g}) $$

i.e. source is the + input, gate is the - input,
open loop gain $g_{m}R_{D}$. The output is sampled
by $R_{1},R_{2}$ and fed to the - input:

$$V_{F}=V_{out}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}} $$

Gate draws no current so this is exact at low frequency.
Let

$$\beta =\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}},\qquad
R_{12}=R_{1}+R_{2}$$

$$v_{g}= \beta v_{out}$$

Error voltage is

$$v_{gs}=v_{g}-v_{s}=V_{F}-V_{in}$$

series mixing, shunt - voltage - sampling.
Voltage-series negative feedback.

Round the loop, $v_{in}=0$:
gate $\to$ drain $-g_{m}R_{out}$, drain $\to$ gate
$\beta$. Loop gain:

$$L = -g_{m}R_{out,open}\beta $$

$$T=-L>0$$

$$R_{out,open}=R_{D}\parallel R_{12}\parallel r_{o}$$

$$T = g_{m}\beta\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{12}\parallel r_{o})$$

Single stage: unconditionally stable.

### DC bias

$$V_{G}= \beta V_{out} =\beta(V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D})$$
$$V_{GS}=V_{G}-V_{IN,DC}$$
$$V_{DS}=V_{out}-V_{IN,DC}$$
$$I_{D}=\frac12 k_{n}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{DS})$$

$V_{SB}=V_{IN,DC}$ if body to GND.

In saturation:

$$V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{D}-V_{S}\ge V_{G}-V_{S}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{D}-V_{G}+V_{TH}\ge 0$$

But $V_{G}=\beta V_{D}$, $0<\beta<1$:

$$V_{out}(1-\beta)+V_{TH} >0$$

always true. $V_{G}<V_{D}$, so $V_{GD}<0$.
M1 cannot go to triode. It can only turn off.

ON requires $V_{GS}>V_{TH}$:

$$\beta(V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D})-V_{IN,DC}>V_{TH}$$

In particular with $I_{D}\to 0$:

$$V_{IN,DC}<\beta V_{DD}-V_{TH}$$

DC feedback is negative: $I_{D}\uparrow\to
V_{out}\downarrow\to V_{G}\downarrow\to V_{GS}\downarrow
\to I_{D}\downarrow$. Self biased.

Note $I_{D}$ must flow out of the source into
the $V_{in}$ source. $V_{in}$ must sink DC current.

### Small signal

Model with $g_{m},g_{mb},r_{o}$, body grounded,
$v_{s}=v_{in}$, $v_{g}=\beta v_{d}$, $v_{d}=v_{out}$,
$v_{bs}=-v_{s}$.

KCL at drain, open output:

$$\frac{v_{d}}{R_{D}}+\frac{v_{d}-v_{g}}{R_{1}}
+g_{m}(v_{g}-v_{s})+g_{mb}(-v_{s})
+\frac{v_{d}-v_{s}}{r_{o}}=0$$

Since $(1-\beta)/R_{1}=1/R_{12}$:

$$v_{d}\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{12}}
+\frac1{r_{o}}+g_{m}\beta\right]
=v_{in}\left[g_{m}+g_{mb}+\frac1{r_{o}}\right]$$

Hence

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m}+g_{mb}+1/r_{o}}
{1/R_{D}+1/R_{12}+1/r_{o}+g_{m}\beta}$$

i.e.

$$A_{v}=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+1/r_{o})\,R_{out,closed}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$, $g_{mb}=0$, $R_{12}\gg R_{D}$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{D}\beta}$$

This is $A_{ol}/(1+A_{ol}\beta)$ with
$A_{ol}=g_{m}R_{D}$ from source to drain.

If $T=g_{m}R_{D}\beta\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac1{\beta}=1+\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}$$

non-inverting, set by resistors. This is exactly
$$V_{out}=A_{ol}(V_{in}-\beta V_{out}).$$
Finite $T$, $r_{o}$, loading $R_{12}$ and
$g_{mb}$ give gain error $1/(1+T)$.
Body effect increases forward gain to
$g_{m}+g_{mb}$ but not loop gain, giving
$A_{v}\approx (1+\eta)/\beta$, $\eta=g_{mb}/g_{m}$.

Supply rejection: with $v_{in}=0$,
$v_{out}/v_{dd}=(1/R_{D})/G_{den}=R_{out}/R_{D}
\approx 1/T$.

### Input resistance

At source, $i_{in}+i_{s}=0$, $i_{s}$ = transistor
source current = drain current:

$$i_{in}=-[g_{m}(v_{g}-v_{s})-g_{mb}v_{s}
+(v_{d}-v_{s})/r_{o}]$$

With $v_{g}=\beta v_{out}$ this gives:

$$\frac1{R_{in}}=\frac{i_{in}}{v_{in}}
=A_{v}\left(\frac1{R_{D}}+\frac1{R_{12}}\right)$$

$$R_{in}= \frac{R_{D}\parallel R_{12}}{A_{v}}$$

Simplified $R_{12}\to\infty$, $r_{o}\to\infty$,
$g_{mb}=0$:

$$R_{in}= \frac{R_{D}}{A_{v}}
=\frac{1+g_{m}R_{D}\beta}{g_{m}}
=\frac1{g_{m}}+\beta R_{D}$$

Series mixing raises $R_{in}$ above $1/g_{m}$ of
the open CG stage. With large $T$,
$R_{in}\approx \beta(R_{D}\parallel R_{12})$.

### Output resistance

Set $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$ at output.
$v_{g}=\beta v_{x}$, $v_{s}=0$.

$$i_{x}=v_{x}/R_{D}+v_{x}/R_{12}
+g_{m}\beta v_{x}+v_{x}/r_{o}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac1{1/R_{D}+1/R_{12}+1/r_{o}+g_{m}\beta}$$

$$=R_{D}\parallel R_{12}\parallel r_{o}\parallel
\frac1{g_{m}\beta}$$

$$=\frac{R_{out,open}}{1+T}$$

Shunt sampling lowers $R_{out}$.
With large $T$, $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m}\beta$.

In sum: self-biased, always saturated,
non-inverting voltage-series amplifier whose
ideal closed-loop gain, input and output
impedances are controlled by $\beta=R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2})$
and desensitized by $1+T$.

answer.text:
This is a NMOS **common-drain, source follower**
with active load. The top device is the input device,
the bottom device is DC bias.

* $M_{1}$: gate $=V_{in}$, drain $=V_{DD}$ AC ground,
  source $=V_{out}$. NMOS follower.

* $M_{2}$: source $=GND$, drain $=V_{out}$, gate $=V_b$ DC.
  With $V_b$ DC it is a constant current source if
  kept in saturation.

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$ in DC steady state.

Implicitly both NMOS bodies are to the p-sub $=GND$.
$M_{2}$ has $V_{SB2}=0$. $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=V_{out}>0$
and therefore suffers body effect unless put in a
separate well with body tied to source.

### Large signal DC

$M_{2}$ in saturation:

$$ I_D = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_b-V_{TH2})^2(1+\lambda_n V_{out}) $$

$V_{GS2}=V_b$, $V_{DS2}=V_{out}$. To stay in saturation:

$$ V_{out} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov2} $$

$M_{1}$ in saturation:

$$ I_D = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{GS1}-V_{TH1})^2(1+\lambda_n(V_{DD}-V_{out})) $$

where

$$ V_{GS1} = V_{in}-V_{out} $$
$$ V_{DS1} = V_{DD}-V_{out} $$
$$ V_{TH1}=V_{TH0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_f+V_{out}}
-\sqrt{2\phi_f}\right) $$

due to $V_{SB1}=V_{out}$. To turn on:

$$ V_{in}-V_{out} \ge V_{TH1} $$

To stay in saturation:

$$ V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{ov1} $$
$$ V_{DD}-V_{out} \ge V_{ov1} $$

Hence, roughly,

$$ V_{ov2} \le V_{out} \le V_{DD}-V_{ov1} $$
$$ V_{out}+V_{GS1}=V_{in} $$

The circuit is a level-shifter follower:

$$ V_{out,DC}=V_{in,DC}-V_{GS1} $$

where $V_{GS1}=V_{TH1}(V_{out})+V_{ov1}$.

Intuitively: if $V_{in}$ goes up, $V_{GS1}$ goes up,
$M_{1}$ supplies more current than the $M_{2}$ sink
and charges up the output node until $V_{GS1}$ falls
back. If $V_{in}$ goes down, $M_{1}$ supplies less current,
the $M_{2}$ sink discharges the output until equilibrium.
Hence $V_{out}$ follows $V_{in}$. It can source large
transient current through $M_{1}$, but sinking is limited
to the DC bias $I_D$ of $M_{2}$.

### Small signal

Drain of $M_{1}$ is AC ground, gate of $M_{2}$ is AC ground.
Let $g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}$ be for $M_{1}$,
$g_{m2},r_{o2}$ for $M_{2}$. $V_{bs2}=0$, so $M_{2}$
has no body effect.

$$ V_{gs1}=V_{in}-V_{out} $$
$$ V_{bs1}=-V_{out} $$
$$ V_{ds1}=-V_{out} $$
$$ V_{gs2}=0 $$
$$ V_{ds2}=V_{out} $$

Drain currents, drain to source:

$$ I_{d1} = g_{m1}V_{gs1}+g_{mb1}V_{bs1}+g_{ds1}V_{ds1} $$
$$ I_{d2} = g_{ds2}V_{ds2} $$

KCL at output: current out of $M_{1}$ source into
node equals current into $M_{2}$ drain out of node:

$$ I_{d1} = I_{d2} $$

$$ g_{m1}(V_{in}-V_{out})-g_{mb1}V_{out}-g_{ds1}V_{out}
= g_{ds2}V_{out} $$

Voltage gain:

$$ A_v = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} =
\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

i.e.

$$ A_v = \frac{g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})}
{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})} <1 $$

Ideal with $r_o\to\infty$, no body: $A_v\to 1$.
With $r_o$ large but body:

$$ A_v \approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}
= \frac{1}{1+\eta} \approx 0.7-0.9 $$

Positive, non-inverting, slightly less than unity.
Body effect is the main gain loss. The varying
$V_{TH1}(V_{out})$ also makes the follower non-linear.

Output resistance: set $V_{in}=0$, drive $V_{out}$
with $V_x$, measure $I_x$.

$$ R_{out} = \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

$$ = \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}} $$

Low, $\sim 1/g_m$. That is the point of the circuit.

Input resistance at low frequency:

$$ R_{in} = \infty $$

into MOS gate.

In summary: ~unity voltage gain buffer, low output
impedance, high input impedance, level shift by $V_{GS1}$,
output swing limited by keeping both devices saturated,
gain reduced by body effect of the input device.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a NMOS common-drain stage with active load.

* $M_{1}$: driver. Drain is ac ground $V_{DD}$,
source is output. Gate is input.
$$V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\;, \; V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out}$$
* $M_{2}$: current source load. Source to ground,
drain to output, gate to DC bias $V_{b}$.
$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}\; , \; V_{GS2}=V_{b}$$

In DC, $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{bias}$, gate draws no current.
$M_{2}$ in saturation presents a DC current

$$I_{bias} \approx \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_b-V_{TH2})^2(1+\lambda_2 V_{out})$$

and small signal impedance $r_{o2}$ to ac ground.

$M_{1}$ must supply that current:

$$I_{bias} \approx \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{GS1}-V_{TH1})^2(1+\lambda_1 V_{DS1})$$

In large signal the output follows the input with a
level shift $V_{GS1}$:

$$V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}$$

This is a voltage follower / buffer.

Assuming both in saturation. In a normal p-sub
process the NMOS bulk is to GND. Then

* $M_{2}$: $V_{SB2}=0$, no body effect.
* $M_{1}$: $V_{SB1}=V_{out}>0$, body effect.

$$V_{TH1}=V_{TH0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_f+V_{SB1}}-
\sqrt{2\phi_f}\right)$$

Saturation requires:

$$V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{OV1}$$
$$V_{DS2} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{OV2}$$

i.e.

$$V_{out} \le V_{DD}-V_{OV1}$$
$$V_{out} \ge V_{OV2}$$

Available output swing for both saturated:

$$V_{OV2} \le V_{out} \le V_{DD}-V_{OV1}$$

Input must keep $M_{1}$ on:

$$V_{in} = V_{out}+V_{GS1} = V_{out}+V_{TH1}+V_{OV1}$$

so minimum input for $M_{2}$ saturated is

$$V_{in,min} \approx V_{OV2}+V_{TH1}+V_{OV1}$$

There is essentially no max, $V_{in}\le V_{DD}+V_{TH1}$.
In practice $V_{in,max}=V_{DD}$.

The advantage over a resistor source load is
a large AC load with a small DC drop $V_{OV2}$.

### Small signal

Small signal model: $V_{dd}=0$, $V_{b}=0$.
Let $g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$ for $M_{1}$,
$g_{m2},r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$ for $M_{2}$, $g_{mb2}=0$.

$M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=0$, $v_{bs2}=0$:

$$i_{d2}=g_{ds2}v_{ds2}=g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

i.e. impedance $r_{o2}$ from output to ground.

$M_{1}$: gate $v_{in}$, source $v_{out}$, drain $0$,
bulk $0$:

$$\begin{aligned}
v_{gs1} &= v_{in}-v_{out}\\
v_{bs1} &= -v_{out}\\
v_{ds1} &= -v_{out}\\
i_{d1} &= g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}
\end{aligned}$$

KCL at output, no external load: the AC source
current of $M_{1}$ equals the AC drain current of
$M_{2}$, $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$:

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{mb1}v_{out}-g_{ds1}v_{out}
= g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

Hence:

$$ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} =
\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

i.e, with $r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2}=1/(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})$,

$$A_v = \frac{g_{m1}(r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2})}
{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2})}=g_{m1}R_{out}$$

If $\lambda=0$, $r_o\to\infty$:

$$A_v \approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}=
\frac{1}{1+\eta}<1$$

$\eta=g_{mb1}/g_{m1}\sim 0.1-0.3$.
Typically 0.7-0.9.

Ignoring body effect as well, $g_{mb1}=0$:

$$A_v \approx \frac{g_{m1}(r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2})}
{1+g_{m1}(r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2})}\approx 1$$

Input impedance at low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

looking into MOS gate.

Output impedance: set $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_x$ at
output, measure $i_x$.

$$v_{gs1}=-v_x,\;v_{bs1}=-v_x,\;v_{ds1}=-v_x$$
$$i_{d1}=-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_x$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{ds2}v_x$$

$i_x$ entering the node leaves into $M_{1}$ source
and $M_{2}$ drain: $i_x = -i_{d1}+i_{d2}$

$$i_x = (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})v_x$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\Vert r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}$$

Neglecting body effect and CLM: $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m1}$.

In summary: near-unity positive gain, very high
$R_{in}$, relatively low $R_{out}$. It serves as
a level-shifting voltage buffer. The gain is degraded
from 1 by finite $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ loading and,
most importantly, by the back-gate $g_{mb1}$ of the
follower, since its source moves with respect to
substrate ground.

answer.text:
This is a NMOS common drain with NMOS
current source load. A voltage buffer.

* $M_{1}$ : driver. Drain to $V_{DD}$ ac ground,
gate the input, source the output.
* $M_{2}$ : load. Source to ground, drain to output,
gate to DC bias $V_{b}$.

Both are N-channel. For $M_{2}$ source is the body,
no back bias. For $M_{1}$ body is normally the
p-substrate = GND, source = $V_{out}$. Hence
back bias.

$$V_{SB1}=V_{out}, \quad V_{SB2}=0$$

In DC, gates draw no current, so

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{B}$$

$M_{2}$ sets the current:

$$I_{B} = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_b - V_{TH2})^2(1+\lambda_2 V_{out})$$

$$V_{GS2}=V_{b},\;V_{DS2}=V_{out}$$

To be saturated:

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov2} \tag{1}$$

$M_{1}$ carries the same current:

$$I_{B} = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{TH1})^2(1+\lambda_1(V_{DD}-V_{out}))$$

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out},\;V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

$$V_{TH1}=V_{TH0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{|2\Phi_F+V_{out}|}
-\sqrt{|2\Phi_F|}\right)$$

by body effect. In saturation:

$$V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}$$
$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{TH1}$$
$$V_{in}\le V_{DD}+V_{TH1} \tag{2}$$

almost always true. To be on:

$$V_{GS1}\ge V_{TH1}$$
$$V_{out}\le V_{in}-V_{TH1} \tag{3}$$

In other words the circuit is a level-shift down:

$$V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}(I_B)$$

$$V_{GS1}\approx V_{TH1}(V_{out})+V_{ov1}$$

$$V_{ov1}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_B}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1}}$$

$V_{GS1}$ is fairly constant, increased by body
effect and modulated slightly by $\lambda$ via
$V_{out}$.

Large signal limits:

Bottom is set by $M_{2}$ trioding. From (1):

$$V_{out,min}\approx V_{ov2}$$

Corresponding

$$V_{in,min}\approx V_{ov2}+V_{TH1}+V_{ov1}$$

The input cannot go near ground. Top is set by
following:

$$V_{out,max}\approx V_{in,max}-V_{TH1}-V_{ov1}$$

With $V_{in,max}\approx V_{DD}$, output can never
reach $V_{DD}$.

Also pull-up / pull-down are asymmetric.
$M_{1}$ can source large transient current to a
load capacitor, $M_{2}$ can sink only DC $I_{B}$.
For $C_L$, negative slew rate:

$$SR_{-}\approx I_B/C_L$$

when $M_{1}$ turns off.

### Small signal

At low frequency, $V_{DD}$, $V_b$ are ac ground.

$M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=0$, $v_{bs2}=0$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}$

$$i_{d2}=g_{ds2}v_{out}=v_{out}/r_{o2}$$

i.e. an impedance $r_{o2}$ to ground.

$M_{1}$: $v_{g1}=v_{in}$, $v_{s1}=v_{out}$,
$v_{d1}=0$, $v_{b1}=0$

$$\begin{aligned}
v_{gs1} &=v_{in}-v_{out}\\
v_{bs1} &=-v_{out}\\
v_{ds1} &=-v_{out}\\
i_{d1} &=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}\\
&=g_{m1}v_{in}-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

KCL at output, no external load: current out of
$M_{1}$ source = current into $M_{2}$ drain:

$$i_{d1}=i_{d2}$$

$$g_{m1}v_{in}-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}
= g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

Hence voltage gain:

$$ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
= \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

Let $R_p = r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}=1/(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})$ :

$$A_v = \frac{g_{m1}R_p}{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})R_p}$$

$g_{m1}=\sqrt{2\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1I_B}$,
$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_1 I_B$, $r_{o2}=1/\lambda_2 I_B$,
$g_{mb1}=\eta g_{m1}$, $\eta\approx 0.1-0.3$.

If $r_{o1},r_{o2}\gg 1/g_m$:

$$A_v\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}=\frac1{1+\eta}<1$$

typically 0.7-0.9. Body effect degrades gain
and makes it nonlinear, since $V_{TH1}$ moves
with $V_{out}$.

Without body effect, e.g. isolated well with body
to source:

$$A_v =\frac{g_{m1}R_p}{1+g_{m1}R_p}$$

and for $R_p\to\infty$, $A_v\to 1$.

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$, drive $v_x$ at
output, measure $i_x$.

$$i_x = (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})v_x$$

$$ R_{out}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2} $$

$$\approx 1/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})$$

Low, as for a follower, but not zero. 
No body: $\approx 1/g_{m1}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$.

Input resistance:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

at low frequency. At high frequency:

$C_{gd1}$ from input to ac ground, $C_{gs1}$
bootstrapped between input and output:

$$C_{in}\approx C_{gd1}+(1-A_v)C_{gs1}$$

small because $A_v\approx 1$. Dominant pole is
usually at the output:

$$\omega_p \approx 1/R_{out}C_L$$

Supply rejection is good: $v_{out}/v_{dd}\approx
R_{out}/r_{o1}\ll 1$.

In summary: near unity gain buffer, large $R_{in}$,
small $R_{out}\sim 1/g_m$, DC shift down by $V_{GS}$,
limited low input range and low output swing,
gain $<1$ due to body effect and finite $r_o$,
and limited sinking capability.

answer.text:
This is the static CMOS logic inverter.

$M_1$ is the NMOS pull-down, $M_2$ is the PMOS pull-up.
Assume bulk to source: $V_{SB1}=0$, $V_{SB2}=0$.

$$k_n=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1 \;\;,\;\; k_p=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2$$
$$V_{TN}>0 \;\;,\;\; V_{TP}=-|V_{TP}|<0$$

$$I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2(1+\lambda_nV_{DS})$$
in saturation, $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TN}$

$$I_{Dn} = k_n\left[(V_{GS}-V_{TN})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2\right]$$
in triode.

PMOS with $V_{SG}, V_{SD}, |V_{TP}|$ dual.

$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$.

Saturation conditions:

NMOS: $V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{TN}$ sat, else linear
PMOS: $V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{in}+V_{TP}$ sat, i.e.
$$V_{out} \le V_{in}-V_{TP}$$
else linear. Since $V_{TP}<0$, the window
$$V_{in}-V_{TN} \le V_{out} \le V_{in}-V_{TP}$$
is where both can saturate.

### 1. Logic operation

$V_{in}=0$ low:
$$V_{GS1}=0<V_{TN} : M_1\; OFF$$
$$V_{GS2}=-V_{DD}<V_{TP} : M_2\; ON$$
Output is pulled via $M_2$ to $V_{DD}$. $V_{SD2}\approx 0$,
$M_2$ deep triode.

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ high:
$$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN} : M_1\; ON$$
$$V_{SG2}=0<|V_{TP}| : M_2\; OFF$$
Output is pulled via $M_1$ to $0$. $M_1$ deep triode.

Hence
$$V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$$
with full rail:
$$V_{OL}\approx 0,\;V_{OH}\approx V_{DD}$$

In a stable state one device is OFF, so ideally
static $I_{DD}=0$. Static power is only leakage.

For $V_{in}$ swept $0\to V_{DD}$:

1. Region 1: $0\le V_{in}<V_{TN}$ : $M_1$ off, $M_2$ linear. $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. Region 2: $M_1$ sat, $M_2$ linear. $V_{out}$ falls from $V_{DD}$.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 = k_p\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\right]$$

3. Region 3: $M_1$ sat, $M_2$ sat. Narrow high gain region.
$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2(1+\lambda_nV_{out})=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2(1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{out}))$$

4. Region 4: $M_1$ linear, $M_2$ sat.
$$k_n\left[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right]=\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2$$

5. Region 5: $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ : $M_1$ linear, $M_2$ off. $V_{out}=0$.

This gives the classic sharp voltage transfer characteristic, VTC.

### 2. Switching threshold

$V_M$ defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$. At that point
both are almost certainly in saturation. Neglecting $\lambda$:

$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{TN})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

$$\sqrt{\frac{k_n}{k_p}}(V_M-V_{TN}) = V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|$$

Let $r=\sqrt{k_n/k_p}$. Then

$$V_M = \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|+r\,V_{TN}}{r+1}$$

In particular if $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|=V_T$ and $k_n=k_p$,
$$V_M=V_{DD}/2$$
Stronger NMOS, larger $k_n$, moves $V_M$ down toward $V_{TN}$.
Stronger PMOS moves $V_M$ up toward $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$.
Since $\mu_n\approx 2$-$3\,\mu_p$, symmetric threshold
requires $(W/L)_p\approx 2$-$3\,(W/L)_n$.

### 3. Small signal in transition

In region 3 both act as common-source, one as load of
the other. Gates common to $v_{in}$, drains common to $v_{out}$,
sources ac ground.

KCL at output gives:

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out}+g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}=0$$

$$A_v =\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$
$$= -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}||r_{o2})$$

with at bias $I_D$:

$$g_m = \sqrt{2kI_D}= \frac{2I_D}{V_{GS}-V_T}$$
$$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_n I_D,\; r_{o2}=1/\lambda_p I_D$$

$|A_v|$ is large, typically 20-50. Hence the VTC is almost
vertical in region 3.

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}||r_{o2},\;\; R_{in}=\infty$$

Biased at $V_M$, e.g. with resistive feedback, it is a
high gain analog inverting amplifier.

$V_{IL}, V_{IH}$ are defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$
in regions 2 and 4. Noise margins:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL},\; NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}$$

approx $V_{DD}/2$ for symmetric high-gain design.

### 4. Power and speed

No static current except during transition where both
conduct briefly: short-circuit current.

Dynamic power to charge load $C_L$ at frequency $f$:

$$P_{dyn}= \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

Propagation delay set by current drive in saturation/triode
charging $C_L$:

$t_{pHL}$: $M_1$ discharging, $t_{pLH}$: $M_2$ charging.
Approximately $0.69 R_{eq}C_L$.

In sum: rail-to-rail inverting gate, zero nominal static power,
high noise margin, high gain in threshold region, the
fundamental CMOS gate.

answer.text:
This is a static CMOS inverter. The fundamental
CMOS gate.

* $M_{1}$ : NMOS pull down. source to $GND$.
$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$
* $M_{2}$ : PMOS pull up. source to $V_{DD}$.
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$
with $V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{DD}$

Bulk is tied to source: $M_{1}$ body to $GND$,
$M_{2}$ n-well to $V_{DD}$. No body effect.

Let

$$ k_{n} = \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}, \quad k_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2} $$
$$ I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS1}-V_{THN})^{2}(1+\lambda_n V_{DS1}) $$
in saturation, $V_{DS} \ge V_{GS}-V_{THN}$,
$$ I_{Dp} = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_p V_{SD2}) $$
in saturation, $V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$.

In steady state $I_{Dn}=I_{Dp}$ because gates draw no DC
current. That defines $V_{out}$ vs $V_{in}$.

### 1. Logic operation

$M_{1}$ is OFF for $V_{GS1}<V_{THN}$, i.e.

$$ V_{in} < V_{THN} $$

$M_{2}$ is OFF for $V_{SG2}<|V_{THP}|$, i.e.

$$ V_{DD}-V_{in}<|V_{THP}| $$
$$ V_{in} > V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| $$

Hence:

* $V_{in}=0$ = Low: $M_1$ OFF, $M_2$ ON. No DC path
to $GND$. Output is pulled to $V_{DD}$ through $M_2$.
$$ V_{OH} \approx V_{DD} $$

* $V_{in}=V_{DD}$ = High: $M_2$ OFF, $M_1$ ON. No DC path
to $V_{DD}$. Output is pulled to $GND$ through $M_1$.
$$ V_{OL} \approx 0 $$

This is a NOT gate with rail-to-rail swing and,
ideally, zero static current in the two logic states.
One transistor is always OFF.

There is push-pull drive in both directions, so
low static output impedance.

### 2. Voltage transfer characteristic

Ignoring $\lambda$ for the shape, we have 5 regions.

I. $0 \le V_{in} < V_{THN}$:
$M_1$ OFF, $M_2$ in linear. $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

II. $V_{THN} \le V_{in} < V_M$:
$M_1$ saturation, $M_2$ triode.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{THN})^2 = 
\frac{k_p}{2}\left[2(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{THP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})-(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2\right] $$
$V_{out}$ falls fast from $V_{DD}$.

$V_M$ is the switching threshold where $V_{in}=V_{out}$.

III. $V_{in}\approx V_M$:
Both saturation.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{THN})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

IV. $V_M < V_{in} \le V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$:
$M_1$ triode, $M_2$ saturation.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}\left[2(V_{in}-V_{THN})V_{out}-V_{out}^2\right]=\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

V. $V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| < V_{in} \le V_{DD}$:
$M_2$ OFF, $M_1$ linear. $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

Boundary II-III: $M_2$ enters saturation:
$V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|$, i.e. $V_{out}=V_{in}+|V_{THP}|$.
Boundary III-IV: $M_1$ enters saturation:
$V_{DS1}=V_{GS1}-V_{THN}$, i.e. $V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{THN}$.

With $\lambda=0$, region III is a vertical line with
infinite gain. With $\lambda_n,\lambda_p>0$ it has a
finite steep slope.

### 3. Switching threshold $V_M$

Put $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$ and $I_{Dn}=I_{Dp}$:

$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{THN})^2(1+\lambda_n V_M)=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|)^2(1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_M)) $$

For $\lambda\approx 0$:

$$ \sqrt{k_n}\,(V_M-V_{THN}) = \sqrt{k_p}\,(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|) $$

$$ V_M = \frac{V_{THN}+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|)}{1+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}} $$

$V_M$ is set by ratio $k_p/k_n$, i.e. by sizing.

For symmetric $V_{THN}=|V_{THP}|=V_T$ and $V_M=V_{DD}/2$:

$$ \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}} = \frac{V_{DD}/2-V_{THN}}{V_{DD}/2-|V_{THP}|} $$

Ideally $k_n\approx k_p$. Since $\mu_n \approx 2\text{-}3\,\mu_p$,
this requires

$$ (W/L)_p \approx 2\text{-}3\,(W/L)_n .$$

Then PMOS is wider to compensate for lower hole mobility,
giving symmetric rise/fall.

### 4. Small-signal gain at $V_M$

At $V_M$ both devices are in saturation, common source,
gates common, drains common.

$$ g_{m1}=k_n(V_M-V_{THN}), \quad g_{m2}=k_p(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|) $$
$$ r_{o1}=1/(\lambda_n I_D), \quad r_{o2}=1/(\lambda_p I_D) $$

Small signal:

$$ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} = -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

Typically $-20$ to $-100$. This is why a CMOS inverter
biased at $V_M$, e.g. with resistive feedback from output
to input, is a high gain inverting amplifier.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$ are defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$,
at the edges of the steep transition, in regions II and IV.
Noise margins:

$$ NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL} $$
$$ NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH} $$

For a symmetric inverter they are close to $V_{DD}/2$,
very large. E.g. with matched $k_n=k_p$, $V_{THN}=|V_{THP}|=V_T$:

$$ V_{IL}=\frac{3V_{DD}+2V_T}{8},\quad V_{IH}=\frac{5V_{DD}-2V_T}{8} $$

### 5. Dynamic and power

In static states $I_{DD}\approx 0$ except leakage.
Current flows only during transition, when both
transistors are momentarily ON - the crowbar / short-circuit
current, maximum near $V_M$.

With a load capacitance $C_L$, the delay is set by
charging/discharging $C_L$ through the saturation current
of $M_2$/$M_1$.

Roughly $t_{p} \propto C_L V_{DD}/I_{D,sat}$.
Symmetric $t_{pLH}\approx t_{pHL}$ if $k_n\approx k_p$.

Dynamic power for activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$:

$$ P_{dyn} = \alpha C_L V_{DD}^{2} f $$

plus short-circuit power during finite input rise/fall.

In summary: rail-to-rail inverting logic, high noise immunity,
essentially zero static power, active pull-up and pull-down,
and very high small-signal gain in the transition region.
That is why it is the core CMOS building block.

answer.text:
This is the static CMOS inverter. The logic NOT gate.

* $M_1$ bottom: NMOS, source to GND, drain to $V_{out}$
* $M_2$ top: PMOS, source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$

Both gates to $V_{in}$. Bodies to their sources,
NMOS body = p-sub = GND, PMOS body = n-well = $V_{DD}$,
so $V_{SB}=0$, no body effect.

Let for long channel square law

NMOS: $V_{TN}>0$, $k_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1$
PMOS: $V_{TP}<0$, $|V_{TP}|=-V_{TP}$,
$k_p = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_2$,
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$,
$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$.

Assume $V_{DD} > V_{TN}+|V_{TP}|$.

### 1. Ideal digital operation

MOS is a switch: NMOS on for gate high, PMOS on
for gate low.

$V_{in}=0$ low:
$V_{GS1}=0 < V_{TN}$: $M_1$ OFF
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{TP}|$: $M_2$ ON
Output pulled to $V_{DD}$ through $M_2$. No DC path
to GND because $M_1$ is off.

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ high:
$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN}$: $M_1$ ON
$V_{SG2}=0 < |V_{TP}|$: $M_2$ OFF
Output pulled to 0 through $M_1$. No DC path
to $V_{DD}$ because $M_2$ is off.

Hence:

```
Vin = 0   -> Vout = VDD
Vin = VDD -> Vout = 0
```

Inverter with rail-to-rail swing, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$,
$V_{OL}=0$, infinite DC input impedance, zero
static supply current except leakage.

During transition both devices are momentarily on,
giving a crowbar current from $V_{DD}$ to GND.

### 2. Voltage transfer characteristic

Equate $I_{DN}=|I_{DP}|$. Neglect $\lambda$ for DC levels.

I. $V_{in}<V_{TN}$:
$M_1$ cut-off, $M_2$ linear with $V_{SD}\approx 0$.
$V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $I_D=0$.

II. $V_{TN}<V_{in}<V_M$:
$M_1$ saturated, $M_2$ linear.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 =
k_p\Big[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\Big] $$
$V_{out}$ falls from $V_{DD}$.

III. $V_{in}\approx V_M$:
Both saturated. High gain.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 =
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

IV. $V_M<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$:
$M_1$ linear, $M_2$ saturated.
$$ k_n\Big[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\Big]=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

V. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$:
$M_2$ cut-off, $M_1$ linear with $V_{DS}\approx 0$.
$V_{out}=0$, $I_D=0$.

That gives the familiar sharp VTC with flat top
and bottom and steep transition. With $\lambda>0$
region III has finite negative slope, regions I,V
are still flat because current is zero.

### 3. Switching threshold $V_M$

Defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$, both in
saturation. Ignoring $\lambda$:

$$\sqrt{k_n}(V_M-V_{TN})=\sqrt{k_p}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)$$

$$V_M = \frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)}
{1+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}} $$

This is set by threshold and $\beta$-ratio.
If $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|=V_T$ and $k_n=k_p$:

$$V_M = V_{DD}/2$$

For equal strength $k_n=k_p$ we need:

$$\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}=\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}\approx 2-3$$

because PMOS mobility is lower.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$, the points where
$dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$, lie in regions II and IV.
Solving the current equation together with slope $=-1$
gives $V_{IL}<V_M<V_{IH}$ symmetrically around $V_M$
in the matched case. Noise margins are:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL}$$
$$NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH}$$

Close to $V_{DD}/2$ for a well sized inverter.

### 4. Small signal as amplifier

Biased at $V_M$, both devices are on in saturation,
forming a push-pull common-source amplifier.

$$A_v = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
= -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

with

$$g_{m1}=k_n(V_M-V_{TN}),\quad
g_{m2}=k_p(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)$$
$$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_n I_D,\quad r_{o2}=1/\lambda_p I_D$$

Typically $|A_v|\sim 20-50$. Output resistance
in transition is $r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, large.
In logic 0 or 1 state, output resistance is the
linear-region $1/[k(V_{GS}-V_T)]$ of the ON device,
low.

Input capacitance is essentially the two gate
capacitances with Miller multiplication in the
transition region.

### 5. Dynamics and power

With load $C_L$, switching charges/discharges $C_L$
through $M_2$, $M_1$.

No static power: $P_{static}\approx 0$.

Dynamic power for activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$:

$$P_{dyn} = \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

plus short-circuit power during the time both
transistors conduct.

Propagation delay $\approx R_{eq}C_L$. Rise time
set by PMOS strength, fall time by NMOS strength.
Equal $t_{pLH}\approx t_{pHL}$ requires
$k_n\approx k_p$, i.e. wider PMOS.

In short: rail-to-rail inverter, zero static
current, large noise margin, high gain in transition,
load-dependent speed and $CV_{DD}^2$ dynamic power.

answer.text:
This is the static CMOS inverter. The NOT gate.

* $M_{2}$, down, is NMOS. Source to GND,
drain to $V_{out}$. Bulk p-sub to GND.
* $M_{1}$, up, is PMOS. Source to $V_{DD}$,
drain to $V_{out}$. Bulk n-well to $V_{DD}$.

Gates common to $V_{in}$, drains common to $V_{out}$.
$V_{SB1}=0$, $V_{SB2}=0$, no back bias in normal
operation.

Let

$$k_n =\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2 ,\quad k_p =\mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_1$$
$$V_{tn}>0,\quad V_{tp}<0,\quad |V_{tp}|=-V_{tp}$$

Square law, for simplicity $\lambda=0$, $\gamma=0$:

$$I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS2}-V_{tn})^2\;(sat)$$
$$|I_{Dp}| = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{SG1}-|V_{tp}|)^2\;(sat)$$

in triode:

$$I_{Dn}=k_n\left[(V_{GS2}-V_{tn})V_{DS2}-V_{DS2}^2/2\right]$$
$$|I_{Dp}|=k_p\left[(V_{SG1}-|V_{tp}|)V_{SD1}-V_{SD1}^2/2\right]$$

KCL at output, no load: $I_{Dn}=|I_{Dp}|$.

$$V_{GS2}=V_{in},\; V_{DS2}=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{in},\; V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

### Large signal logic operation

$V_{in}=0$ :

$V_{GS2}=0<V_{tn}$ : M2 OFF.
$V_{SG1}=V_{DD}>|V_{tp}|$ : M1 ON.
No DC path to ground, $I_D=0$, so $V_{SD1}=0$.
$$V_{out}=V_{DD}$$

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ :

$V_{SG1}=0<|V_{tp}|$ : M1 OFF.
$V_{GS2}=V_{DD}>V_{tn}$ : M2 ON.
No DC path to $V_{DD}$, $I_D=0$, so $V_{DS2}=0$.
$$V_{out}=0$$

So logically:

0 -> 1, 1 -> 0.

This is ratioless, rail-to-rail logic with in steady
state one device always OFF. Hence ideally zero
static power, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$.

For $V_{tn}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$ both are ON
and must satisfy $I_{Dn}=|I_{Dp}|$. This gives
the voltage transfer characteristic $V_{out}(V_{in})$.

M2 saturates when $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{tn}$.
M1 saturates when $V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$.

i.e.

1. Region 1: $V_{in}<V_{tn}$
   M2 off, M1 linear, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. Region 2: $V_{in}$ just $>V_{tn}$, $V_{out}$ high.
   M2 sat, M1 linear:

$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{tn})^2 =
k_p\big[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\big]$$

Steep falling $V_{out}$.

3. Region 3: around the middle, both sat:
$$V_{in}-V_{tn}\le V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$$

$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{tn})^2=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)^2$$

This is independent of $V_{out}$ for $\lambda=0$.
It defines only one $V_{in}$, the switching
threshold $V_M$ where $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$:

$$\sqrt{k_n}(V_M-V_{tn})=\sqrt{k_p}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{tp}|)$$

$$V_M=\frac{V_{tn}+r\,(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)}{1+r}$$

$$r=\sqrt{k_p/k_n}$$

VTC is vertical here for $\lambda=0$. With
$\lambda>0$ it has finite large negative slope.

4. Region 4: M2 linear, M1 sat, symmetric of 2.

$$k_n\big[(V_{in}-V_{tn})V_{out}-V_{out}^2/2\big]=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)^2$$

5. Region 5: $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$
   M1 off, M2 linear, $V_{out}=0$.

This is the classic high-gain inverter VTC.

For the symmetric case $V_{tn}=|V_{tp}|=V_t$,
$k_n=k_p$:

$$V_M = V_{DD}/2$$

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$, the unity-gain points
$dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$, are in regions 2 and 4.
E.g. for symmetric, $V_t\ll V_{DD}$:

$$V_{IL}\approx \frac{3V_{DD}}{8},\quad
V_{IH}\approx \frac{5V_{DD}}{8}$$

Noise margins:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL}$$
$$NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH}$$

$\approx 0.375\,V_{DD}$, approaching ideal $V_{DD}/2$.
Very robust logic.

### Small signal at $V_M$

Bias at $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$ both are in
saturation. It is a push-pull common-source
amplifier.

$$g_{m1}=k_p(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{tp}|)$$
$$g_{m2}=k_n(V_M-V_{tn})$$
$$g_{ds1}=\lambda_p I_D,\; g_{ds2}=\lambda_n I_D$$

Input sees gates: $R_{in}=\infty$.
Output sees both $r_o$ in parallel:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
=\frac{1}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

Voltage gain:

$$A_v = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

Typically -20 to -100. Ideally $-\infty$ if
$\lambda=0$.

That is why biased with resistive feedback from
output to input to force $V_{in}\approx V_M$,
the inverter becomes a high-gain analog
inverting amplifier.

### Dynamic and power

Load with $C_L$. Rise is charging $C_L$ through
M1, fall is discharging through M2. With
matched $k_n\approx k_p$, rise/fall symmetric.

Approximate propagation delays:

$$t_{pHL}\approx \frac{C_L V_{DD}}{2 I_{Dn,av}},
\quad t_{pLH}\approx \frac{C_L V_{DD}}{2 |I_{Dp,av}|}$$

Static $I_{DD}=0$ except leakage.
During switching both conduct briefly: short-circuit
current spike. Dominant power is dynamic:

$$P_{dyn}= \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

for activity factor $\alpha$.

In short: push-pull, full-swing, zero static current
inverter with threshold set by device ratio, large
noise margin, large transition gain, and $C_LV_{DD}^2$
dynamic energy per transition. The basis of all
CMOS logic.

answer.text:
This is the static CMOS logic gate - the CMOS inverter.

```
           VDD
            |
       S    |
     M1 PMOS pull-up
       D    |
Vin --G     +-- Vout
     G      |
     M2 NMOS pull-down
       S    |
            |
           GND
```

* $M_1$ : PMOS, source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$,
  bulk to $V_{DD}$
* $M_2$ : NMOS, source to GND, drain to $V_{out}$,
  bulk to GND
* Gates common: $V_{GS2}=V_{in}$, $V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$
* Drains common: $V_{DS2}=V_{out}$, $V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$

There is no body effect because source = bulk for both
devices. The junctions stay reverse biased.

It is push-pull common-source. One transistor is always
off in steady state, so ideally zero static current.

### 1. Logic operation

Let $V_{TN}>0$ be NMOS threshold, $V_{TP}<0$ PMOS threshold,
$|V_{TP}|=-V_{TP}$.

NMOS ON if $V_{GS}>V_{TN}$ : $V_{in}>V_{TN}$
PMOS ON if $V_{SG}>|V_{TP}|$ : $V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$

$V_{in}=0$, logic 0:

$$V_{GS2}=0 < V_{TN} \to M_2 OFF$$
$$V_{SG1}=V_{DD} > |V_{TP}| \to M_1 ON$$

$M_2$ is open, $M_1$ connects $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$.
$V_{SD1}\approx 0$, $M_1$ in linear triode. 
$$V_{out}=V_{DD}\;\; \text{logic 1}$$

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$, logic 1:

$$V_{GS2}=V_{DD} > V_{TN} \to M_2 ON$$
$$V_{SG1}=0 < |V_{TP}| \to M_1 OFF$$

$M_1$ is open, $M_2$ connects $V_{out}$ to GND.
$V_{DS2}\approx 0$, $M_2$ in linear.
$$V_{out}=0\;\; \text{logic 0}$$

Hence:

Vin | M1 | M2 | Vout
0 | ON | OFF | VDD
VDD | OFF | ON | 0

NOT gate with full rail swing.

### 2. Voltage transfer characteristic

For $V_{TN} < V_{in} < V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ both devices are ON.
Drain currents must be equal: $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D$.

Neglect channel-length modulation for DC:

$I_{Dn} = k_n[(V_{GS}-V_{TN})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2]$ linear
$I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2$ saturation

$k_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2$, $k_p = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_1$.

5 regions as $V_{in}$ sweeps 0 to $V_{DD}$:

1. $V_{in}<V_{TN}$: $M_2$ off, $M_1$ linear, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $I_D=0$
2. $V_{TN}<V_{in}<V_M$: $M_2$ saturated, $M_1$ linear. $V_{out}$ falling.
3. $V_{in}\approx V_M$: both saturated. Very high gain.
4. $V_M<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$: $M_2$ linear, $M_1$ saturated.
5. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$: $M_1$ off, $M_2$ linear, $V_{out}=0$, $I_D=0$

$V_M$ is the switching threshold where $V_{in}=V_{out}$,
both in saturation:

$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{TN})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)^2$$

$$\displaystyle V_M = \frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)}{1+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}} $$

For matched drive $k_n=k_p$ and $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|=V_T$:

$$V_M \approx V_{DD}/2$$

This is the point of maximum crowbar current.

The gain in transition is that of two common-source
devices in parallel:

$$A_v = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

typically -20 to -50. This steep transition gives large
noise margins. $V_{IL}$, $V_{IH}$ are defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL}$$
$$NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH}$$

$V_{OL}=0$, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$.

### 3. Current and power

Static: in state 0 or 1, one transistor is OFF, so:

$$I_{DD,static}\approx 0 \text{ leakage only}$$
$$P_{static}\approx 0$$

This is the great advantage of CMOS.

Dynamic: during switching the load capacitance $C_L$
is charged through $M_1$ and discharged through $M_2$.

Energy per 0->1 transition from $V_{DD}$: $C_L V_{DD}^2$,
half stored, half dissipated in $M_1$. 1->0: stored energy
dissipated in $M_2$.

$$P_{dyn}= \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

plus short-circuit crowbar current during the time both
are ON in regions 2-4:

$$P_{sc}= I_{peak}t_{sc}V_{DD}f$$

Propagation delay is set by charging $C_L$:

$t_{pHL}$ : $M_2$ discharging, $t_{pLH}$ : $M_1$ charging,
$\approx 0.69 R_{eq}C_L$ in first order.

Symmetrical rise/fall requires $k_p\approx k_n$, i.e.
$(W/L)_p \approx (\mu_n/\mu_p)(W/L)_n \approx 2\text{-}3\,(W/L)_n$.

### 4. As amplifier

If biased at $V_M$, both ON in saturation, it is a
high-gain CMOS push-pull amplifier with self load
$r_{o1}||r_{o2}$. Not normally used that way because
$V_M$ is supply and process sensitive.

In short: complementary pull-up / pull-down gives
rail-to-rail inversion with essentially zero static power,
high input impedance, low output impedance in ON state,
and power dissipation only during switching.

answer.text:
This is not a CMOS inverter. From the direction
of the body arrows both devices are $n$-channel.

* $M_{2}$ : drain to $V_{out}$, source to GND, gate to $V_{in}$,
  body to GND. Common source driver.
* $M_{1}$ : drain to $V_{DD}$, source to $V_{out}$, gate to $V_{in}$,
  body to source. Common drain pull up.

Put for simplicity, $\lambda =0$,

$$k_{1}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1},\;\;k_{2}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$$

$$V_{GS2}=V_{in},\;\;V_{DS2}=V_{out}$$
$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out},\;\;V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

No body effect on $M_{2}$. No body effect on $M_{1}$
if it is isolated with body tied to source. In a
p-sub $M_{1}$ would have body to GND and suffer body
effect, which only makes things worse.

DC KCL at the output, no load:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$$

### 1. $V_{in}<V_{Tn}$

$$V_{GS2}<V_{Tn}\;\Rightarrow\; M_{2}\;{\rm off}$$

$M_{1}$ on requires

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out}>V_{Tn}$$

i.e. $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{Tn}<0$, impossible.
So $M_{1}$ is also off.

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=0$$

The output is floating, high impedance. It retains
previous charge on a load capacitance. There is no
active pull-up.

In particular there is no $V_{OH}$. To have $M_{2}$ off
you need $V_{in}<V_{Tn}$. To have $M_{1}$ on to pull
high you need $V_{in}>V_{out}+V_{Tn}$. The two cannot
be satisfied simultaneously for $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$.
The circuit can never pull to $V_{DD}$. The maximum
source-follower voltage is $V_{in}-V_{Tn}$.

### 2. $V_{in}>V_{Tn}$

Both devices can be on. $V_{out}$ settles where the
source-follower current of $M_{1}$ equals the
pull-down current of $M_{2}$.

$M_{1}$ : $V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$,
$V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}=V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{Tn}$.

Saturation condition:

$$V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}\iff V_{DD}\ge V_{in}-V_{Tn}$$

always true for $0\le V_{in}\le V_{DD}$. So if $M_{1}$
is on it is saturated:

$$I_{D1}=\frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{Tn})^{2}$$

$M_{2}$ : $V_{DS2}=V_{out}$,
$V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}=V_{in}-V_{Tn}$.

Assume both saturated:

$$ \frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{Tn})^{2}
   =\frac{k_{2}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{Tn})^{2} $$

This requires $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{Tn}$, i.e. $M_{2}$
triode. Contradiction. In fact $M_{2}$ is always
triode when on.

Hence for $V_{in}>V_{Tn}$:

* $M_{1}$ saturation
* $M_{2}$ triode

$$ \frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{Tn})^{2}
   =k_{2}\left[(V_{in}-V_{Tn})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^{2}}{2}\right] \tag{1}$$

This defines the transfer characteristic. $V_{out}$
is low. E.g. for $V_{in}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}$ from

$$\frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{OL}-V_{Tn})^{2}
   =k_{2}\left[(V_{DD}-V_{Tn})V_{OL}-\frac{V_{OL}^{2}}{2}\right]$$

For $V_{OL}$ small,

$$V_{OL}\approx \frac{k_{1}}{k_{2}}\frac{V_{DD}-V_{Tn}}{2}$$

To get $V_{OL}\approx 0$ you need $k_{2}\gg k_{1}$,
a strong ratioed pull-down, as in NMOS-only logic.

Static current when on:

$$I_{DD}=\frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{Tn})^{2}
      \approx \frac{k_{1}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{Tn})^{2}$$

large, ratioed power.

In summary VTC is:

* $0<V_{in}<V_{Tn}$ : $I=0$, $V_{out}$ = hi-Z, undefined.
* $V_{in}>V_{Tn}$ : $V_{out}\approx$ low, $\sim V_{OL}>0$,
  determined by (1). Monotonically stays low.

No high output, no noise margin, no regenerative
switching threshold.

Small signal about an on-point, $v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{out}$,
$v_{ds1}=-v_{out}$, $v_{gs2}=v_{in}$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}$,
$i_{d1}=i_{d2}$:

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{ds1}v_{out}
   =g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}-g_{m2}}
            {g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$M_{2}$ is in deep triode, $g_{ds2}$ is large,
$\approx k_{2}(V_{in}-V_{Tn})$. Gain is small, $<1$
in magnitude. It is a common-source device loaded by
the low $\approx 1/g_{m1}$ impedance of a source follower,
not a useful amplifier.

This is a push-pull of common-drain + common-source
NMOS. It cannot function as a logic inverter because
the pull-up is an NMOS source-follower whose gate
is driven by the same input. When the input is low it
is off, when the input is high it fights the pull-down.

A proper CMOS inverter needs $M_{1}$ to be PMOS with
source/body to $V_{DD}$.

answer.text:
This is a common source stage with a diode
connected load. It is the CMOS version of the
classical saturated-load inverter.

```
M1 : driver, common-source, VGS1 = Vin, VDS1 = Vout
M2 : load, VSG2 = VSD2 = VDD-Vout
```

Body of NMOS to GND, body of PMOS to $V_{DD}$,
so normally no back-gate effect.
$V_{DD}$ is ac ground.

M2 with gate tied to drain is always in saturation
when on, because for PMOS

$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|$$

is satisfied with $V_{SD}=V_{SG}$.

It presents a small signal impedance of $\approx 1/g_m$.

### 1. Large signal

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. In square law, neglecting $\lambda$:

M1 on saturation:
$$I_{D1}=\frac12 k_n'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1(V_{in}-V_{Tn})^2$$
$$V_{in}>V_{Tn},\; V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{Tn}$$

M2 on saturation:
$$I_{D2}=\frac12 k_p'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$$
$$V_{DD}-V_{out}>|V_{Tp}|$$

where $k_n'=\mu_nC_{ox},\;k_p'=\mu_pC_{ox}$.

Hence in saturation-saturation:

$$\frac12 k_n'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1(V_{in}-V_{Tn})^2
 =\frac12 k_p'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$$

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|-k\,(V_{in}-V_{Tn})$$

with

$$k=\sqrt{\frac{k_n'(W/L)_1}{k_p'(W/L)_2}}$$

This is inverter-like with slope $-k$.

Regions of the VTC:

* I. $V_{in}<V_{Tn}$: M1 off. $I_D=0$. Ideally
any $V_{out}>V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$ gives zero current.
In practice leakage pulls $V_{out}\to V_{DD}$.

* II. Normal: M1 sat, M2 sat. Above equation.
Valid until M1 enters triode, $V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{Tn}$, i.e.

$$V_{in,max}=V_{Tn}+\frac{V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|}{k+1}$$

Input range for high gain is very narrow.

* III. $V_{in}>V_{in,max}$: M1 triode, M2 sat.

$$k_n'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1\left[(V_{in}-V_{Tn})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right]
 =\frac12 k_p'\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$$

$V_{out}$ falls slowly to a $V_{OL}>0$:

for small $V_{out}$,
$$V_{OL}\approx\frac{\frac12 k_p'(W/L)_2(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)^2}
{k_n'(W/L)_1(V_{DD}-V_{Tn})}$$

Useful output high with both on:

$$V_{OH,max}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$$

There is a threshold drop at the top. This is the
saturated-load loss. The circuit is ratioed.

### 2. Small signal

Bias at a Q-point in region II with bias current $I_D$.

M1: $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{ds1}=v_{out}$
$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out}$$

M2: source ac ground, gate=drain=$v_{out}$
$$v_{sg2}=-v_{out},\;v_{sd2}=-v_{out}$$
$$i_{sd2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{out}$$

KCL at output: current down into M1 = current down from M2:
$i_{d1}=i_{sd2}$ :

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out}=-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{out}$$

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{m2}}$$

If body effect on M2 cannot be neglected, $g_{m2}\to g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

Since typically $g_m\gg g_{ds}$:

$$A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}$$

For long channel:

$$g_m=\sqrt{2k'(W/L)I_D}$$

$$|A_v|\approx\sqrt{\frac{k_n'(W/L)_1}{k_p'(W/L)_2}}=k$$

i.e. the large signal slope. To get gain, make driver
strong, load weak. Typically only a few.

This is M1 transconductance driving the impedance
presented by the diode:

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}}$$

Proof: zero $v_{in}$, apply $v_x$ at output. Current drawn:
$i_x=(g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_x$.

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

at low frequency, gate of M1.

In words: gain = $-g_{m1}R_{out}$.

### 3. Frequency, etc.

Dominant pole at output:

$$\omega_p\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{L,tot}}$$

$R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2}$ is relatively small, so
bandwidth is larger than a current-source loaded CS,
at expense of gain.

$C_{L,tot}=C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{gs2}+C_{gb1,2}+C_{gd1}(Miller)+C_L$.
Note $C_{gd2}$ is shorted by gate-drain connection.

Input capacitance has Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$:
$C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+ (1+|A_v|)C_{gd1}$.

### Summary

* Inverting amplifier, self-biased load.
* Load $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, gain $\approx -g_{m1}/g_{m2}$.
* Low gain, low output resistance.
* Limited swing: cannot pull higher than $V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$ while maintaining gain.
* Static current $I_D$ whenever on: ratioed power.
* Q-point set by $V_{in,DC}$, very sensitive to $V_T$, $k'$, $W/L$.

Used where a small on-chip resistor is needed, as level
shifter, in differential loads, old saturated-load logic.
Replaced by current-source load for high gain op-amps.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a common-source stage with an active,
diode-connected load.

* $M_1$ : NMOS driver. Source to GND, drain to $V_{out}$,
gate to $V_{in}$.
* $M_2$ : PMOS load. Source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$,
gate tied to drain.

$M_2$ is always diode-connected. Neglect body effect,
body of $M_1$ to GND = source of $M_1$, body of $M_2$
to $V_{DD}$ = source of $M_2$. No $V_{SB}$.

It is like a CMOS inverter except the PMOS gate
is not driven by $V_{in}$ but shorted to output.
It draws static current.

### 1. Large signal DC

Let for $M_1$ NMOS:

$$ I_{D1} = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{GS1}-V_{THN})^2 (1+\lambda_n V_{DS1}) $$

in saturation, and for $M_2$ PMOS:

$$ I_{D2} = \frac12 \mu_p C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|)^2 (1+\lambda_p V_{SD2}) $$

in saturation.

Here:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1} &= V_{in} \\
V_{DS1} &= V_{out} \\
V_{SG2} &= V_{DD}-V_{out} \\
V_{SD2} &= V_{DD}-V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

$M_2$: $V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}$, so

$$V_{SD2} \ge V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|$$

is always true. $M_2$ is in saturation if it is on,
i.e. if:

$$V_{SG2} > |V_{THP}| \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; V_{out} < V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$$

$M_1$ is in saturation if:

$$V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN} \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{THN}$$

Neglect $\lambda$ for DC transfer. $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$:

$$\frac12 \beta_1 (V_{in}-V_{THN})^2 =
\frac12 \beta_2 (V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|)^2$$

where $\beta_1 = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1$,
$\beta_2 = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_2$.

Hence, when both saturated and on:

$$ V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}| = \sqrt{\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}}\,
(V_{in}-V_{THN}) $$

$$V_{out}= V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|-\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n(W/L)_1}{\mu_p(W/L)_2}}\,
(V_{in}-V_{THN})$$

This is a linear decreasing transfer with large-signal
slope $-\sqrt{\beta_1/\beta_2}$.

DC bias current is set by $V_{in}$ DC level:

$$I_D = \frac12 \beta_1 (V_{in}-V_{THN})^2$$

The circuit is ratioed. $V_{out}$ DC depends on device sizes.

For both in saturation:

$V_{in} > V_{THN}$,
$$V_{in} \le V_{THN} + \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|}{1+\sqrt{\beta_1/\beta_2}}$$

$$V_{out,min,sat}= V_{in,max}-V_{THN}
 = \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|}{1+\sqrt{\beta_1/\beta_2}}$$

If $V_{in} = V_{THN}$, $I_D=0$ and:

$$V_{out,max} = V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$$

It can never go up to $V_{DD}$. If $V_{in}$ is too large,
$M_1$ goes to triode:

$$\beta_1\left[(V_{in}-V_{THN})V_{out}-V_{out}^2/2\right]
 = \frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|)^2$$

$V_{out}$ falls further but slowly.

If $V_{in}<V_{THN}$, $M_1$ is off, current is zero,
output floats to $\approx V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$.

### 2. Small signal

$M_2$ diode connected between $V_{DD}$ AC ground and output
looks like an impedance. Apply $v_x$ at drain (=gate):

$$i_x = g_{m2}v_x + g_{ds2}v_x$$

$$Z_2 = \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}}\parallel r_{o2}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

since $g_m \gg g_{ds}$. $M_2$ acts as a resistor $\approx 1/g_{m2}$.

The stage is $M_1$ CS with source grounded loaded by
$r_{o1} \parallel Z_2$.

KCL at output:

$$g_{m1}v_{in} + (g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{m2})v_{out}=0$$

$$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$R_{out} = r_{o1} \parallel \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

$$R_{in} = \infty \; \text{at low frequency}$$

Because $g_{m2} \gg g_{ds1},g_{ds2}$:

$$A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}$$
$$R_{out} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

This is inverting, low gain.

With square law, $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D$:

$$g_m = \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$$

$$|A_v| \approx \sqrt{\frac{\mu_n(W/L)_1}{\mu_p(W/L)_2}}$$

Independent of $I_D$ to first order. Same as large-signal
slope. In overdrive terms $g_m =2I_D/V_{ov}$:

$$A_v \approx -\frac{V_{ov2}}{V_{ov1}}$$

To get $|A_v|>1$ you need $M_1$ much stronger than $M_2$.
Typically $|A_v|$ is 2-10.

Dominant pole at output:

$$\omega_p \approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{tot}}$$

$C_{tot}$ = $C_{DB1}+C_{GD1}+C_{DB2}+C_{GS2}+C_{GD2}+C_L$.
$C_{GS2}$ goes to AC ground. Input capacitance includes Miller:

$$C_{in} = C_{GS1}+(1+|A_v|)C_{GD1}$$

Miller is small because $|A_v|$ is small.

### 3. Swing, pros/cons

* Max output: $V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$. Loss of one threshold.
Limited swing.
* Min output for saturation: $(V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|)/(1+\sqrt{\beta_1/\beta_2})$.
Can go lower in triode but non-linear.
* Low small-signal gain set by geometry ratio.
* Low output resistance $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, good to drive
capacitive load, bad for gain.
* Static power: $V_{DD}I_D$ always when on. Unlike a CMOS
inverter.
* Input common-mode range very narrow for high gain.

It saves area vs a passive resistor and tracks process,
and is linear if $\lambda=0$. But it is inferior to a
current-source load, which gives $A_v=-g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$
much larger, and full swing.

Used as level shifter, biasing element, diode load
inverter in old NMOS logic, active load for differential
pairs where low common-mode gain is wanted, not for
high-gain op-amps.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a Common Source stage with a diode
connected load.

* $M_1$ : NMOS driver. Source to GND, drain to $V_{out}$,
  gate to $V_{in}$. Body to GND.
* $M_2$ : PMOS load. Source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$,
  gate to $V_{out}$. Body to $V_{DD}$.

So $V_{SB1}=V_{SB2}=0$, no back gate effect.

$M_2$ gate=drain is always in saturation when on.
Indeed for a PMOS

on: $V_{SG} > |V_{THP}|$
sat: $V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$

With $V_G=V_D$, $V_{SD}=V_{SG}$ so sat is always
satisfied.

$M_1$ is a normal common source:

on: $V_{GS1}=V_{in} > V_{THN}$
sat: $V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN}$ i.e.

$$ V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{THN} $$

The two drains are in series, so in DC steady state

$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2} $$

With square law, neglecting $\lambda$ for DC:

$$ I_{D1} = K_n (V_{GS1}-V_{THN})^2 $$
in saturation,
$$ I_{D1} = K_n\left[2(V_{GS1}-V_{THN})V_{DS1}-V_{DS1}^2\right] $$
in triode,
$$ I_{D2} = K_p (V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$
in saturation,

where

$$K_n=\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1,\quad
  K_p=\frac12\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2$$
$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\; V_{DS1}=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{out},\; V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

### Large signal VTC, inverting

1. $V_{in}<V_{THN}$ : $M_1$ off.
$I_{D1}=0$ forces $I_{D2}=0$. $M_2$ charges the output
until it turns itself off:

$$ V_{out,H}=V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| $$

This is the highest output. Not $V_{DD}$ due to the
$V_{TH}$ drop in the diode connected PMOS.

2. $M_1$ sat, $M_2$ sat. Both on:

$$ K_n (V_{in}-V_{THN})^2 = K_p (V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

i.e.

$$ V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|-\sqrt{\frac{K_n}{K_p}}\,(V_{in}-V_{THN}) $$

Output falls linearly with $V_{in}$.

This holds as long as $V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{THN}$.
The edge is at

$$ V_{in,H}=V_{THN}+\frac{V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|}{1+\sqrt{K_n/K_p}} $$

3. $V_{in}>V_{in,H}$ : $M_1$ triode, $M_2$ sat:

$$ K_n[2(V_{in}-V_{THN})V_{out}-V_{out}^2]
 = K_p(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

$V_{out}$ continues to fall to a low value $V_{OL}>0$.
For $V_{in}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}$ is small if $K_n\gg K_p$.

In short: inverter with degraded high level,
finite low level, gradual transition, static current
when on. Not a good logic gate.

### Small signal

Bias at a $Q$-point in region 2, apply small $v_{in}$.
$M_1$: $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{ds1}=v_{out}$.
$M_2$: source ac ground, $v_g=v_d=v_{out}$,
$v_{sg}=-v_{out}$, $v_{sd}=-v_{out}$.

KCL at output, no load:

PMOS source-to-drain ac current:
$i_{sp}=g_{m2}v_{sg}+g_{ds2}v_{sd}=-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{out}$
entering the output node.

NMOS drain current:
$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out}$
leaving the output node.

$i_{sp}=i_{d1}$ :

$$ -(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{out}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out} $$

Voltage gain:

$$ A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{m2}} $$

Output resistance, $v_{in}=0$, test $v_x$ at output:

$$ R_{out}= \frac{1}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{m2}} $$

i.e. $r_{o1}$ in parallel with the impedance looking
into the diode connected $M_2$, $1/(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})$.

Since normally $g_m \gg g_{ds}$ :

$$ R_{out}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}},\quad A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} $$

With $g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ and $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$:

$$ |A_v|\approx \sqrt{\frac{\mu_n(W/L)_1}{\mu_p(W/L)_2}} $$

To get gain, make the driver stronger than the load.
Gain is independent of bias to first order.

Input resistance:

$$ R_{in}=\infty $$

Dominant high frequency pole at output is approximately

$$ \omega_H \approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{L,tot}} $$

where $C_{L,tot}$ includes $C_{db1},C_{db2},C_{gd1}(1+|A_v|)$,
$C_{gs2}$, wiring and next stage.

Summary: inverting low-gain amplifier, gain set by
device ratio, low output impedance $\sim 1/g_{m2}$,
limited swing $V_{OL}$ to $V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$,
dissipates static power $V_{DD}I_D$. Useful as active
load amplifier, level shifter, bias element, not as a
full-swing CMOS inverter.
