answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a PMOS common-source stage with a
PMOS ``diode'' load.

* $M_{2}$ : gate $=V_{in}$, source $=V_{DD}$,
drain $=V_{out}$. Body to $V_{DD}$ - or to
source in its own well.
Standard CS, source AC ground.

* $M_{1}$ : source $=V_{out}$, drain $=GND$,
gate $=GND$. Body to source - or to $V_{DD}$.

Upper terminal carries the arrow, i.e. the
$p$-source. $M_{1}$ gate is shorted to
drain. It is diode connected, but upside down:
the signal is applied to the source, drain/gate
are AC ground.

Put for PMOS $|V_{DS}|=V_{SD}$, $|V_{GS}|=V_{SG}$,
$|V_T|=-V_{Tp}>0$,
$$ I_{SD}= \frac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
 (V_{SG}-|V_T|)^{2}(1+\lambda V_{SD}) $$
in saturation.

DC large signal

$M_{1}$: 
$$ V_{SG1}=V_{S1}-V_{G1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out} $$
$$ V_{SD1}=V_{S1}-V_{D1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out} $$
Hence
$$V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}$$
$M_{1}$ is in saturation whenever it is on:
$$ V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{T1}| $$
is automatically satisfied. ON requires
$$ V_{out}>|V_{T1}| $$

$M_{2}$:
$$ V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in} $$
$$ V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out} $$
ON requires
$$ V_{DD}-V_{in}>|V_{T2}| $$
Saturation requires
$$ V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{T2}| $$
i.e.
$$ V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}| $$
$$ V_{out}-V_{in}\le |V_{T2}| $$

The two are in series, DC:
$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2} $$
$$ \frac12\mu_pC_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
 (V_{out}-|V_{T1}|)^2(1+\lambda_1V_{out}) $$
$$ =\frac12\mu_pC_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
 (V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|)^2
 [1+\lambda_2(V_{DD}-V_{out})] \tag{1}$$

This is the $V_{out}$ vs $V_{in}$ characteristic.
Neglecting $\lambda$:
$$ \sqrt{\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1}\,(V_{out}-|V_{T1}|)
 =\sqrt{\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2}\,
 (V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|) $$
$$ V_{out}=|V_{T1}|+ \sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}
 \,(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|) \tag{2} $$

As $V_{in}$ goes up, $V_{SG2}$ goes down,
current goes down, the drop $V_{SG1}=V_{out}$
required by $M_{1}$ to carry that current goes
down. The stage is inverting.

It is not a good logic inverter. If $M_{2}$ is
off, $M_{1}$ discharges $V_{out}$ to $|V_{T1}|$
and then cuts off. Low level $\approx |V_{T1}|$,
high level $<V_{DD}$.

Small signal

Bias in saturation, small signal model for a
PMOS is the same as NMOS:
$$ i_d = g_m v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds} $$
entering the drain.

$M_{2}$ is conventional CS: $v_s=0$ AC,
$v_g=v_{in}$, $v_d=v_{out}$,
$$ i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out} $$
leaving the output node into $M_{2}$.

$M_{1}$: signal at source. $v_g=0$, $v_d=0$,
$v_s=v_{out}$. With its own well, $v_b=v_s$,
no back gate. In general $v_b=0$ AC if well
to $V_{DD}$.
$$ v_{gs1}= -v_{out} $$
$$ v_{ds1}= -v_{out} $$
$$ v_{bs1}= v_{b}-v_{s}= -v_{out} \;\;{\rm common\;well} $$
$$ i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1} $$
$$ =-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{out} $$
$i_{d1}$ enters the drain from ground. The
current entering the source from the output
node is $-i_{d1}$:
$$ i_{s1} = (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{out} $$

i.e. looking into the source of a gate-grounded
device you see
$$ Z_{1}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}
 \approx \frac1{g_{m1}} $$
This is exactly the diode-connected impedance.
With body to source, $g_{mb1}=0$.

KCL at output:
$$ i_{d2}+i_{s1}=0 $$
$$ g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}
 +(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}=0 $$

$$ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
 = -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

With no body effect:
$$ A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

Output resistance at the drain of $M_{2}$ loaded
by $Z_{1}$:
$$ R_{out}= r_{o2}\parallel Z_{1}
 = \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$
$$ \approx \frac1{g_{m1}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2} $$

Input resistance:
$$ R_{in}=\infty $$

Neglecting $\lambda$, $g_m=\sqrt{2\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$,
same $I_D$:
$$ A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}
 = -\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}} $$
same as (2). To get $|A_v|>1$ you need
$(W/L)_2>(W/L)_1$.

In short: inverting CS amplifier, gain set
by $g_m$ ratio, low $R_{out}\sim 1/g_m$,
limited output swing, static current.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Identifies both devices as PMOS, M2 as the common-source input device, and M1 as a diode-connected PMOS load with gate and drain at ground. It derives the expected inverting gain, approximately −gm2/gm1; the additional logic-pulldown framing is explicitly acceptable.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a PMOS common-source stage with a PMOS
diode-connected load. It is the PMOS version of the
enhancement-load inverter.

* Symbol: the arrow is on the source lead.
Both arrows point away from the channel. Both
are PMOS.
* M2 top: body + source to $V_{DD}$, drain to
$V_{out}$, gate to $V_{in}$.
* M1 bottom: body + source to $V_{out}$,
drain to GND, gate to GND.

So M1 has gate shorted to drain. But the ``top"
of the device is the source. It sits upside down
between $V_{out}$ and GND.

Let for PMOS

$$I_{SD}=\frac12 \mu_pC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
(V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|)^2(1+\lambda V_{SD})$$

in saturation, $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|$,
$V_{SG}>|V_{thp}|$.

Put $k_{p}= \mu_pC_{ox}W/L$, $|V_{T}|=-V_{thp}>0$.

No body effect: $V_{SB2}=0$, $V_{SB1}=0$ because
body is tied to source in both cases. This requires
two separate n-wells: M2 well to $V_{DD}$, M1 well
to $V_{out}$. Well to p-sub remains reverse biased
as long as $V_{out}>0$.

KCL at output, no external load:

$$I_{D2}=I_{D1}=I_D$$

conventional current downward from $V_{DD}$ to
$V_{out}$ to GND.

For M1:
$$V_{SG1}=V_{S1}-V_{G1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SD1}=V_{S1}-V_{D1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}$$
So $V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}$. M1 is:

- off if $V_{out}<|V_{T1}|$
- saturated if $V_{out}>|V_{T1}|$

It is always saturated when on.

For M2:
$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$
On if $V_{DD}-V_{in}>|V_{T2}|$, i.e.
$$V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{T2}|$$
Saturated if $V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{T2}|$, i.e.
$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|$$
$$V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{T2}|$$

### Large signal $V_{out}$ vs $V_{in}$

1. M2 off: $V_{in}\ge V_{DD}-|V_{T2}|$

$I_{D2}=0$ so $I_{D1}=0$. If $V_{out}>|V_{T1}|$
M1 is on and discharges the output node to GND
until it turns itself off. Equilibrium:

$$V_{out}\approx |V_{T1}|$$

both devices (ideally) off.

2. Both saturated, ignoring $\lambda$:

$$\frac12k_{p2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|)^2
 =\frac12k_{p1}(V_{out}-|V_{T1}|)^2$$

i.e.

$$V_{out}=|V_{T1}|+\sqrt{\frac{k_{p2}}{k_{p1}}}
\,(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|)$$

This is linear inverting, slope
$-A$ with

$$A=\sqrt{k_{p2}/k_{p1}}
 =\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}$$

assuming same $\mu_pC_{ox}$.

Valid while M2 stays saturated,
$V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{T2}|$, i.e.

$$V_{in}\ge V_L =\frac{A}{1+A}V_{DD}
 +\frac{|V_{T1}|}{1+A}-|V_{T2}|$$

Upper end is $V_H=V_{DD}-|V_{T2}|$, where
$V_{out}=|V_{T1}|$.

Input range for high-gain mode:
$$V_H-V_L =\frac{V_{DD}-|V_{T1}|}{1+A}$$

Output at lower $V_{in}$ edge, still saturated:
$$V_{out,H,sat}=V_L+|V_{T2}|
 =\frac{A\,V_{DD}+|V_{T1}|}{1+A}$$

If $A\gg 1$ this is $\approx V_{DD}$.

3. M2 triode, M1 saturated: $V_{in}<V_L$

$$k_{p2}\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{T2}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\right]
 =\frac12k_{p1}(V_{out}-|V_{T1}|)^2$$

$V_{out}$ keeps rising toward $V_{DD}$ as
$V_{in}$ falls, compressively. Minimum $V_{out}$
is $|V_{T1}|$, maximum $\approx V_{DD}$.

In digital terms: low in $\to$ high out $\approx V_{DD}$,
high in $\to$ low out $=|V_{T1}|\ne 0$. Ratioed,
asymmetric, static current in the low-input state.
Not a good logic gate.

### Small signal

In saturation, M2 is a common-source device,
source AC ground. M1 has gate AC ground, drain
AC ground, source at output. It is a diode.

Look into source of M1 with test $v_x$:
$v_g=0$, $v_d=0$, $v_s=v_x$, $v_b=v_x$,
$v_{gs}=-v_x$, $v_{ds}=-v_x$,
$i_d=g_m v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$ entering drain.

Current entering source $i_x=-i_d$:

$$i_x = (g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_x$$

i.e.

$$R_{1}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

$g_{mb1}=0$. M2 output resistance $r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$.

Total at output:

$$R_{out}=R_{1}\parallel r_{o2}
 =\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
 \approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

Voltage gain:

$$A_v = -g_{m2}R_{out}
 =-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
 \approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}$$

With same $I_D$:

$$\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}\approx
\sqrt{\frac{k_{p2}}{k_{p1}}}=A$$

same as large signal slope. Input resistance
is infinite at low frequency, gate of M2.

In essence: CS with $R_D$ replaced by $1/g_{m1}$.
To get $|A_v|>1$ need $(W/L)_2>(W/L)_1$.

Dominant pole is at output:

$$\omega_p \approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{tot}}$$

$C_{tot}$ = $C_{db2}+C_{gd2}$ + well capacitance
of M1 + $C_{gs1}$ + load + Miller effect of
$C_{gd2}$ to input. Input capacitance
$\approx C_{gs2}+(1+|A_v|)C_{gd2}$.

Summary: inverting amplifier, low intrinsic
gain set by device ratio, limited output
swing $|V_{T1}|$ to $V_{DD}$, no body effect,
$R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m1}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a PMOS common source stage with a PMOS
diode connected load. It is the PMOS dual of the
old NMOS enhancement load inverter.

* $M_{2}$ : gate $V_{in}$, source to $V_{DD}$,
drain to $V_{out}$, bulk to $V_{DD}$.
It must be PMOS. NMOS body must go to the
lowest supply. Here bulk is to $V_{DD}$.

* $M_{1}$ : top terminal to $V_{out}$, bottom
terminal to GND, gate to GND, bulk to top terminal.
Bulk cannot be grounded for a PMOS. Therefore
bulk is not grounded. The grounded bottom
terminal is drain alone.

Top = source = bulk = $V_{out}$
Bottom = drain = GND
Gate = GND

i.e. gate shorted to drain. $M_{1}$ is a
diode connected PMOS. Its current flows
from $V_{out}$ to GND. $M_{2}$ current flows
from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$. In DC they are
in series.

Both have source tied to bulk, so

$$V_{SB1}=0,\quad V_{SB2}=0$$

no back gate effect. This needs two separate
n-wells: $M_{2}$ well to $V_{DD}$, $M_{1}$
well to $V_{out}$.

$M_{1}$ is always saturated when on because
gate = drain.

For PMOS in saturation, ignoring $\lambda$:

$$I_D = \frac12 \mu_pC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
(V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

Put $V_{TH}=|V_{THP}|$, same for both.

$$V_{SG1}=V_{S1}-V_{G1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SD1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

DC with no load: $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D$.

$$ \frac12\mu_pC_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{out}-V_{TH})^2(1+\lambda_1V_{out}) = $$
$$\frac12\mu_pC_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{TH})^2(1+\lambda_2(V_{DD}-V_{out})) $$

Neglect $\lambda$:

$$V_{out}=V_{TH}+ \sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}
\,(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{TH}) \tag{1}$$

when both on and $M_{2}$ saturated.

On conditions:

$$V_{SG1}>V_{TH}\to V_{out}>V_{TH}$$
$$V_{SG2}>V_{TH}\to V_{in}<V_{DD}-V_{TH}$$

$M_{1}$ saturation is automatic:
$V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}\ge V_{SG1}-V_{TH}$.

$M_{2}$ saturation:
$$V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{out}\le V_{in}+V_{TH} \tag{2}$$

Let

$$A_r=\sqrt{(W/L)_2/(W/L)_1}$$

(1)+(2) give for saturation-mode operation:

$$V_{in}\ge \frac{A_r}{A_r+1}(V_{DD}-V_{TH})$$
$$V_{in}\le V_{DD}-V_{TH}$$

In that interval (1) holds, i.e. an inverting
linear characteristic with slope $-A_r$.

* for $V_{in}\ge V_{DD}-V_{TH}$, $M_2$ off,
$I_D=0$, $M_1$ pulls $V_{out}$ down until it
turns itself off:
$$V_{out}\approx V_{TH}$$
This is the $V_{OL}$, not 0.

* for $V_{in}$ below the lower limit, $M_2$
goes to triode. $V_{out}$ rises toward $V_{DD}$.
With $V_{in}=0$,
$$V_{OH}\approx V_{DD}-\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{TH}}{2}$$
close to $V_{DD}$ if $(W/L)_2\gg (W/L)_1$.

So large signal it is an inverter with degraded
low level, degraded high gain region, static
current. Gain magnitude in the high slope
region is $A_r$.

Small signal: bias in saturation.

$M_2$: $v_{g2}=v_{in}$, $v_{s2}=0$,
$v_{d2}=v_{out}$, $v_{b2}=0$.

$$v_{gs2}=v_{in},\;v_{ds2}=v_{out}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$
into drain.

$M_1$: $v_{s1}=v_{out}$, $v_{d1}=0$,
$v_{g1}=0$, $v_{b1}=v_{out}$.

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{out},\;v_{ds1}=-v_{out},\;v_{bs1}=0$$
$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}
=-(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}$$
into drain.

KCL at output: current leaving node into $M_2$
drain + into $M_1$ source $=0$.
Source current $=-$drain current:
$$i_{d2}-i_{d1}=0$$

$$g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}
=-(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}$$

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

The diode device presents

$$R_{L}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

to AC from source, so $A_v=-g_{m2}(r_{o2}\Vert R_L)$.

Output resistance:

$$R_{out}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
= \frac1{g_{m1}}\Vert r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}}$$

Input resistance:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

Since $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$,

$$g_m=\sqrt{2\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$$

$$|A_v|\approx \frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}
= \sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}=A_r$$

$\lambda$ reduces it slightly.

In words: low gain set by geometry ratio, inverting,
low output resistance $\sim 1/g_m$, poor output
swing $V_{TH}$ to $\sim V_{DD}$, narrow input
range for saturation, static power, PSRR $\approx 0$dB
because supply variation is amplified by $\approx g_{m2}/g_{m1}$.

With load capacitance $C_L$ the dominant pole is
approximately

$$\omega_p \approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{tot}}$$

where $C_{tot}$ is $C_L$ plus $C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{gs1}$
plus $C_{gd2}$ Miller, etc.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies both devices as PMOS, M2 as the common-source input device, and M1 as a diode-connected PMOS load with gate and drain at ground. It also derives the expected gain, approximately −gm2/gm1.

answers.question: Find Rout in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a PMOS cascode. Put $V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}$
ac ground and drive the output, the drain of $M_{1}$,
with a test source.

```
      +---- ac gnd
      |
     S2
  0--G  M2
     D2
      |
      X
      |
     S1
  0--G  M1
     D1
      |
     Vx Ix up
```

Let $V_{X}$ be the small signal voltage at $X$, source
of $M_{1}$, drain of $M_{2}$. $V_{x}$ be the test
voltage, $I_{x}$ the current entering the drain of $M_{1}$.

For a MOS, entering the drain,

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

$M_{1}$: $v_{s1}=V_{X},\;v_{d1}=V_{x},\;v_{g1}=0$

$$v_{gs1} = -V_{X}$$
$$v_{ds1} = V_{x}-V_{X}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}(-V_{X})+\frac{V_{x}-V_{X}}{r_{o1}} \tag{1}$$

$i_{d1}$ entering the drain is $I_{x}$.

At node $X$ there is only $D_{2}$ and $S_{1}$.
KCL gives

$$i_{d2}+i_{s1}=0$$

$i_{s1}=-i_{d1}$ , so

$$i_{d2}=i_{d1}=I_{x} \tag{2}$$

$M_{2}$: $v_{s2}=0,\;v_{g2}=0,\;v_{d2}=V_{X}$

$$v_{gs2}=0$$
$$v_{ds2}=V_{X}$$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}\cdot 0+\frac{V_{X}}{r_{o2}}=\frac{V_{X}}{r_{o2}} \tag{3}$$

From (2)(3)

$$V_{X}=I_{x}r_{o2}$$

Put in (1) with $i_{d1}=I_{x}$:

$$I_{x} = -g_{m1}I_{x}r_{o2}+\frac{V_{x}-I_{x}r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}$$

$$I_{x}\left[1+g_{m1}r_{o2}+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}\right]=\frac{V_{x}}{r_{o1}}$$

$$\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

i.e. the common-gate $M_{1}$ degenerated by the
$r_{o2}$ in its source:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}+ (1+g_{m1}r_{o1})r_{o2}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the PMOS cascode with M1 as the common-gate device and derives Rout = ro1 + ro2 + gm1 ro1 ro2, with the correct large-gm approximation. Omitting body effect is allowed.

answer.text:
This is the small signal impedance looking into the drain
of a cascode with the gates at ac ground.

Put $V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}$ to ac ground and drive
the output, the drain of $M_{1}$, with $V_{t}$ and
measure $I_{t}$.

$M_{2}$ : source to ac ground, gate to ac ground,
drain to $X$.  With $v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=0$

$$ R_{X} = \frac{v_{x}}{-i_{sd2}} = r_{o2}$$

i.e. looking into the drain of $M_{2}$ you see $r_{o2}$
to ground.

$M_{1}$ : gate grounded, source to $R_{X}=r_{o2}$,
drain to output.  It is a common gate with source
degeneration.

Let the source of $M_{1}$, node $X$, be $V_{X}$.
For the PMOS in saturation use $v_{sg},v_{sb},v_{sd}$,
current $i_{sd}$ entering the source, leaving the drain:

$$i_{sd}=g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+g_{ds}v_{sd}$$

$M_{1}$:
$$v_{sg1}=V_{X},\quad v_{sb1}=V_{X},\quad v_{sd1}=V_{X}-V_{t}$$
$$i_{sd1}=g_{m1}V_{X}+g_{mb1}V_{X}+g_{ds1}(V_{X}-V_{t})$$

$M_{2}$:
$$v_{sg2}=0,\quad v_{sb2}=0,\quad v_{sd2}=-V_{X}$$
$$i_{sd2}=-g_{ds2}V_{X}$$

KCL at $X$ and at the output gives, with $I_{t}$
entering the drain of $M_{1}$,

$$i_{sd1}=i_{sd2}=-I_{t}$$

Hence
$$-I_{t} = -g_{ds2}V_{X}$$
$$V_{X} = \frac{I_{t}}{g_{ds2}} = I_{t}r_{o2}$$

and
$$-I_{t} = (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})V_{X}-g_{ds1}V_{t}$$

$$g_{ds1}V_{t}=(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})V_{X}+I_{t}$$

$$\frac{V_{t}}{I_{t}}=
\frac{1}{g_{ds1}}\left[\frac{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{ds2}}+1\right]$$

i.e. with $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$,

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}+[1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}]r_{o2}$$

the familiar common-gate with $R_{S}=r_{o2}$ result.
With $g_{mb}=0$,

$$R_{out}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

answer.text:
Looking into the drain with the gate at ac ground

Put $V_{DD}, V_{b1}, V_{b2}$ to ac ground. Put a
Thevenin $V_{x}$ at the output and measure $I_{x}$.

For the PMOS, with conventional current directions,
in saturation

$$I_{d}=g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{mb}V_{bs}+g_{ds}V_{ds}$$

entering the drain.

$M_{2}$ has source to ac ground, gate to ac ground.
Let $X$ be the $M_{2}$ drain $=M_{1}$ source node.

For $M_{2}$ : $V_{g2}=V_{s2}=0$ ac. Looking into
its drain,

$$I_{d2}=g_{ds2}(V_{X}-0)$$

i.e. the impedance from $X$ to ground is

$$R_{X}=r_{o2}$$

$M_{1}$ is a common gate device whose source sees
$R_{X}$ to ground. Let the output node be $V_{x}$,
the source node be $V_{s1}=V_{X}$.

Gate grounded: $V_{g1}=0$.
Bulk at ac ground for a PMOS in the $n$-well to $V_{DD}$:
$V_{b1}=0$.

$$V_{gs1}= -V_{s1}, \quad V_{bs1}= -V_{s1}, \quad
V_{ds1}=V_{x}-V_{s1}$$

The small signal drain current entering $M_{1}$ is
the test current $I_{x}$. Since gate and bulk draw
no current, it must all exit at the source and go
through $R_{X}$ to ground:

KCL at source: $I_{x}$ flows out the source into $R_{X}$,

$$V_{s1}=I_{x}R_{X}$$

KCL at drain:

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{x} &= g_{m1}V_{gs1}+g_{mb1}V_{bs1}+g_{ds1}V_{ds1}\\
&= -g_{m1}V_{s1}-g_{mb1}V_{s1}+g_{ds1}(V_{x}-V_{s1})
\end{aligned}$$

$$g_{ds1}V_{x}=I_{x}+V_{s1}(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})$$

With $V_{s1}=I_{x}R_{X}$,

$$\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=\frac{1+R_{X}(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})}{g_{ds1}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}+R_{X}+ (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}R_{X}$$

Here $R_{X}=r_{o2}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+ (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$=r_{o1}+[1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}]r_{o2}\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

Without body effect, $g_{mb1}=0$.

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
For $M_{2}$ this is a PMOS common source with
a PMOS common gate cascode $M_{1}$ on top of it.

Put source positive. A PMOS is on and saturated if

$$V_{SG} > |V_{THp}|$$
$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THp}| = V_{OV}$$

For $M_{2}$ :

* source: $V_{DD}$
* gate: $V_{b2}$
* drain: $V_{X}$

$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}$$

Saturation requires

$$V_{DD}-V_{X} \ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THp2}|$$

i.e.

$$ V_{X} \le V_{b2}+|V_{THp2}| \tag{1}$$

The drain voltage of $M_{2}$ must be low enough to
support the required $V_{SD}$.

$V_{X}$ is not independent. It is the source
voltage of the cascode $M_{1}$. For $M_{1}$:

* source: $V_{X}$
* gate: $V_{b1}$

If $M_{1}$ is on,

$$V_{SG1}=V_{X}-V_{b1}=|V_{THp1}|+V_{OV1}$$

where $V_{OV1}$ is set by the series dc current
and $(W/L)_{1}$. Hence

$$ V_{X}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}=V_{b1}+|V_{THp1}|+V_{OV1} \tag{2}$$

i.e. $V_{X}$ follows $V_{b1}$.

Put (2) in (1):

$$V_{b1}+|V_{THp1}|+V_{OV1} \le V_{b2}+|V_{THp2}|$$

$$V_{b1} \le V_{b2} +|V_{THp2}|-|V_{THp1}|-V_{OV1}$$

With matched $|V_{TH}|$,

$$V_{b2}-V_{b1} \ge V_{OV1}$$

In words: lower $V_{b1}$ to lower $V_{X}$ to increase
$V_{SD2}$. Do not make $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$ so
large - for the required current use large enough
$(W/L)_{2}$ - that the required $V_{SD2}\ge V_{OV2}$
cannot be supported.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies both devices as PMOS, derives M2’s saturation condition, relates VX to Vb1 through M1, and obtains the equivalent bias condition Vb2 − Vb1 ≥ M1’s overdrive.

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
Both devices are PMOS. The current flows down.

* $M_{2}$ : source to $V_{DD}$, gate to $V_{b2}$,
drain to $X$
* $M_{1}$ : source to $X$, gate to $V_{b1}$,
drain to the output

For high impedance $R_{out}$ both must be
saturated, with high $r_{o}$.

For a PMOS in saturation

$$V_{SG}>|V_{TH}|$$
$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{TH}| = V_{OV}$$

i.e. with signed $V_{THP}<0$, $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}+V_{THP}$.

For $M_{2}$:

$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}$$

Saturation requires

$$V_{DD}-V_{X} \ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TH2}|$$

$$V_{X} \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}| \tag{1}$$

i.e. the drain of $M_{2}$ must be low enough to
support $\approx V_{OV2}$ across it.

$V_{X}$ is the source voltage of the cascode $M_{1}$.
If $M_{1}$ is on:

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}$$

with, in saturation,

$$V_{SG1}=|V_{TH1}|+V_{OV1}$$

set to first order by the bias current and
$(W/L)_{1}$. Body is tied to source for both
devices, so no back gate effect.

Put in (1):

$$V_{b1}+V_{SG1} \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|$$

$$V_{b1} \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|-V_{SG1}$$

In particular if $|V_{TH1}|\approx |V_{TH2}|$:

$$V_{b2}-V_{b1} \ge V_{SG1}-|V_{TH1}|=V_{OV1}$$

If $V_{b1}$ is too high, $V_{X}$ follows it up,
$V_{SD2}$ falls and $M_{2}$ goes to triode.

So for given current, i.e. given $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$,
we must keep the cascode gate $V_{b1}$ sufficiently
below $V_{b2}$, by at least one $M_{1}$ overdrive.
At the edge:

$$V_{X}\approx V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|=V_{DD}-V_{OV2}$$
$$V_{SD2}\approx V_{OV2}$$

Making $V_{b1}$ lower only helps $M_{2}$ stay
saturated, but it lowers the maximum allowed output
voltage for $M_{1}$ saturation, $V_{out}\le V_{b1}+
|V_{TH1}|$. Hence $V_{b1}$ is chosen just low
enough.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies both devices as PMOS, gives M2’s saturation condition, and uses VX = Vb1 + |VGS1| to derive the required condition on Vb1, including the equal-threshold overdrive form.

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
$M_{2}$ is the PMOS current source, $M_{1}$ is the
PMOS cascode. With conventional current flowing down:

* $M_{2}$ : source $V_{DD}$, gate $V_{b2}$, drain $V_{X}$
* $M_{1}$ : source $V_{X}$, gate $V_{b1}$, drain $V_{out}$

For a PMOS in saturation

$$V_{SG} > |V_{THP}|$$
$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}| = V_{OV}$$

For $M_{2}$:

$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}$$

Saturation is

$$V_{DD}-V_{X} \ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TH2}|$$

i.e.

$$ V_{X} \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}| \tag{1}$$

$M_{2}$ stays saturated iff its drain, node $X$,
is low enough to leave $\ge V_{OV2}$ across
source-drain:

$$V_{DD}-V_{X} \ge V_{OV2}$$

$V_{X}$ is set by the cascode $M_{1}$. If $M_{1}$ is
on and saturated it carries the $M_{2}$ current with
an essentially fixed $V_{SG1}$:

$$V_{X}=V_{S1}=V_{G1}+V_{SG1}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}$$

$$V_{SG1}=|V_{TH1}|+V_{OV1}$$

Put in (1):

$$V_{b1}+V_{SG1} \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|$$

$$V_{b2} \ge V_{b1}+V_{SG1}-|V_{TH2}|$$

With no body effect, $|V_{TH1}|\approx |V_{TH2}|$:

$$V_{b2} \gtrsim V_{b1}+V_{OV1}$$

In other words, for a given current, i.e. given
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$, you must keep $V_{b1}$
low enough that

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}\le V_{DD}-V_{OV2}$$

$$V_{b1}\le V_{DD}-V_{SG1}-V_{OV2}$$

That leaves $V_{SD2}\ge V_{OV2}$.

At the edge of saturation,

$$V_{b1,opt}=V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|-V_{SG1}$$

E.g. same size and current, $V_{SG1}=V_{SG2}=
|V_{TH}|+V_{OV}$:

$$V_{b1}=V_{b2}-V_{OV}=V_{DD}-|V_{TH}|-2V_{OV}$$

$V_{b1}$ cannot be made arbitrarily low or $M_{1}$
loses headroom. $M_{1}$ saturation needs
$V_{X}-V_{out}\ge V_{OV1}$, i.e.

$$V_{out}\le V_{X}-V_{OV1}=V_{b1}+|V_{TH1}|$$

So $V_{b1}$ is chosen as high as (1) allows.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies both devices as PMOS, gives M2’s saturation condition, and relates VX to Vb1 to derive the corresponding bias condition. This satisfies the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a common-source stage $M_{1}$ with
cascode device $M_{2}$ and active load $I_{1}$.

* $M_{1}$ is the input transconductor. Its source
is ac ground.
* $M_{2}$ is common-gate. $V_{b1}$ is ac ground.
Its source is node $X$, its drain is $v_{out}$.
* $I_{1}$ is the dc bias current and the ac load.
Let its small signal impedance to $V_{DD}$ ac
ground be $R_{1}$. For an ideal source $R_{1}=\infty$.

Assume all in saturation. Let

$$ g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1},\; g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$$

$M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$, no back gate.
$M_{2}$ in a common p-sub has $V_{SB2}>0$,
back gate $g_{mb2}\ne 0$ unless in own well.

DC: neglecting mismatch

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}$$

$V_{GS1}$ is set by $V_{in,DC}$ to support $I_{1}$:

$$ I_{1}\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}
(V_{GS1}-V_{TH1})^{2}(1+\lambda_{1}V_{DS1}) $$

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$$

Saturation needs:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{X} &\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{OV1} \\
V_{out} &\ge V_{X}+V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{X}+V_{OV2}\\
V_{out} &\le V_{DD}-V_{sat,I1}
\end{aligned}$$

i.e.

$$V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{GS2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$$

With $\lambda=0$ and ideal $I_{1}$ the dc $V_{out}$
is undefined. In practice it is set by
$\lambda$ and $R_{1}$. It is a high gain node,
bias sensitive.

Small signal, low frequency.

Put $v_{in}$ at gate of $M_{1}$, $v_{x}$ at $X$,
$v_{out}$ at output. For $M_{2}$:

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x},\quad v_{bs2}=-v_{x},\quad
v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

Define the $M_{2}$ drain-to-source ac current:

$$i_{2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$$i_{2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

For $M_{1}$:

$$i_{1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$

flowing from $X$ to ground.

KCL at $X$: current entering $X$ from $M_{2}$
equals current leaving $X$ into $M_{1}$:

$$i_{2}=i_{1} \tag{1}$$

KCL at output: current leaving output into $M_{2}$
plus current leaving into $R_{1}$ = 0:

$$i_{2}+v_{out}/R_{1}=0 \tag{2}$$

for open circuit load. Hence from (1)-(2):

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{2} &= -v_{out}/R_{1} \\
g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x} &= -v_{out}/R_{1}
\end{aligned}$$

and

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})+v_{out}/R_{1}=0 $$

i.e. with $N=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}$:

$$v_{out}(g_{ds2}+1/R_{1}) = v_{x}N \tag{3}$$

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$, drive
output with test source. Putting $v_{in}=0$
in above gives with $B=g_{ds1}$, $C=g_{ds2}$,
$G_{1}=1/R_{1}$:

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{G_{1}+\dfrac{BC}{B+N}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{out}=R_{1}\parallel R_{cas}$$

where $R_{cas}$ is the impedance looking into
the cascode drain:

$$R_{cas} = r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$\approx [1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]r_{o1}$$

This is the classic common-gate with source
resistance $r_{o1}$ result:

$$R_{d}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}]R_{S}$$

For $R_{1}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

Ignoring body effect: $(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1}$.

Voltage gain: from (3) and (1):

$$-v_{out}G_{1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+v_{x}B$$
$$v_{x}=v_{out}\frac{G_{1}+C}{N}$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m1}N}{G_{1}(N+B)+BC}$$

This can be written as

$$A_{v} = -G_{m}R_{out}$$

where the short-circuit transconductance is

$$G_{m}=g_{m1}\frac{N}{N+B}=g_{m1}
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}
{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\approx g_{m1}$$

since $g_{m2}\gg g_{ds1,2}$. Hence to very good
approximation:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\,[R_{1}\parallel
\{(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2})r_{o1}\}]$$

Ideal load:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]$$

$\approx -(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$.
This is the intrinsic gain squared.

In practice $R_{1}$ is finite, e.g. a PMOS
current source with $r_{op}$. Then

$$R_{out}\approx r_{op}\parallel g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}
\approx r_{op}$$

and $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{op}$, only about
2x the simple CS with active load. The big
gain increase comes only if the load is also
cascoded.

Intuition:

$M_{1}$ produces $g_{m1}v_{in}$. Almost all
flows into $R_{out}$ to give $-g_{m1}R_{out}$.
$M_{2}$ shields the output from $X$, raising
the impedance seen at the drain by $\approx
g_{m2}r_{o2}$.

Node $X$: From (3),

$$\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=A_{v}\frac{G_{1}+C}{N}$$

If $R_{1}$ is of order $r_{o}$, $|v_{x}/v_{in}|
\approx g_{m1}/g_{m2}\sim 1$. The Miller
multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $1-A_{v1}\sim 2$,
not $1+g_{m1}R_{out}$. This pushes the input
pole out and is the main bandwidth advantage
of cascode.

If $R_{1}\to\infty$, $G_{1}\to 0$, then
$v_{x}/v_{in}\to -g_{m1}r_{o1}$, large, because
with an open drain the CG source impedance
becomes large: $R_{x}\approx (R_{1}+r_{o2})/
[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]\parallel r_{o1}$.
Low $R_{x}\approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$ requires
low $R_{1}$.

Frequency: $R_{in}=\infty$ at low frequency.
Dominant pole usually at output:

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$

$C_{out}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{I1}+C_{L}$.
Non-dominant pole at $X$:

$$\omega_{p,X}\approx \frac{1}{R_{x}C_{x}}$$

$C_{x}=C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}$ (Miller),
$R_{x}$ as above, generally much higher than
$\omega_{p,out}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source input device and M2 as the common-gate cascode, and derives both the general gain approximation and the equivalent ideal-load expression. The additional bias and frequency discussion does not undermine the essential result.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a single-ended telescopic cascode.

* $M_{1}$ : NMOS common-source input device
* $M_{2}$ : NMOS common-gate cascode device, gate DC bias $V_{b1}$
* $I_{1}$ : active load from $V_{DD}$ to output. In small signal
it is an AC ground through $R_{I1}$. Ideal $R_{I1}=\infty $.
Realistic PMOS: $R_{I1}=r_{op}$, for PMOS cascode: $\approx g_{mp}r_{op}^{2}$.

Assume all in saturation. $\lambda \ne 0$. Bulk of NMOS
is p-sub = GND, so $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$, $M_{2}$
has $V_{SB2}=V_{X}>0$ and suffers body effect, $g_{mb2}\ne 0$.
If triple well with body to source, put $g_{mb2}=0$.

### Intuition

$M_{1}$ converts $v_{in}$ to current. $M_{2}$, with AC
grounded gate, conveys that current to the high impedance
output node with $\approx 1$ current gain, but presents a
low impedance to the drain of $M_{1}$.

Hence:

* gain is $g_{m1}\times$ impedance at output,
* impedance at output is boosted by cascode,
* Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $\approx 1+g_{m1}R_{X}$
with $R_{X}$ small, bandwidth is much larger than simple
common source.

### DC operation

Let DC bias current be $I_{D}$.

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}=I_{D}$$

$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$

For $M_{1}$ sat:

$$V_{X}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{ov1}$$

For $M_{2}$ sat:

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{b1}-V_{X}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$$

$V_{TH2}>V_{TH0}$ due to body effect.

Combined, to keep both saturated:

$$V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{GS2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out,min}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$

This is the beauty of cascode: minimum output is sum
of overdrives.

Maximum output is set by $I_{1}$ staying in saturation.
For PMOS $I_{1}$:

$$V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-|V_{ovp}|$$

So usable swing:

$$V_{ov1}+V_{ov2} \le V_{out}\le V_{DD}-|V_{ovp}|$$

Note: the DC value of $V_{out}$ is ill defined.
It is a high-$Z$ node fed by two nominally equal DC
currents: the cascode and $I_{1}$. Any mismatch drives
$V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ or to triode. In practice the
stage cannot be open-loop biased; it needs feedback /
following stage to define $V_{out}$.

### Low frequency small signal

Gate $M_{2}$ AC ground. Source $M_{1}$ AC ground.
$v_{gs1}=v_{in}$.

Let $r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$, $r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$.

#### Impedance looking down from output

Turn off $v_{in}$, apply $v_{x}$ at $V_{out}$, measure $i_{x}$.

$M_{1}$ presents $r_{o1}$ from node $X$ to ground.

$M_{2}$ is a common-gate with source degeneration $R_{S}=r_{o1}$
and body effect.

KCL gives:

$$i_{x}=g_{m2}(-v_{S})+g_{mb2}(-v_{S})+g_{ds2}(v_{x}-v_{S})$$
$$i_{x}=v_{S}/r_{o1}$$

Hence:

$$R_{down}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]r_{o1}$$

$$R_{down}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}$$

$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}$$

This is $\approx g_{m}r_{o}$ times larger than $r_{o1}$ alone.

Total output resistance:

$$R_{out}=R_{down}\parallel R_{I1}$$

If $I_{1}$ ideal, $R_{out}=R_{down}$. If $I_{1}$ is
simple PMOS, $R_{I1}=r_{op}\ll R_{down}$ and
$R_{out}\approx r_{op}$.

#### Voltage gain

With $v_{in}$ applied, let $v_{S}$ be small signal at $X$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{S}$$
$$i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{S}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{S})$$

KCL $X$: $i_{d2}=i_{d1}$
KCL out, open: $i_{d2}+v_{out}/R_{I1}=0$

Solving, the Norton short circuit current into a shorted
output is:

$$I_{sc}=-g_{m1}v_{in}\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\approx -g_{m1}v_{in}$$

Then $v_{out}=I_{sc}R_{out}$:

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}R_{out}\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

Explicitly:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left\{\left[r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}\right]\parallel R_{I1}\right\}$$

Special cases:

* Ideal load, no body: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)\approx -(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$
Intrinsic gain squared.
* Finite PMOS load $R_{I1}=r_{op}$: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}(r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\parallel r_{op})\approx -g_{m1}r_{op}$ if $r_{op}$ dominates. Cascode does not increase low frequency gain much but still helps bandwidth.
* PMOS cascode load $R_{I1}\approx (g_{mp}+g_{mbp})r_{op}^{2}$: both sides $\sim g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$, $R_{out}\approx \tfrac12 g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$, very high gain.

Input resistance:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

at low frequency.

#### Voltage at cascode node

$$ \frac{v_{X}}{v_{in}}\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -1 $$

Thus $V_{DS1}$ hardly moves - cascode shielding. Gain from gate to $X$ is small.

Impedance looking into source of $M_{2}$:

$$R_{X}=\frac{R_{I1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

for moderate $R_{I1}$. In parallel with $r_{o1}$.

### High frequency intuition

Low frequency dominant pole at output:

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$

$$C_{out}\approx C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}+C_{I1}+C_{L}$$

$R_{out}$ large, so dominant.

Non-dominant pole at $X$:

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{C_{X}}$$

$$C_{X}\approx C_{DB1}+C_{SB2}+C_{GS2}+C_{GD1}(1-A_{v1}^{-1})$$

Since $R_{X}$ is $\sim 1/g_{m}$, this pole is much higher than in a non-cascode stage. Miller effect of $C_{gd1}$ is only $(1+g_{m1}R_{X})\approx 2$, not $(1+g_{m1}R_{out})$.

Hence cascode achieves high gain and wide bandwidth simultaneously.

In summary: high-gain, high-output-impedance inverting amplifier with $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$, $R_{in}=\infty$, $R_{out}$ boosted to $\sim g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a single ended cascode with active load.

* $M_{1}$ : input common-source, source grounded.
* $M_{2}$ : common-gate cascode device, gate at AC ground $V_{b1}$.
* $I_{1}$ : DC load current from $V_{DD}$. AC impedance $R_{P}$.

$r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}$ . The current flows downward:
$I_{D2}=I_{D1}=I_{1}$ in DC steady state.

Bulk of an n-well NMOS is normally the p-sub = GND.
$M_{1}$: $V_{SB1}=0$, no back gate.
$M_{2}$: $V_{SB2}=V_{X}>0$,

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x}\;, \quad v_{bs2}=-v_{x}$$

unless M2 is put in its own well tied to $X$. Keep
$g_{mb2}$ in formulas. Put $g_{mb2}=0$ if no body effect.

### 1. DC bias

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in,DC}>V_{TH1}$$
$$I_{D1}=\frac12 \mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}V_{ov1}^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS1})$$
$$V_{X}=V_{DS1}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$$

For saturation:

$$V_{X}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{ov1}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov2}$$

Hence

$$V_{out,min}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$
$$V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{GS2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}$$

for minimum headroom. Above:

$$V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-V_{SDsat,I1}$$

to keep the PMOS current source in saturation.

Note the DC problem: the output node sees two high
impedances to $V_{DD}$ and to GND. $V_{out,DC}$ is floating.
Any $\Delta I = I_{1}-I_{D1}$ is multiplied by the large $R_{out}$
and drives $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ or to triode.
In practice the bias needs feedback.

Large signal gain is very sharp. Linear input range is
$\sim V_{ov1}$.

### 2. Small signal low frequency

Model $M_{1}$: $g_{m1}v_{in}$ from $X$ to ground in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

Model $M_{2}$: gate grounded, source $X$, drain $V_{out}$:

drain to source current

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$
$$=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}$$

$I_{1}$ : $R_{P}$ to AC ground.

KCL $X$:

$$i_{d2}=g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}} \tag{1}$$

KCL $V_{out}$, open:

$$i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=0 \tag{2}$$

Hence from (1)-(2)

$$ -\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}} $$

#### Output resistance

Set $v_{in}=0$, drive $v_{out}=v_{t}$, measure $i_{t}$.
$M_{1}$ is $r_{o1}$ from $X$ to ground.

From above with $v_{in}=0$:

$$\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{t}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}$$

$$v_{t}=v_{x}\left[1+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]$$

The current supplied by the test source into $M_{2}$ drain
is $v_{x}/r_{o1}$. So impedance looking into $M_{2}$ drain is:

$$R_{casc}=\frac{v_{t}}{v_{x}/r_{o1}}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$R_{out}=R_{casc}\parallel R_{P}$$

i.e. the standard CG with source degeneration $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{casc}\approx \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]r_{o1}$$

This is $(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$ times larger than a simple
common source $r_{o1}$. $M_{2}$ shields $M_{1}$ drain from $v_{out}$.

#### Voltage gain

From (2):

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=0$$

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o2}}+\frac1{R_{P}}\right)=v_{x}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)$$

Let $A=1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$, $G=A/r_{o2}$.
Using $v_{x}=-r_{o1}(v_{out}/R_{P}+g_{m1}v_{in})$:

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}= -\frac{g_{m1}r_{o1}R_{P}A}{R_{P}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

with $r_{o2}+r_{o1}A=R_{casc}$. In other words

$$A_{v}=-g_{m1}R_{out}\,\frac{r_{o1}A}{r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

$$\frac{r_{o1}A}{r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}A}}\approx 1$$

because $A\approx g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$. Hence to very good
approximation

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

The cascode passes the $M_{1}$ signal current almost
entirely to the load. The effective $G_{m}\approx g_{m1}$.

Special cases:

* Ideal load $R_{P}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}A,\quad A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}A$$
$$=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]$$

Neglect body:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\approx -(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$$

if devices matched.

* Realistic single PMOS load $R_{P}=r_{o3}\sim r_{o1,2}$:

$$R_{casc}\gg r_{o3}\;\Rightarrow\; R_{out}\approx r_{o3}$$
$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o3}$$

i.e. cascoding the input alone does not raise the gain
much if the load is not cascoded. To get $(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$
gain you need cascode load as well – telescopic cascode.

Input resistance low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

### 3. What the cascode buys

Voltage at intermediate node $X$:

$$A_{x}=\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{R_{P}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

If $R_{P}\sim r_{o}$:

$$A_{x}\approx -g_{m1}\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{A}\approx -1\;{\rm to}\;-{\rm few}$$

versus $-g_{m1}R_{out}$ for a simple CS. Hence:

* Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $1-A_{x}$, small.
  Input capacitance $\approx C_{gs1}+(1-A_{x})C_{gd1}$
  is much reduced. Input pole pushed out.
* Reverse isolation improved, stage almost unilateral.
* Output impedance greatly increased.
* Drain of $M_{1}$ sees only small swing, suppressing
  $\lambda$-effect on $M_{1}$ and improving current-mirror accuracy.

Cost is headroom $V_{ov2}$, an extra non-dominant pole at $X$,
and bias complexity.

Frequency estimate: dominant pole at output

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$
$$C_{out}\approx C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{db,I1}+C_{gd,I1}+C_{L}$$

Pole at $X$:

$$C_{X}\approx C_{db1}+C_{gd1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gb2}$$
$$R_{X}\approx \left[\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\right]\parallel r_{o1}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{1}{R_{X}C_{X}}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{C_{X}}$$

Much higher than $\omega_{p,out}$ because $R_{X}$ is low.
That is why the cascode has wider bandwidth than a CS
with the same gain.

answer.text:
Yes. It is the textbook NMOS cascode with
resistive load.

* $M_{1}$ : gate = $V_{in}$, source = GND, drain = to $M_{2}$.
  That is a common-source input device.

* $M_{2}$ : gate = $V_{b1}$ AC ground, source = to $M_{1}$ drain,

current. Signal current generated by $M_{1}$ is fed
into the source of $M_{2}$ and taken out of the drain
of $M_{2}$ into $R_{D}$.

CS + CG with the same current = cascode.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a single common-source / common-emitter the Miller effect is large because there is large inverting gain across the same capacitor that connects input to output.

A cascode breaks that connection: it gets large gain overall, but small gain across the input device.

Recall Miller's theorem: an impedance $Z$ connected between input and output of a stage with voltage gain $A_v = v_o/v_i$ looks like:

$$ Z_{in} = \frac{Z}{1-A_v} \quad , \quad Z_{out} = \frac{Z}{1-1/A_v} $$

to ground.

For a MOSFET the culprit is $C_{gd}$, for a BJT $C_\mu$ between base and collector. Physically, if gate goes up by $v_i$ and drain goes down by $|A_v|v_i$, the voltage across $C_{gd}$ changes by $(1+|A_v|)v_i$. The input source has to supply $(1+|A_v|)$ times more charge than for $C_{gd}$ to ground.

For a simple common-source with load $R_D'$:

$$ A_v = -g_m R_D' $$

large, e.g. -20 to -100. So at the input:

$$ C_{in} \approx C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1-A_v) = C_{gs} + (1+g_m R_D')C_{gd} $$

$(1+g_m R_D')C_{gd}$ can be 10s-100s of fF, and with the source resistance $R_{sig}$ it creates a low input pole:

$$ f_H \approx \frac{1}{2\pi R_{sig} C_{in}} $$

This is bandwidth killer.

### Cascode: CS driving CG

A cascode is:

```
M1: common-source input device
M2: common-gate device stacked on top, gate at AC ground
```

Total voltage gain is still $-g_{m1} R_{out}$, even larger than before because $R_{out} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1} || R_D$ is very large.

But Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ depends only on the *local* gain from gate1 to drain1, not the overall gain to the output.

Drain1, call it node X, does not see $R_D$. It sees the impedance looking into the source of a common-gate stage with gate grounded:

$$ R_X \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} || r_{o1} || r_{o2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} $$

very low. So the voltage gain of M1 alone is:

$$ A_{v1} = \frac{v_X}{v_{g1}} = -g_{m1} R_X \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1 $$

if devices are similar.

Therefore for $C_{gd1}$:

$$ C_{in} \approx C_{gs1} + C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) \approx C_{gs1} + 2 C_{gd1} $$

instead of $C_{gs1} + (1+g_m R_D')C_{gd1}$.

Intuitively: M2 holds the drain of M1 almost constant. M1 converts $v_{in}$ to current, M2 passes that current to $R_D$ to make large voltage swing at the output. Since the two plates of $C_{gd1}$ don't swing in opposite large directions anymore, little extra current is needed to charge it.

The same for BJT: Q1's collector sees $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, so its gain is $\sim -1$, and $C_{\mu 1}$ is multiplied by $\sim 2$ instead of $(1+g_m R_C')$.

### Why doesn't M2 add Miller?

M2 is common-gate / common-base. Its gate/base is AC ground.

Its $C_{gd2}$ / $C_{\mu 2}$ goes between output and AC ground, not between output and signal input. So it is just a capacitive load on the output, no Miller multiplication to the input.

Its $C_{gs2}$ / $C_{\pi 2}$ goes between node X and AC ground, just load on the intermediate node.

Feedthrough from output to input now has to go through $C_{gd2}$ to node X, then $C_{gd1}$ to input, and node X is shunted to ground by the low $1/g_{m2}$ impedance. Reverse isolation is therefore much improved. The amplifier is almost unilateral.

### Cost: intermediate pole

We added node X with capacitance:

$$ C_X \approx C_{db1}+C_{sb2}+C_{gs2}+ (1+1/|A_{v1}|)C_{gd1} \approx ... $$

But the resistance is $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, so the pole

$$ f_{pX} \approx \frac{g_{m2}}{2\pi C_X} $$

is at very high frequency, typically non-dominant. The dominant input and output poles are pushed way out.

In short: cascode keeps high overall $g_m R_{out}$ but puts almost all of the voltage swing across the common-gate device, which has no Miller effect, and almost none across the input device.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The main explanation is correct: the low-impedance node at M1’s drain makes its local gain about −1, so Cgd1 is multiplied by roughly 2 rather than by the full stage gain. However, the answer later overstates this by describing that node as nearly fixed and the input-device swing as almost absent; it also has a secondary inconsistency about Cgd2 feedthrough.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is feedback through the transistor's own capacitance from output back to input.

In a common-emitter / common-source the $C_{\mu}$ / $C_{gd}$ capacitor bridges input to output:

```
                Cmu
        base o--||--o collector
```

Let the voltage gain from base to collector be

$$ K = V_c / V_b = A_v \approx -g_m R_C $$

The voltage *across* the capacitor is not $V_b$, it is

$$ V_b - V_c = V_b(1 - A_v) $$

So for the same $V_b$, $(1-A_v)$ times more AC current is forced through $C_{\mu}$ than if the other end were grounded. By Miller's theorem the capacitor looks, from the input, like a capacitor to ground of:

$$ C_{in,Miller} = C_{\mu}(1 - A_v) \approx C_{\mu}(1+g_m R_C) $$

$$ C_{out,Miller} = C_{\mu}(1-1/A_v) \approx C_{\mu} $$

If $A_v = -100$ and $C_{\mu}=2pF$, the input sees $\sim 200pF$. Driven by source resistance $R_{sig}$, that creates a low-pass dominant pole:

$$f_H \approx \frac{1}{2\pi R_{sig} [C_{\pi}+C_{\mu}(1+g_mR_C)]}$$

That is why a high-gain single stage is slow.

A cascode separates current gain and voltage gain:

```
                 RC
                  |
Vin -> Q1 CE -> Q2 CB -> Vout
     base in   base AC gnd
```

Q1 is common-emitter, Q2 is common-base. In MOS: CS + CG. They carry the same signal current, the overall transconductance is still $\approx g_{m1}$ and the overall gain is still $\approx -g_{m1}R_C$.

But they do NOT share the same voltage gain.

1. Q1 sees almost no voltage gain

Q1's collector load is not $R_C$, it is the input impedance looking into the emitter of a common-base stage:

$$ R_{in2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$$

very low, $\sim 1/g_m$.

So the voltage gain of Q1 *alone* is:

$$ A_{v1} = \frac{v_{c1}}{v_{b1}} \approx -g_{m1} R_{in2} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} $$

If the two devices are biased at the same current, $g_{m1}=g_{m2}$ and

$$ A_{v1} \approx -1 $$

Intuitively, Q2 holds Q1's collector almost still. Q1's collector moves up only a little when its base moves down.

Therefore the Miller multiplication for Q1's $C_{\mu1}$ is:

$$ C_{in1} \approx C_{\mu1}(1 - A_{v1}) \approx 2 C_{\mu1} $$

not $101 C_{\mu1}$. In our example, 4pF instead of 202pF, independent of $R_C$. The voltage swing happens elsewhere.

2. Q2 has no Miller effect

Q2 is common-base: its base is AC ground. Its $C_{\mu2}$ goes from collector - output - to AC ground, not from output to input.

In hybrid-pi terms:
- $C_{\mu2}$ : collector to grounded base = grounded output cap
- $C_{\pi2}$ : emitter to grounded base = grounded cap on the intermediate node

There is no capacitor bridging its input, the emitter, to its output, the collector. Its voltage gain, $\approx +g_{m2}R_C$, does not Miller-multiply back to Q1.

In other words, the device that has voltage gain has no input-output capacitor, and the device that has an input-output capacitor has no voltage gain.

The price is a new intermediate node: collector1 / emitter2. Its capacitance to ground is $\approx C_{\mu1}+C_{\pi2}+C_{cs}$ etc., but its resistance to ground is $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, very small, so its pole

$$ f_{pX} \approx \frac{g_{m2}}{2\pi C_X} $$

is very high frequency, usually non-dominant.

Result: input pole is pushed far out, reverse feedthrough is greatly reduced, the stage is much more unilateral and stable, while still getting the full gain $-g_{m1}R_C$ and even higher output resistance.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and the roughly −1 gain across the input transistor’s Cgd, yielding about 2× Miller multiplication rather than multiplication by the full-stage gain. Phrases like “almost no voltage gain” slightly overstate the effect, but the answer’s quantitative explanation is correct.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a common-emitter / common-source the trouble is the
capacitor directly bridging input to output: $C_{\mu}$, $C_{bc}$,
$C_{gd}$.

By the Miller theorem, an impedance $Z_f$ bridging
an amplifier of voltage gain $A_v = v_o/v_i$ looks like

$$ \frac{Z_f}{1-A_v} \;\; \text{to ground at the input} $$
$$ \frac{Z_f}{1-1/A_v} \;\; \text{to ground at the output} $$

For a capacitor:

$$C_{in,Miller} = C_f (1-A_v)$$
$$C_{out,Miller} = C_f (1-1/A_v)$$

For an inverting stage $A_v = -g_m R_L$, large and negative:

$$C_{in} \approx C_{\pi} + (1+g_m R_L)C_{\mu}$$

i.e. you have to charge $C_{\mu}$ with $v_i - v_o \approx (1+|A_v|)v_i$, so it draws $(1+|A_v|)$ times more current from the source. With source resistance that makes a low-frequency dominant input pole. That is the Miller effect.

A cascode is:

```
       Rc
        |
      Q2 C  <- common-base / common-gate
Vbias - Q2 B AC ground
      Q2 E / Q1 C  <- intermediate node
Vin - Q1 B  <- common-emitter / common-source
      Q1 E
```

It has about the same overall $A_v \approx -g_m R_C$ as a single stage, but the gain is distributed in a way that kills the Miller multiplication.

1. **The lower device has voltage gain $\approx -1$.**
Q1 is a CE stage loaded not by $R_C$ but by the input impedance of a CB stage:

$$R_{in2} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}} \;\; \text{roughly}$$

for BJT: $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, for MOS: $\approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.

So:

$$A_{v1} = \frac{v_{c1}}{v_{in}} = -g_{m1}(R_{in2}\parallel r_{o1}) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

The Miller multiplication for $C_{\mu1}$ of Q1 is therefore:

$$C_{M1,in} = C_{\mu1}(1-A_{v1}) \approx 2C_{\mu1}$$

instead of $(1+g_m R_C)C_{\mu1}$ which might be $100\,C_{\mu1}$.

Physically, Q2 holds Q1's collector almost constant. There is very little voltage swing across $C_{bc1}$, so very little current is needed to charge it.

The output side of that Miller cap, $\approx C_{\mu1}$, lands on the intermediate node Q1C-Q2E. That node impedance is $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, very low, so its pole $1/2\pi R C$ is at very high frequency.

2. **The upper device has no Miller multiplication at all.**
Q2 is common-base. Its $C_{bc2}$ goes from collector - output to base - AC ground. Its $C_{be2}$ goes from emitter - intermediate node to base - AC ground.

Neither capacitor bridges input to output. They are just capacitances to ground. No $(1-A_v)$ factor.

Q2 is a current buffer with $\approx 1$ current gain. It takes the signal current of Q1 and drops it across $R_C$ to make the large voltage gain:

$$A_{v2} = \approx g_{m2}R_C$$

$$A_{v,total}=A_{v1}A_{v2} \approx -g_m R_C$$

In short: Miller multiplication depends on the gain *across the capacitor itself*, not on the overall circuit gain. The cascode gives the large output swing with a device that has no input-output capacitor, and gives the input device a load so small it has essentially no voltage gain to multiply.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the cascode’s low-impedance intermediate node and the lower device’s gain of about −1, giving a Miller factor of roughly 2 rather than the full-stage gain. However, it overstates the effect by saying the node is almost constant and there is essentially no voltage gain; the swing across the input device’s Cgd is not negligible.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a CMOS common-gate stage with active load.

* $M_{2}$ : NMOS amplifying device. Gate is ac ground
by $V_{b1}$, source is the input, drain is the output.
* $M_{1}$ : PMOS current source load. Source to $V_{DD}$,
gate ac ground by $V_{b2}$, drain to output.

Put $V_{b1},V_{b2}$ ac ground. Assume long channel,
both in saturation. The symbols show source tied
to body, so

* $M_{1}$ : $n$-well to $V_{DD}$, no back gate
* $M_{2}$ : $p$-well to source, no back gate

If $M_{2}$ is in common $p$-sub, replace $g_{m2}$ by
$g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ below. Include channel length
modulation:

$$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_{p}I_{D},\quad r_{o2}=1/\lambda_{n}I_{D}$$

### DC operation

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$$

$$I_{D2} = \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{2}
(V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}-V_{THN})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}(V_{out,DC}-V_{in,DC}))$$

$$I_{D1} = \frac12\mu_{p}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}
(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}(V_{DD}-V_{out,DC}))$$

This defines $V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}$ and
$V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}$ for a given $I_{D}$.
Like any current-source loaded stage, the
DC output voltage is poorly defined. The output
node sees two current sources in parallel, impedance
$r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$. Any mismatch in $I_{D1},I_{D2}$
drives $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ or to triode.
In practice bias must be stabilized by feedback.
Ideally assume matching gives desired $V_{out,DC}$.

Saturation headroom:

$M_{2}$ : $V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{THN}$

$$V_{out}-V_{in} \ge V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{THN}$$

$$V_{out,min}=V_{b1}-V_{THN}$$

$M_{1}$ : $V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$

$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|$$

$$V_{out,max}=V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$$

$M_{2}$ stays on for $V_{in}\le V_{b1}-V_{THN}$.

### Small signal low frequency

Gate of $M_{2}$ grounded, source $v_{in}$,
drain $v_{out}$:

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{in},\quad v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

drain-to-source current:

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+\frac{v_{ds2}}{r_{o2}}
=-g_{m2}v_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}$$

$M_{1}$ : source ac ground, gate ac ground,
drain $v_{out}$:

$$v_{gs1}=0,\quad v_{ds1}=v_{out}$$

$$i_{d1}= \frac{v_{ds1}}{r_{o1}}=\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}$$
from output node to $V_{DD}$.

KCL at output node, no external load. Both $i_{d1}$
and $i_{d2}$ leave the node:

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-g_{m2}v_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o1}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
= v_{in}\left(g_{m2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)$$

Hence non-inverting gain:

$$ A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

$$A_{v}=g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}
\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

Intuitively: $v_{in}\uparrow \to V_{GS2}\downarrow \to
I_{D2}\downarrow$. $M_{1}$ sources more than $M_{2}$
sinks, $v_{out}$ charges up. $M_{1}$ provides high
load impedance $\approx r_{o1}$ to get large gain.

### Input resistance

With $i_{in}$ into the source, KCL at input gives
$i_{in}=-i_{d2}$:

$$i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{in}-\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}$$

Using $v_{out}=A_{v}v_{in}$:

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}$$

This is the classic CG formula $R_{in}=(R_{D}+r_{o})/(1+g_{m}r_{o})$
with $R_{D}=r_{o1}$. For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$:

$$R_{in}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}}\left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right)$$

If $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$, $R_{in}\approx 2/g_{m2}$.
Ignoring CLM, $r_{o}\to\infty$, $R_{in}\to 1/g_{m2}$.

Low input $Z$, current-buffer behavior.

### Output resistance

Look into output with $v_{in}=0$. Source of $M_{2}$
grounded, gate grounded, so $v_{gs2}=0$ and
$M_{2}$ presents $r_{o2}$. In parallel with $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\quad \text{for }R_{S}=0$$

In general with source resistance $R_{S}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel\left[r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_{S}\right]$$

High output $Z$.

In summary: non-inverting voltage amplifier,
low $R_{in}$, high $R_{out}$, gain $\approx g_{m}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$.
No Miller effect, gate grounded, good high frequency
current to voltage conversion.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, places the input at M2’s source, and gives the non-inverting gain, low input resistance, and equivalent gain expression required for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a single stage **common-gate with active load**.

* $M_2$ : NMOS input device. Gate is DC biased at
$V_{b1}$, i.e. ac ground. Source is input. Drain is
output.
* $M_1$ : PMOS load. Source to $V_{DD}$, gate DC
biased at $V_{b2}$, i.e. ac ground. Drain to output.

$M_1$ is a DC current source biasing $M_2$.
AC-wise it is just an impedance to ac ground.

Let

$$V_{in}=V_{IN,DC}+v_{in}\;,\;\;V_{out}=V_{OUT,DC}+v_{out}$$

$V_{b1},V_{b2},V_{DD}$ are ac ground.

DC current path is:

$$V_{DD}\to M_1 \to M_2 \to V_{in} \;source\to GND$$

So the input source must sink the DC bias current $I_D$.
In practice the input is AC coupled and the bias is
provided separately. For small signal we assume an
ideal $v_{in}$ source with $R_S=0$ and open output.

### DC

Same current flows in both devices: $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D$.

$M_1$ PMOS, bulk tied to source, $V_{SB1}=0$, no
back-bias:

$$V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}>|V_{THP}|$$
$$I_D =\tfrac12 \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_1(V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|)^2
(1+\lambda_p V_{SD1})$$

$M_2$ NMOS, bulk = p-sub = GND. Source is at
$V_{IN,DC}>0$, so $V_{SB2}=V_{IN,DC}>0$.
There is body effect:

$$V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{IN,DC} > V_{THN2}$$
$$V_{THN2}=V_{TH0}+\gamma
\left(\sqrt{2\phi_f+V_{IN,DC}}-\sqrt{2\phi_f}\right)$$
$$I_D =\tfrac12 \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2
(V_{GS2}-V_{THN2})^2(1+\lambda_n V_{DS2})$$

Saturation requires:

$M_2$: $V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{THN2}$, i.e.

$$V_{out}-V_{IN,DC}\ge V_{b1}-V_{IN,DC}-V_{THN2}$$

$$V_{OUT,DC}\ge V_{b1}-V_{THN2}$$

$M_1$: $V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$, i.e.

$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|$$

$$V_{OUT,DC}\le V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$$

Output DC is the high impedance intersection of
$I_{D1}(V_{SD1})$ and $I_{D2}(V_{DS2})$ and is
sensitive to mismatch.

Small signal parameters: $g_{m1},r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$,
$g_{mb1}=0$, and $g_{m2},g_{mb2},r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$.

### Small-signal model

Gate of $M_2$ grounded, bulk grounded:
$$v_{gs2}=-v_{in}\;,\;\;v_{bs2}=-v_{in}\;,\;\;
v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

NMOS drain current into drain:
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$M_1$: source, gate, bulk ac ground,
drain at $v_{out}$. With $v_{sg1}=0$, $v_{sb1}=0$,
$v_{sd1}=-v_{out}$:

current source to drain $i_{sd1}=g_{ds1}v_{sd1}$,
i.e. current into drain:
$$i_{d1}= -i_{sd1}=g_{ds1}v_{out}$$

In other words $M_1$ looks like $r_{o1}$ to ground.

KCL at output, open load:
$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$$

### Voltage gain

$$g_{ds1}v_{out}+g_{m2}(-v_{in})+g_{mb2}(-v_{in})
+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})=0$$

$$(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})v_{out}
=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{in}$$

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$A_v=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$
$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

Positive, i.e. non-inverting. Intuitively:
$v_{in}\uparrow \to V_{GS2}\downarrow \to I_{D2}\downarrow
\to$ less pull-down $\to v_{out}\uparrow$ toward $V_{DD}$.

If $\gamma=0$:
$$A_v\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

Note channel-length modulation must be kept,
otherwise with two ideal current sources in series
the gain is infinite.

### Input resistance

Put test $v_x$ at source, drain loaded by $r_{o1}$.
$v_d$ at drain:

$$(g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})v_d=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_x$$

Current into source $i_x = -i_{d2}$ because
$i_g=i_b=0$:

$$i_x=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_x-g_{ds2}v_d$$

$$i_x=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})
\frac{g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}v_x$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_x}{i_x}
=\frac{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})}$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}$$
$$\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right)$$

This is low but larger than $1/(g_m+g_{mb})$.
With ideal load $r_{o1}\to\infty$, $R_{in}\to\infty$
because the AC drain current is forced to zero,
hence AC source current is zero.

If $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$, $R_{in}\approx 2/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.

With finite load $R_L$ to ground, replace $r_{o1}$
by $r_{o1}\parallel R_L$.

### Output resistance

With $v_{in}=0$, i.e. source of $M_2$ grounded,
$v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=0$. Looking into drain of $M_2$
is just $r_{o2}$. In parallel with $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

Large, typical of active load. With source
resistance $R_S$:
$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel [r_{o2}+(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2})R_S]$.

In summary: common-gate current-buffer / voltage
amplifier, non-inverting, large voltage gain $\sim g_m r_o/2$,
low input impedance, high output impedance, no
Miller effect, good for high frequency and for
e.g. 50-ohm RF input matching.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, source-side input, bias voltages, non-inverting gain, and low input resistance. Its gain and input-resistance expressions are equivalent to the golden formulas, including body effect and finite output resistance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a CMOS common-gate stage with active load.

* $M_{2}$ : NMOS amplifying device.
Source is the input, gate is ac ground, drain is the
output.
* $M_{1}$ : PMOS current source load.
Source to $V_{DD}$, gate dc biased, drain to output.

$V_{b1}, V_{b2}$ are dc bias, ac ground. $V_{b2}$
sets the dc current. $V_{b1}$ sets the $V_{GS2}$.

Body:
$M_1$ is in its own n-well, body to source to $V_{DD}$.
No backgate.
$M_2$ is NMOS, body is p-sub to GND. Source is
at signal level. Hence $V_{SB2}\ne 0$ and
backgate exists.

Assume both in saturation.

DC:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D$$

$$I_{D1} = \frac12 \mu_p C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
 (V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|)^2(1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{out}))$$

$$I_{D2} = \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
 (V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{THN})^2(1+\lambda_n(V_{out}-V_{in}))$$

For saturation:

$M_2$ ON: $V_{GS2}>V_{THN}$ :
$$V_{in} < V_{b1}-V_{THN}$$

$M_2$ saturated: $V_{DS2} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{THN}$ :
$$V_{out}-V_{in} \ge V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{THN}$$
i.e.
$$V_{out} \ge V_{b1}-V_{THN}$$

$M_1$ saturated: $V_{SD1} \ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$ :
$$V_{DD}-V_{out} \ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|$$
i.e.
$$V_{out} \le V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$$

Hence proper output dc level must satisfy

$$V_{b1}-V_{THN} \le V_{out} \le V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$$

This is a high gain node, bias sensitive.

Small signal: put $V_{DD}, V_{b1}, V_{b2}$ to ac
ground.

$M_1$ : $v_{gs1}=0$, $v_{bs1}=0$. It is just
$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$ from output to ground.

$M_2$ : common gate:
$$v_{g2}=0,\; v_{s2}=v_{in},\; v_{d2}=v_{out}$$
$$v_{gs2}= -v_{in}$$
$$v_{bs2}= -v_{in}$$
$$v_{ds2}= v_{out}-v_{in}$$

The drain small signal current into the drain is
$$i_d = g_m v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

So
$$i_{d1} = g_{ds1}v_{out} = \frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}$$
$$i_{d2} = -g_{m2}v_{in}-g_{mb2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})$$

KCL at output: currents into output node from
the two drains are $-i_{d1}-i_{d2}=0$, i.e.

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$$

Hence:
$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}
+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

Voltage gain:

$$A_v =\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} =
\frac{(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

i.e.

$$A_v \approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) >0$$

Non-inverting. This is a $g_m R_D$ stage where
$R_D = r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ is very large. Neglecting body:

$$A_v \approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

With $\lambda=0$, $r_o\to\infty$, gain $\to\infty$.
In practice limited by parallel output resistance.

Input resistance: current into source is $i_{in}=i_{s2}=-i_{d2}$.
But $i_{d2}=-i_{d1}$, so $i_{in}=i_{d1}=v_{out}/r_{o1}$.

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}=\frac{r_{o1}}{A_v}$$

$$R_{in}= \frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}$$

This is the classic CG result with $R_D=r_{o1}$:
$$R_{in} = \frac{1+R_D/r_{o2}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/r_{o2}}$$

Intuition: with ideal load $r_{o1}\to\infty$,
the dc current is fixed, ac current cannot flow,
$R_{in}\to\infty$. With finite $r_{o1}$, $R_{in}$
is on the order of $1/(g_m+g_{mb})$ to a few times
that. If $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o$,
$R_{in}\approx 2/(g_m+g_{mb})$.

If driven from source resistance $R_S$, the divider
$R_{in}/(R_{in}+R_S)$ applies.

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$. Then $M_2$ has
source and gate grounded, $v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=0$.
It is just $r_{o2}$ to ground, in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

In summary: current buffer, positive high gain,
high output impedance, relatively low - but load
boosted - input impedance, no Miller multiplication,
good for high frequency.

answer.text:
The small–signal circuit is 2nd order.

Put $s$ for the Laplace variable.

* $M_{1}$ : common source. Gate $=A$, drain $=B$,
source ac gnd.
* $M_{2}$ : common gate load. Gate ac gnd,
source ac gnd, drain $=B$.

Let $A$ be the $M_{1}$ gate node after $R_{S}$,
$B$ be the common-drain node $=V_{out}$.

* $A$ to gnd : $C_{GS}$
* $A$ to $B$ : $C_{GD}$
* $B$ to gnd : $C_{DB}$ from $M_{1}$
* $B$ to ac gnd : $C_{DB2}$ from $M_{2}$
* $B$ to ac gnd : $C_{GD2}$ from $M_{2}$, since the
$M_{2}$ gate is ac gnd

i.e. to ac ground

$$C_{L}=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}$$

in parallel at the output.

KCL at $A$ and KCL at $B$, with $g_{m1},r_{o1},r_{o2}$,
are two first order equations in $V_{A},V_{out}$:

$$ \frac{V_{A}-V_{in}}{R_{S}}+sC_{GS}V_{A}+sC_{GD}(V_{A}-V_{out})=0 $$

$$g_{m1}V_{A}+G_{o}V_{out}+sC_{GD}(V_{out}-V_{A})+sC_{L}V_{out}=0$$

Eliminating $V_{A}$ gives $V_{out}/V_{in}$ with a
quadratic denominator.

There is one capacitive node at the input,
one capacitive node at the output. The 3 caps
at the output are in parallel, and $C_{GS},C_{GD},C_{L}$
form one capacitive loop, $3-1=2$ independent states.

One input pole, one output pole.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two poles from the gate and output nodes, and assigns the capacitors to the appropriate nodes; the coupling capacitor does not create a third independent state.

answer.text:
The small signal circuit has 2 capacitive nodes.

Put all supplies to ac ground.

* $M_{1}$ : common source, source grounded
* $M_{2}$ : active load, source to $V_{DD}$ ac ground,
  gate to dc bias ac ground. $v_{sg2}=0$.

Capacitances, in small signal :

* gate of $M_{1}$, node $X$:
  $C_{GS}$ $X$ to ground
* gate-drain of $M_{1}$:
  $C_{GD}$ $X$ to $Y$ , $Y$ = output, drain of $M_{1}$
* drain of $M_{1}$ :
  $C_{DB}$ $Y$ to ground
* gate-drain of $M_{2}$ :
  gate ac ground, drain $Y$ : $C_{GD2}$ $Y$ to ground
* drain-bulk of $M_{2}$ :
  bulk $V_{DD}$ ac ground, drain $Y$ : $C_{DB2}$ $Y$ to ground

i.e. to first order

* $X$ - gnd : $C_{GS}$
* $X$ - $Y$ : $C_{GD}$
* $Y$ - gnd : $C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}$

KCL $X$, $Y$ with $R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ :

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_x-V_{in}}{R_S}+sC_{GS}V_x+sC_{GD}(V_x-V_y)&=0\\
g_{m1}V_x+\frac{V_y}{R_{out}}+s(C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2})V_y
+sC_{GD}(V_y-V_x)&=0
\end{aligned}$$

The determinant is quadratic in $s$, with a 
$s^{2}$ term $\approx (C_{GS}+C_{GD})C_{tot'}-C_{GD}^{2}\ne 0$.
3 capacitors with one $C$-only loop $X$-gnd-$Y$-$X$ gives
2 independent state variables.

2nd order denominator, i.e. 2 poles, plus 1 zero
from $C_{GD}$ feedforward.

answer.text:
The small signal circuit has 2 capacitive nodes.

$M_{2}$ has $v_{gs2}=0$. It is $r_{o2}$
to ac ground.

At the output node $Y$:

* $C_{DB}$ : $Y$ to gnd
* $C_{DB2}$ : $Y$ to ac gnd
* $C_{GD2}$ : $Y$ to ac gnd

are in parallel. Put

$$ C_{L}= C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2} $$

At the input node $X$:

* $C_{GS}$ : $X$ to gnd
* $C_{GD}$ : $X$ to $Y$

Put $R_{D}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$. KCL at $X,Y$:

$$\frac{V_{x}-V_{in}}{R_{S}}+V_{x}sC_{GS}
+(V_{x}-V_{y})sC_{GD}=0$$

$$ \frac{V_{y}}{R_{D}}+V_{y}sC_{L}
+(V_{y}-V_{x})sC_{GD}+g_{m1}V_{x}=0$$

i.e.

$$\left[\frac1{R_{S}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD})\right]V_{x}
-sC_{GD}V_{y}= \frac{V_{in}}{R_{S}} $$

$$(g_{m1}-sC_{GD})V_{x}
+\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+s(C_{L}+C_{GD})\right]V_{y}=0$$

The determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}
D(s)=&\left[\frac1{R_{S}}+s(C_{GS}+C_{GD})\right]
\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+s(C_{L}+C_{GD})\right] \\
&+sC_{GD}(g_{m1}-sC_{GD})
\end{aligned}$$

$$D(s)=\frac1{R_{S}R_{D}}+s\left[\frac{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}{R_{D}}
+\frac{C_{L}+C_{GD}}{R_{S}}+g_{m1}C_{GD}\right]$$
$$+s^{2}\left[(C_{GS}+C_{GD})(C_{L}+C_{GD})-C_{GD}^{2}\right]$$

2nd order in $s$. There are 2 capacitive state
variables $V_{x},V_{y}$, one Miller input pole
and one output pole, and one RHP zero from
$C_{GD}$.
