answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a resistor loaded common source stage.
Both devices are NMOS. The lower device $M_{1}$
has source grounded. The upper device $M_{2}$
has drain at the output, source at the drain
of $M_{1}$. Both gates are driven by $V_{in}$.

```
VDD - RD - D2 - S2 - D1 - S1 - GND
             G2=G1=Vin
```

Body is strapped to source for both devices,
so no back gate. Put

$$k_{1}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1},\quad
  k_{2}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$$

Large signal, square law, neglect $\lambda$ for bias:

$V_{in}<V_{TH}$ : $M_{1},M_{2}$ off,
$$V_{out}=V_{DD}$$
$I_{D}=0$. Node $X=S_{2}=D_{1}$ is floating.

For $V_{in}>V_{TH}$ current flows in $R_{D}$-$M_{2}$-$M_{1}$.
Let

$$V_{ov}=V_{GS1}-V_{TH}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{X}=V_{DS1}$$
$$V_{GS2}-V_{TH}=V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH}=V_{ov}-V_{X}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}$$

$M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ carry the same $I_{D}$.
They cannot both be saturated with the same
size. Indeed $V_{GS2}<V_{GS1}$. This is the
self-cascode or composite transistor.

The consistent high gain bias is

* $M_{1}$ in triode
* $M_{2}$ in saturation

Then

$$I_{D1}=k_{1}\left(V_{ov}V_{X}-\frac{V_{X}^{2}}{2}\right)$$
$$I_{D2}=\frac{k_{2}}{2}(V_{ov}-V_{X})^{2}$$

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$ gives:

$$(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{X}^{2}-2(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{ov}V_{X}
+k_{2}V_{ov}^{2}=0$$

i.e.

$$V_{X}=V_{ov}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}}\right]$$

Put

$$\alpha =\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}}$$

$$V_{X}=V_{ov}(1-\alpha)<V_{ov}$$
$$V_{GS2}-V_{TH}= \alpha V_{ov}$$

$$I_{D}=\frac{k_{2}}{2}\alpha^{2}V_{ov}^{2}
      =\frac12\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}V_{ov}^{2}$$

i.e. the composite behaves as one transistor
with

$$k_{eq}=\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}$$
$$I_{D}=\frac{k_{eq}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^{2}$$

and

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}
 =V_{DD}-\frac{k_{eq}R_{D}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^{2}$$

This is valid while $M_{2}$ stays saturated:

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge \alpha V_{ov}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$$

same headroom as a single transistor. This is
the virtue of the self-cascode.

When $V_{out}$ falls to $V_{in}-V_{TH}$, $M_{2}$
enters triode. Then both devices are in triode
and $V_{out}$ is low:

$$V_{out}\approx V_{DD}\frac{R_{on1}+R_{on2}}
{R_{D}+R_{on1}+R_{on2}}$$

For $R_{D}\gg R_{on}$, $V_{OL}\approx 0$.
The circuit is therefore an inverter.

Small signal in the high gain region: $M_{1}$
triode, $M_{2}$ sat.

$$g_{m1}=k_{1}V_{X},\quad
  g_{ds1}=k_{1}(V_{ov}-V_{X})$$
$$g_{m2}=k_{2}(V_{ov}-V_{X}),\quad
  g_{ds2}=\lambda_{2}I_{D}$$
$g_{ds1}$ contains $1/R_{on}$ plus $\lambda$.
$g_{mb}=0$.

Small signal model: $v_{g1}=v_{g2}=v_{in}$,
$v_{s1}=0$, $v_{d1}=v_{s2}=v_{x}$,
$v_{d2}=v_{out}$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

KCL at $X$ and at output:

$$i_{d1}=i_{d2}$$
$$i_{d2}+v_{out}/R_{D}=0$$

Eliminating $v_{x}$,

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$
$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}
-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{x}$$

Hence

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\,R_{D}\,
\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}
{(g_{m2}+g_{ds2}+g_{ds1})+R_{D}g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

This is exact, no body effect.

Output resistance with $v_{in}=0$ is $R_{D}$
in parallel with the impedance looking into $M_{2}$,
whose source is degenerated by $r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$:

$$R_{core}=r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1}$$
$$=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$
$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{core}$$

$r_{o1}$ is the triode $1/g_{ds1}$, small.
With $g_{ds1}=k_{1}\alpha V_{ov}$,
$g_{m2}=k_{2}\alpha V_{ov}$,

$$R_{core}\approx r_{o2}\left(1+\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}\right)$$

i.e. $1$ to $3\times r_{o2}$. In practice
$R_{D}\ll R_{core}$ and $R_{out}\approx R_{D}$.

Input resistance at low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

If $r_{o1},r_{o2}\gg R_{D}$, $g_{ds2}\approx 0$:

$$A_{v}\approx -R_{D}\,g_{m2}\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}
{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}$$

But for triode $g_{m1}+g_{ds1}=k_{1}V_{ov}$.
Hence

$$A_{v0}=-k_{eq}V_{ov}R_{D}$$

which is $dV_{out}/dV_{in}$ from large signal.
Effective transconductance is

$$G_{m}=k_{eq}V_{ov}$$

In general

$$A_{v}=-G_{m}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{core})$$

Intuition: $M_{2}$ cascodes $M_{1}$ but its gate
moves with the input, so it does not increase
$G_{m}$. The pair acts as a single longer device
with $k_{eq}$, saturation voltage $\approx V_{ov}$,
somewhat larger $r_{o}$ than $r_{o2}$ alone,
at the price of somewhat smaller $G_{m}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS pair, with M1 in triode and M2 saturated, and derives an equivalent transconductance factor that corresponds to the summed effective channel length for equal widths.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is two $N$-channel devices in series with
a resistive load.

* $M_{1}$ : source to ground, drain to $X$, gate to $V_{in}$
* $M_{2}$ : source to $X$, drain to $V_{out}$, gate to $V_{in}$
* $R_{D}$ : $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$

Put the bulks to the sources so there is no back gate.
Put

$$g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}\qquad g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$$

$V_{in}$ is both the small signal input and the d.c. bias.
In series

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D}}$$

Large signal, in saturation, ignoring $\lambda$,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D} &\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}
(V_{in}-V_{TH1})^{2} \\
&\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{2}
(V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH2})^{2}
\end{aligned}$$

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$$

For $V_{in}<V_{TH1}$, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.
For $V_{in}$ large, current grows and $V_{out}$ falls.
It is an inverting amplifier.

Saturation conditions are

$$\begin{align*}
M_{1}:&\quad V_{X} \ge V_{in}-V_{TH1} \\
M_{2}:&\quad V_{out}-V_{X} \ge V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH2}\\
      &\quad V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{TH2}
\end{align*}$$

and $M_{2}$ on needs

$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X}>V_{TH2}$$

i.e. $V_{X}<V_{in}-V_{TH2}$.

Hence $M_{1}$ saturated and $M_{2}$ on needs

$$V_{in}-V_{TH1} \le V_{X} < V_{in}-V_{TH2}$$

which requires $V_{TH2}<V_{TH1}$.
With identical enhancement thresholds both devices
cannot be saturated at the same time. In practice
with identical $V_{TH}$ the operating point with
both on is

* $M_{1}$ in triode
* $M_{2}$ in saturation, as long as $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH}$

until $V_{out}$ falls enough to put $M_{2}$ in triode.

For small signal we can still use $g_{m1},r_{o1},
g_{m2},r_{o2}$, evaluated in the actual region.
Formally assume saturation for the formulas.

Small signal: $v_{g1}=v_{g2}=v_{in}$,
$v_{s1}=0$, $v_{d1}=v_{s2}=v_{x}$,
$v_{d2}=v_{out}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{d1} &= g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1} \\
&= g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x} \\
i_{d2} &= g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2} \\
&= g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})
\end{aligned}$$

KCL at $X$ : no other branch, so

$$i_{d2}=i_{d1}$$

KCL at output: current in $R_{D}$ is $-v_{out}/R_{D}$,
so

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}} = i_{d2}=i_{d1}$$

Hence

$$\begin{cases}
g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}+\dfrac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=0\\
g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})+\dfrac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=0
\end{cases}$$

Eliminating $v_{x}$,

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})}
{\dfrac{r_{o1}}{R_{D}}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})+g_{ds2}+\dfrac1{R_{D}}}$$

i.e.

$$ A_{v}= -R_{D}\,
\frac{g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
{R_{D}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}} $$

Output resistance with $v_{in}=0$ is the
resistance looking into $M_{2}$ drain with
$R_{S}=r_{o1}$ in its source, in parallel with $R_{D}$:

$$R_{out,2}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$ R_{o}=R_{D}\parallel R_{out,2} $$

This is exactly the cascode $R_{o}$. $R_{in}=\infty$
at low frequency.

If $\lambda=0$, $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$,

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in},\quad i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})$$

$$v_{x}=v_{in}\left(1-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right)$$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{D}$$

$M_{2}$ drops out to first order.

In general for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$,

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{out,2})$$

with $R_{out,2}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$.

Indeed the conventional cascode with $M_{2}$ gate
ac ground has

$$A_{v,cas}=-g_{m1}(R_{D}\parallel R_{out,2})$$

Our numerator is $g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}+
g_{m1}r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$ versus
$g_{m1}R_{out,2}=g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m1}r_{o2}+
g_{m1}r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$.
They are identical if $g_{m1}=g_{m2}$.

In that matched case, to first order $v_{x}=0$.
The intermediate node is ac ground, like a cascode,
but obtained by driving the cascode gate.

The price:

* bias is difficult, see above, $I_{D}$ is very
sensitive to $V_{in}$;
* input capacitance is $C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}$ plus Miller.
$C_{gd1}$ sees gain $v_{x}/v_{in}\approx 1-g_{m1}/g_{m2}$,
$\approx 0$ if matched, but $C_{gd2}$ connects
output directly back to input and sees the full
$1-A_{v}\approx 1+g_{m1}R_{D}$ Miller multiplication.
A conventional cascode with $M_{2}$ gate ac ground
has no such Miller effect.

With body effect for $M_{2}$ in common p-sub,
$g_{mb2}\ne 0$, replace $g_{m2}$ by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$
in $R_{out,2}$ and in the denominator terms:

$$R_{out,2}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$A_{v}=-R_{D}\frac{g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}+
g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})}
{R_{D}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}r_{o2}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})}$$

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the series, common-gate topology and the actual M1-triode/M2-saturation operating regions. But it then analyzes the stack as a true cascode and claims a gm·ro-multiplied output resistance, missing the key longer-effective-channel behavior.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is two $n$MOS in series with a common gate
drive and a resistive load. Put

$$V_X = V_{D1}=V_{S2}$$

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\; V_{DS1}=V_X$$
$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X,\; V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_X$$

$M_{1}$ source is grounded, no back bias.
$M_{2}$ body is grounded, source is $>0$,
$$V_{TH2}\ge V_{TH1} .$$

### 1. $M_{1}$ cannot saturate

Suppose both devices are on with finite current.
For $M_{1}$ to saturate

$$V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}$$

i.e.

$$V_X \ge V_{in}-V_{TH1} .$$

Then

$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X \le V_{TH1}\le V_{TH2}$$

so $M_{2}$ is off. Contradiction.

Hence, if there is current:

* $M_{1}$ is in triode,
* $M_{2}$ can be in saturation or triode.

The stack behaves as one composite long device.
$M_{2}$ is the saturating device, $M_{1}$ is a
gate-driven source degeneration resistor.

For $V_{in}<V_{TH}$ : $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

For $V_{in}>V_{TH}$, $M_{1}$ pulls $V_X$ down,
$M_{2}$ turns on, current flows in $R_D$.

$M_{2}$ saturates when

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}-V_X \ge V_{in}-V_X-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH2} .$$

With small current $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$ this is
satisfied. As $V_{in}$ grows $V_{out}$ falls and
$M_{2}$ eventually goes triode.

### 2. Large signal, square law

Neglect $\lambda,\gamma$ for insight. Let
$k_{n1}=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1$, $k_{n2}$ similarly,
$V_{od}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$.

$M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ sat:

$$I_D = k_{n1}\left(V_{od}V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right)
      =\frac{k_{n2}}{2}(V_{od}-V_X)^2 .$$

This gives

$$(k_{n1}+k_{n2})V_X^2-2(k_{n1}+k_{n2})V_{od}V_X
   +k_{n2}V_{od}^2=0$$

$$V_X = V_{od}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{k_{n1}}{k_{n1}+k_{n2}}}\right]$$

independent of $V_{out}$. Then

$$I_D = \frac{k_{n,eq}}{2}V_{od}^2$$

where

$$\frac{1}{k_{n,eq}}=\frac1{k_{n1}}+\frac1{k_{n2}} .$$

I.e. $1/k$ adds, $L_{eq}=L_1+L_2$ for same $W$.
And

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_D\frac{k_{n,eq}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^2$$

as long as $V_{out}\ge V_{od}$. This is a normal
resistive-load inverter characteristic but with
reduced $k$.

E.g. identical devices: $k_{n1}=k_{n2}=k_n$,
$$V_X\approx 0.29\,V_{od},\quad I_D=\frac{k_n}{4}V_{od}^2.$$

The effective $g_m$:

$$g_{m,eq}=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{in}}
 =k_{n,eq}V_{od}=\sqrt{2k_{n,eq}I_D}.$$

For larger $V_{in}$, $V_{out}<V_{od}$, both triode,
$V_{out}\to 0$ as $\approx V_{DD}/[1+R_Dk_{n,eq}V_{od}]$.

Body effect on $M_{2}$ makes $V_{TH2}(V_X)>V_{TH1}$
and reduces current further.

### 3. Small signal

Low frequency, $R_{in}=\infty$.

Let $v_x$ be small signal at $X$.
$$v_{gs1}=v_{in}$$
$$v_{gs2}=v_{in}-v_x,\; v_{bs2}=-v_x$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_x$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_x)-g_{mb2}v_x+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_x)$$

Series: $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$, and at output
$$v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_D.$$

Note $g_{m1},g_{ds1}$ are triode values:
$$g_{m1}=k_{n1}V_X,\quad g_{ds1}=k_{n1}(V_{od}-V_X).$$
$g_{m2},g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$ are saturation values.
$g_{mb2}$ is $M_{2}$ back-gate.

From $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$:

$$v_x\big[g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}\big]
 =(g_{m2}-g_{m1})v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}.$$

Let $D=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}$. Then

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_x.$$

Eliminating $v_x$,

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
 -R_D\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{mb2}+g_{m1}g_{ds2}+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}
 {D+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}R_D}. \tag{1}$$

### 4. Output resistance

Set $v_{in}=0$, drive output with $v_t$.
Same $D$ gives $v_x=g_{ds2}v_t/D$,
$i_t=v_t/R_D+g_{ds1}v_x$, so

$$R_{out}=R_D\parallel\frac{D}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

$$\frac{D}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}
 =r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}.$$

Formally the same as a cascode, but $r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$
is the small triode resistance of $M_{1}$. Hence

$$R_o\approx r_{o2}\left[1+\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{g_{ds1}}\right]$$

only a few times $r_{o2}$, not $(gm\,r_o)r_o$.

Then (1) is $A_v=-G_mR_{out}$ with

$$G_m=\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}{D}.$$

If $r_{o2}\to\infty$:

$$A_v\approx -R_D\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}
 {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}}.$$

Neglect $g_{mb2}$:

$$A_v\approx -R_D\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}.$$

Using the square-law triode/sat expressions this is
exactly $-k_{n,eq}V_{od}R_D=-g_{m,eq}R_D$.

Intuition: $M_{2}$ is a common-source device
degenerated by $R_{s1}\approx 1/g_{ds1}$ of $M_{1}$:
$$A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m2}R_D}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}}$$
plus a small boost from driving $M_{1}$ gate,
$g_{m1}$.

If both devices were wrongly assumed saturated
with $g_{ds}\to0$, (1) gives $A_v=-g_{m1}R_D$.
In reality $M_{1}$ is triode, $g_{ds1}$ is large,
and effective $g_m$ is $k_{n,eq}V_{od}$, i.e.
smaller than a single device. E.g. identical
devices give half the $g_m$ for the same $V_{od}$.

In short: the circuit is a common-source stage
made from a composite $L_1+L_2$ transistor.
It has lower $G_m$, somewhat higher $R_o$,
lower voltage gain with resistive load, larger
saturation $V_{od}$ and smaller swing than a
simple CS, but emulates a long-channel device.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate-driven series NMOS stack, with M1 in triode and M2 able to saturate, and derives the key result that the stack behaves approximately like a device with effective length L1 + L2. Its output-resistance discussion is also consistent with the modest increase expected for this structure.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS long tailed pair with resistive load
on one side only.

```
M1 : Vin to gate, drain to VDD ac gnd, source to tail
M2 : Vb DC to gate ac gnd, drain to RD to VDD, source to tail
tail : I1 to gnd, sources common
```

Assume M1,M2 matched, in saturation, body to source,
no back gate. $V_{G1DC}\approx V_{G2DC}=V_{CM}$.
Let

$$g_{m1},g_{m2},r_{o1},r_{o2}, R_{EE}$$

be the small signal parameters of M1,M2 and the
output impedance of $I_{1}$. Ideal $R_{EE}\to\infty$.

M1 is a common drain, M2 a common gate. The
follower drives the common gate.

$V_{in}\uparrow \rightarrow V_{S1}\uparrow \rightarrow
V_{S2}\uparrow \rightarrow V_{GS2}\downarrow \rightarrow
I_{D2}\downarrow \rightarrow V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D \uparrow$.

It is non-inverting. It is a differential to
single-ended converter.

### DC bias

Neglect $\lambda$ mismatch. At balance:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1/2$$

$$V_{OV}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}{\mu_nC_{ox}W/L}}
 =\sqrt{\frac{I_1}{\mu_nC_{ox}W/L}}$$

$$V_S = V_{CM}-V_{GS}=V_{CM}-V_{th}-V_{OV}$$

$$V_{D1}=V_{DD}$$
$$V_{D2}=V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D$$

Strictly $V_{DS1}\ne V_{DS2}$ gives systematic
offset due to $\lambda$.

Saturation requires

$$V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}$$

$$V_{DD}-V_S \ge V_{OV} \;\;{\rm for\; M1}$$
$$V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D-V_S \ge V_{OV} \;\;{\rm for\; M2}$$

i.e.

$$V_{CM}\le V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D+V_{th}$$

Lower $V_{CM}$ is limited by the headroom of $I_1$:

$$V_S \ge V_{I1,min}$$
$$V_{CM}\ge V_{th}+V_{OV}+V_{I1,min}$$

### Small signal

Put $v_{g1}=v_{in}$, $v_{g2}=0$, $v_{d1}=0$,
$v_{s1}=v_{s2}=v_x$, $v_{d2}=v_{out}$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x)+g_{ds1}(-v_x)$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}(-v_x)+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_x)$$

KCL at output:

$$i_{d2}+v_{out}/R_D=0$$

KCL at common source :

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=v_x/R_{EE}$$

From the first:

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}=-g_{m2}v_x+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_x)$$

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_D}+g_{ds2}\right)=(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_x$$

$$v_{out}=K v_x,\quad
K=\frac{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds2}+1/R_D}
=(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})(R_D\parallel r_{o2})$$

This is the common-gate gain from source to drain.

Then

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x)-g_{ds1}v_x-\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}
=\frac{v_x}{R_{EE}}$$

$$g_{m1}v_{in}=v_x\left(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+\frac1{R_{EE}}\right)
+\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}$$

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{Kg_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+1/R_{EE}+K/R_D}$$

Ideal case $r_{o}\to\infty$, $R_{EE}\to\infty$:

$$K=g_{m2}R_D$$

$$v_x=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in}$$

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$$

$$A_v = \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}g_{m2}R_D$$

For matched $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$:

$$v_x\approx \frac12 v_{in}$$

$$A_v \approx +\frac{g_mR_D}{2}$$

i.e. half the common-source gain, positive.

Intuitively the tail forces $i_{d1}=-i_{d2}$ so
the source moves half way to satisfy both
$V_{GS}$.

With $r_o$ : let $g_m1=g_m2=g_m$,
$r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o$, $R_{EE}\to\infty$,

$$A_v = g_m\frac{R_D r_o}{R_D+2r_o}
 =\frac{g_m}{2}\,(R_D\parallel 2r_o)$$

$\approx g_mR_D/2$ if $R_D\ll r_o$.
This is slightly larger than the symmetric
loaded case $(g_m/2)(R_D\parallel r_o)$ because
$M_1$ has no $R_D$ and $r_{o1}$ does not load
the output.

Finite $R_{EE}$ reduces gain:

$$A_v\approx g_{m2}R_D\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}+1/R_{EE}}$$
to first order.

Decomposition: $v_{id}=v_{in}$, $v_{icm}=v_{in}/2$.
Differential gain to drain 2 is $+g_mR_D/2$,
common-mode gain $\approx -R_D/2R_{EE}$.
High $R_{EE}$ gives high CMRR.

### Terminal impedances

Gate input:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

at low frequency.

Output: look into drain of M2 whose source sees
to ground

$$R_{S2}=R_{EE}\parallel\frac1{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

Impedance looking into a common-gate drain
with source resistance $R_S$ is

$$R_{d}=r_o+(1+g_mr_o)R_S$$

Hence

$$R_{out2}=r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_{S2}$$

$$R_{out}=R_D\parallel R_{out2}$$

Matched, $R_{EE}$ large:

$$R_{S2}\approx 1/g_m$$
$$R_{out2}\approx 2r_o$$
$$R_{out}\approx R_D\parallel 2r_o\approx R_D$$

### Summary

* single-ended differential pair, output on
quiet side.
* non-inverting gain $\approx +g_mR_D/2$.
* high $R_{in}$, $R_{out}\approx R_D$.
* no Miller effect: M1 is follower, M2 is
common-gate. Dominant pole at output,
$1/R_{out}C_{out}$, high pole at common
source $\approx (g_{m1}+g_{m2})/C_x$.
Wideband.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled pair as a source follower driving a common-gate stage, with the output at M2’s drain. It gives the correct non-inverting gain, approximately +gmRD/2 for matched devices.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS source coupled pair with
a resistive load on one side. $M_{1}=M_{2}$,
$V_{b}$ is dc, ac ground. $I_{1}$ is the tail
bias, nominally ideal.

$M_{1}$ drain is ac ground at $V_{DD}$.
$M_{2}$ drain is loaded by $R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$.
Gates are $V_{in}$ and ac ground.

In the dc balance $V_{in,DC}=V_{b}$,
$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$$
$$V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}{2}R_{D}$$

Let $k=\frac12 \mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L$. In saturation

$$I_{D1}=k(V_{GS1}-V_{TH})^{2},\; I_{D2}=k(V_{GS2}-V_{TH})^{2}$$
$$I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{1}$$

Overdrive at balance:

$$V_{ov}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{1}/2}{k}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{\mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L}}$$
$$V_{GS1,0}=V_{GS2,0}=V_{TH}+V_{ov}$$
$$V_{S1,0}=V_{S2,0}=V_{in,DC}-V_{TH}-V_{ov}$$

For saturation need $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TH}$.
For $M_{2}$:

$$V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}{2}R_{D}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$$

i.e. upper limit on input common mode.
Lower limit is set by headroom of $I_{1}$:
$V_{S}\ge V_{I1,min}$.

Large signal, with $V_{id}=V_{in}-V_{b}=V_{GS1}-V_{GS2}$,
in saturation:

$$I_{D1,2}=\frac{I_{1}}{2}\pm \frac{kV_{id}}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{k}-V_{id}^{2}},\quad |V_{id}|\le\sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{k}}$$

Beyond, all current steers to one side.
Hence

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D2}$$

goes from $V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$.
When $V_{in}$ goes up, $I_{D1}$ goes up,
$I_{D2}$ must go down because $I_{D1}+I_{D2}\approx I_{1}$,
drop on $R_{D}$ goes down, $V_{out}$ goes up.
Non-inverting.

Small signal: put $v_{g1}=v_{in}$, $v_{g2}=0$,
$v_{d1}=0$, $v_{d2}=v_{out}$, $v_{s1}=v_{s2}=v_{x}$.
Tail impedance $R_{SS}$. $g_{m1},g_{m2},g_{ds1},g_{ds2}$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds1}(-v_{x})$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}(-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

KCL output: $v_{out}/R_{D}+i_{d2}=0$
KCL tail: $i_{d1}+i_{d2}=v_{x}/R_{SS}$

i.e. $i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_{D}$ and

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

$$v_{x}=v_{out}\frac{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{R_{D}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})}$$

$$g_{m1}v_{in}=(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+1/R_{SS})v_{x}+v_{out}/R_{D}$$

Hence

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}R_{D}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})}
{(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})+(1+g_{ds2}R_{D})
(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+1/R_{SS})}$$

Matched, $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$, $g_{ds1}=g_{ds2}=g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$,
$R_{SS}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2+g_{ds}R_{D}}
 =\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2+R_{D}/r_{o}}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}\approx +\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2}$$

Intuition: $v_{in}=V_{c}+V_{d}/2$, $0=V_{c}-V_{d}/2$
with $V_{c}=v_{in}/2$, $V_{d}=v_{in}$. Ideal tail
rejects common mode. Differential half circuit gives
$v_{x}\approx v_{in}/2$, $v_{gs2}=-v_{in}/2$,
$\Delta I_{D2}=-g_{m}v_{in}/2$, $v_{out}=+g_{m}R_{D}v_{in}/2$.

It is a source follower $M_{1}$ driving a common gate
$M_{2}$. Impedance looking into $M_{2}$ source is
$\approx 1/g_{m}$, so follower divides by 2.

Input resistance at gate is infinite at low frequency.

Output resistance: look into $M_{2}$ drain with $v_{in}=0$.
Impedance looking into $M_{1}$ source with gate and drain
grounded is $1/(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})$. This in parallel with
$R_{SS}$ degenerates $M_{2}$ common gate:

$$R_{o2}=r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})
\left[R_{SS}\parallel \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\right]$$

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o2}$$

For $R_{SS}\to\infty$, matched:

$$R_{o2}=2r_{o},\quad R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\approx R_{D}$$

Finite $R_{SS}$ gives common-mode gain. For $v_{in}=v_{b}=v_{ic}$,
half circuit with $2R_{SS}$ degeneration:

$$A_{cm}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+2(g_{m}+g_{ds})R_{SS}+g_{ds}R_{D}}
\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{2R_{SS}}$$

so CMRR $\approx g_{m}R_{SS}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled pair and the equivalent source-follower M1 driving common-gate M2, with the correct non-inverting signal path and gain sign.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a source coupled NMOS differential pair
with a passive load, used single-ended.

* $M_{1}-M_{2}$ matched, tail $I_{1}$
* $M_{1}$ drain to AC ground $V_{DD}$
* $M_{2}$ drain to $R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$, output there
* $M_{1}$ gate = signal $V_{in}$
* $M_{2}$ gate = DC bias $V_{b}$, AC ground

I.e. a differential input $V_{id}=V_{in}-V_{b}$ to
single-ended output. With ideal tail it rejects
common mode. It can be seen as a common-drain
$M_{1}$ driving a common-gate $M_{2}$.

Assume 3-terminal devices, body to source, no backgate.
Assume in saturation.

### DC point

Put for balance DC $V_{in,CM}=V_{b}=V_{CM}$.

Then
$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_{1}}{2}=I_{D} $$

$$ V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}R_{D}}{2} $$

Common source node DC:
$$ V_{S}=V_{CM}-V_{GS1} $$

$M_{1}$: $V_{D1}=V_{DD}$
$$ V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{S}=V_{DD}-V_{CM}+V_{GS1} $$
saturated if $V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH}$, i.e.
$$ V_{CM}\le V_{DD}+V_{TH} $$ normally true.

$M_{2}$: $V_{D2}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$
$$ V_{DS2}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}-V_{S} $$
saturated if
$$ V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}-V_{CM}\ge -V_{TH} $$
$$ V_{CM}\le V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}+V_{TH} $$
This sets the upper input common-mode limit.
The lower limit is set by keeping the tail source
in saturation:
$$ V_{S}=V_{CM}-V_{GS}\ge V_{tail,min} $$

Large signal, the pair steers $I_{1}$ from one side
to the other. Linear for $|V_{in}-V_{b}|$ on order
of overdrive. Beyond, all $I_{1}$ goes in $M_{1}$,
$V_{out}=V_{DD}$, or all in $M_{2}$,
$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$.

### Small signal differential mode

Put $v_{b}=0$, $v_{in}$ small. Let $v_{s}$ be the
common source node, $v_{out}$ the output.

To first order $\lambda=0$:
$$ i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{s}) $$
$$ i_{d2}=g_{m2}(0-v_{s}) $$

Tail ideal AC open: the sum of source currents
leaving into the node must be zero:
$$ i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0 $$
since source current $=$ drain current.

Hence
$$ g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{s})-g_{m2}v_{s}=0 $$
$$ v_{s}=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in} $$

For matched $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$:
$$ v_{s}=\frac{v_{in}}{2} $$

The source follows half the input. The current
in $M_{2}$:
$$ i_{d2}=-g_{m}v_{s}=-\frac{g_{m}}{2}v_{in} $$

This flows in $R_{D}$. At output node,
$$ v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_{D} $$

Hence
$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=+\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2} $$

Non-inverting. This is half the gain of a simple
common source with same $R_{D}$, because only
half the $v_{in}$ appears as $V_{GS}$ and the
differential pair has effective $G_{m}=g_{m}/2$.

In half-circuit language: a single ended drive
$V_{id}$ = common-mode $V_{id}/2$ + differential
$\pm V_{id}/2$. Ideal tail kills the common mode.
Each half to its own drain has $-g_{m}R_{D}$.
So $M_{2}$ side with $-V_{id}/2$ gives
$+g_{m}R_{D}V_{id}/2$.

With channel length modulation, $g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$:

$$ i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}-(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{s} $$
$$ i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})v_{s}+g_{ds2}v_{out} $$

$$ i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0 $$
$$ i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_{D} $$

Solving,
$$ A_{v}=\frac{g_{m1}}{\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}(g_{ds2}+1/R_{D})-g_{ds2}} $$

Matched $g_{m},g_{ds}$:
$$ A_{v}=\frac{g_{m}}{g_{ds}+2/R_{D}} = g_{m}\left(r_{o}\parallel \frac{R_{D}}{2}\right) $$

If $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$, $\approx g_{m}R_{D}/2$.

### Impedances

Gate input:
$$ R_{in}=\infty $$

Output: $R_{D}$ in parallel with impedance looking
into $M_{2}$ drain. With $v_{in}=0$, $M_{1}$ presents
$\approx 1/g_{m1}$ at the source. The common-gate
with source resistance $R_{S}\approx 1/g_{m1}$ has
$$ R_{o2}\approx r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_{S}\approx 2r_{o} $$
matched. So
$$ R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o2}\approx R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\approx R_{D} $$

### Common mode

With finite tail impedance $R_{SS}$, common-mode
gain, $v_{in}=v_{b}=v_{cm}$:

By symmetry $i_{d1}=i_{d2}=i_{d}$, $v_{s}=2i_{d}R_{SS}$,
$$ i_{d}\approx \frac{g_{m}}{1+2g_{m}R_{SS}}v_{cm} $$
$$ A_{cm}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{cm}}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+2g_{m}R_{SS}}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{2R_{SS}} $$

Ideal $R_{SS}\to\infty$, $A_{cm}\to 0$.

Differential single-ended gain $A_{d}=g_{m}R_{D}/2$,
$$ {\rm CMRR}=\left|\frac{A_{d}}{A_{cm}}\right|\approx g_{m}R_{SS} $$

That is the merit of the differential pair: large
tail impedance gives large common-mode rejection.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair, equivalently a source follower driving a common-gate stage, and gives the correct non-inverting gain.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
This is a source follower $M_{1}$ with active load
$M_{2}$ driven from a source of resistance $R_{S}$.

For $Z_{out}$ put $V_{in}=0$ and drive the output
with $V_{x}$. Let $V_{g}$ be the small signal gate
voltage of $M_{1}$.

At low frequency $C_{gs1}$ is open, the gate is
a.c. ground through $R_{S}$,

$$V_{gs} = -V_{x}$$

A rise in $V_{x}$ cuts $V_{gs}$ and cuts the
$M_{1}$ drain current by $g_{m}V_{x}$. $M_{1}$
fights the change in $V_{x}$ strongly:

$$Z_{out0}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

At a.c. $C_{gs1}$ couples source to gate.
Neglect for the moment all capacitances except
$C_{gs1}$. KCL at the gate :

$$\frac{V_{g}}{R_{S}}+(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs1}=0$$
ignoring $C_{gd1}$ to a.c. ground, i.e.

$$ V_{g}=V_{x}\frac{sC_{gs}R_{S}}{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}} \tag{1}$$

This is a high-pass. Well below the gate pole
$1/R_{S}C_{gs}$,

$$V_{g}\approx sC_{gs}R_{S}V_{x}$$

i.e. in time domain

$$v_{g}\approx R_{S}C_{gs}\frac{dv_{x}}{dt}$$

A change in output voltage is differentiated
and fed to the gate.

The small signal current that $M_{1}$ pulls
from the output node is to first order

$$i_{d}\approx g_{m}(v_{g}-v_{x})$$

i.e. the current leaving the $V_{x}$ node to
enter the transistor is $-i_{d}$. Up to sign:

$$i_{out}\approx g_{m}(v_{x}-v_{g})
      \approx g_{m}v_{x}-g_{m}R_{S}C_{gs}\frac{dv_{x}}{dt} \tag{2}$$

This is the key. For a rising $v_{x}$, $C_{gs}$
pushes current into $R_{S}$, $v_{g}$ goes
positive, $|v_{gs}|$ is reduced, $M_{1}$ reacts
less. The faster $v_{x}$ rises, the less current
$M_{1}$ absorbs.

Compare to a resistor $R$ in series with an
inductor $L$:

$$v = Ri+L\frac{di}{dt}$$

i.e. to first order in $L$,

$$i \approx \frac{v}{R}-\frac{L}{R^{2}}\frac{dv}{dt} \tag{3}$$

Eq.2 is of the same form with

$$R=\frac{1}{g_{m}},\qquad \frac{L}{R^{2}} = g_{m}R_{S}C_{gs}$$

i.e.

$$L\approx \frac{R_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}}$$

In phasors, $I_{out}=(g_{m}-j\omega g_{m}R_{S}C_{gs})V_{x}$.
The admittance has a $-j\omega$ term. Negative
imaginary admittance is inductive: $Y_{L}=1/j\omega L=-j/\omega L$.
Current lags voltage.

In $s$-domain, including $r_{o}$, $g_{mb}$,
$sC_{gs}$ itself, from (1) :

$$I_{x} = V_{x}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+1/r_{o}+sC_{gs})
        -V_{g}(g_{m}+sC_{gs})$$

giving with $C_{gd}=0$:

$$Z_{1}(s)=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=
\frac{1+sR_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+1/r_{o}+sC_{gs}}$$

i.e. apart from body effect and $r_{o}$,

$$Z_{1} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}\,
\frac{1+s/\omega_{z}}{1+s/\omega_{p}}$$

$$\omega_{z}=\frac{1}{R_{S}C_{gs}},\quad
\omega_{p}=\frac{g_{m}}{C_{gs}}$$

At DC, $Z_{1}=1/g_{m}$. At $s\to\infty$,
$C_{gs}$ shorts gate to source and
$Z_{1}\to R_{S}$.

If $R_{S}>1/g_{m}$, $\omega_{z}<\omega_{p}$.
Between zero and pole $|Z|$ rises at $\sim$
20 dB/dec and $\angle Z>0$. Indeed for
$\omega_{z}\ll\omega\ll\omega_{p}$:

$$Z_{1}\approx \frac{1+sR_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}}
 =\frac{1}{g_{m}}+s\frac{R_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}}$$

a resistor $1/g_{m}$ in series with an inductor
$R_{S}C_{gs}/g_{m}$.

In feedback terms, the source follower is
series-shunt feedback. Open loop output resistance
$\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ is divided by
$1+Loop(s)$. Loop gain $\approx g_{m}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$
rolls off with the gate pole $1/R_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})$.
Falling loop gain with frequency means rising
closed loop $Z_{out}$ with frequency - inductive.

The full $Z_{out}$ is $Z_{1}$ in parallel with
the load of $M_{2}$, $r_{o2}\parallel s(C_{db2}+C_{gd2})$,
plus $C_{sb1},C_{db1}$ etc. At very high
frequency $C_{gd1}$ shorts the gate and the
load capacitances dominate and $Z_{out}$ becomes
capacitive again. Over a mid band it is inductive
and can resonate with load capacitance to give
peaking.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source follower and explains that Zout transitions from about 1/gm at low frequency to RS at high frequency as Cgs couples the gate to the source. It gives the correct RS > 1/gm condition for the rising, inductive region; minor approximation issues do not change this conclusion.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
This is a common drain stage with active load.
$M_1$ is the follower, $M_2$ is ac ground gated,
i.e. essentially $r_{o2}$ to ground. $M_1$
drain is ac ground.

For $Z_{out}$ put $V_{in}=0$, $V_b=0$ and
drive the output with $V_x$ and measure $I_x$.
Neglect for intuition all high frequency effects
except $C_{gs1}$ of the follower. The body
effect and $r_o$ only change values.

At low frequency $C_{gs}$ is open. The gate of
$M_1$ is tied to ac ground through $R_S$.
A change $V_x$ at the source appears
entirely as $V_{gs}$:

$$ v_{gs} = V_g-V_x \approx -V_x $$

The transistor responds with a drain current,
drain to source,

$$i_{ds} \approx g_m v_{gs} \approx -g_m V_x$$

KCL at the source essentially requires the
test source to supply this difference,
$I_x \approx g_m V_x$, i.e.

$$ Z_{s1} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}$$

resistive. In full, $1/(g_m+g_{mb}+g_{ds1})
\parallel r_{o2}$.

At high frequency $C_{gs}$ can no longer be
ignored. It connects the output node, the
source, back to the gate, which goes to ground
through $R_S$. So $V_x$ is divided to the
gate.

KCL at the gate: the only paths are $R_S$ to
ground and $C_{gs}$ to the source:

$$ \frac{V_g}{R_S} + (V_g-V_x)sC_{gs}=0 $$

i.e.

$$ V_g = V_x \frac{R_S sC_{gs}}{1+R_S sC_{gs}} \tag{1}$$

At $\omega =0$, $V_g=0$. As $\omega$ grows,
$V_g$ follows $V_x$ more and more. That
means the effective $v_{gs}$ driving the
transistor falls with frequency:

$$ v_{gs}=V_g-V_x = -V_x\frac{1}{1+R_S sC_{gs}} $$

The transistor therefore supplies less and
less small-signal current for the same $V_x$.
Less current for same voltage means the
magnitude of the impedance grows with
frequency. That is inductive behavior.

Indeed, KCL at the source node. Let currents
$d\to s$ in the transistor and $g\to s$ in
$C_{gs}$ be positive into $s$:

$$ I_{ds}=g_m(V_g-V_x) $$
$$ I_{cgs}=(V_g-V_x)sC_{gs} $$

With $I_x$ injected into $s$,
$-I_{ds}-I_{cgs}-I_x=0$, i.e.

$$ I_x = -(g_m+sC_{gs})(V_g-V_x)
      =(g_m+sC_{gs})(V_x-V_g) $$

Using (1),

$$ I_x = (g_m+sC_{gs})V_x\frac{1}{1+R_S sC_{gs}} $$

$$ Z_{s1} = \frac{V_x}{I_x}= \frac{1+R_S sC_{gs}}{g_m+sC_{gs}} \tag{2}$$

$M_2$ is in parallel with this, essentially
$r_{o2}\parallel C_{db2},C_{gd2}$. It does not
change the form at moderate frequencies.

For frequencies where the transistor still
has gain, $|s|C_{gs}\ll g_m$, i.e.
$\omega \ll g_m/C_{gs}\approx \omega_T$,

$$ Z_{s1} \approx \frac{1+R_S sC_{gs}}{g_m}
       =\frac{1}{g_m}+s\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m} $$

This is a resistor $1/g_m$ in series with
an inductor

$$ L_{eq} \approx \frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m} $$

In full with $g_{mb},r_{o1}$:

$$ Z_{s1}\approx \frac{1}{g_m+g_{mb}+g_{ds1}}
 + s\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m+g_{mb}+g_{ds1}} $$

In time domain: $V_{gs}$ cannot change
instantaneously because the voltage across
$C_{gs}$ cannot. A step $\Delta V$ on $V_x$
is initially transferred entirely to $V_g$,
keeping $V_{gs}$ unchanged, so the transistor
change in current is initially zero. $C_{gs}$
then discharges through $R_S$ with $\tau=R_S
C_{gs}$, $V_g\to 0$, allowing $V_{gs}\to
-\Delta V$ and the transistor current to build
up gradually. Current lags voltage, like an
inductor.

Both $R_S$ and $C_{gs}$ are essential. If
$R_S=0$, $V_g\equiv 0$, (2) is
$1/(g_m+sC_{gs})$, i.e. $1/g_m \parallel
1/sC_{gs}$, capacitive.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the source follower, gives the correct simplified Zout expression, and explains the Cgs–RS gate-following mechanism and low-to-high impedance transition. Its approximate inductance drops a denominator contribution, but the core explanation meets the golden full-credit rule.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
This is a source follower with an active load.
For $Z_{out}$ put $V_{in}=0$. Look into the source
of $M_{1}$ with the gate tied to ac ground through $R_S$.

At low frequency ignore all caps. A $ \Delta V_{out} $
at the source with the gate grounded gives

$$\Delta V_{gs} = -\Delta V_{out}$$

The transistor changes its drain current by

$$\Delta I_d = g_m \Delta V_{gs} = -g_m \Delta V_{out}$$

i.e. flowing out of the source terminal into the
external node. To support $\Delta V_{out}$ the external
circuit must supply $\approx -\Delta I_d$, so

$$Z_{out, LF} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

with $g_{mb}$ added to $g_m$ if the body is grounded.

The inductance comes from $C_{gs1}$ and $R_S$.
$R_S$ must be non-zero.

Let $V_x$ be a test source at the output, $V_g$ the
gate voltage. Neglect for the essence $r_o$, body,
$C_{gd}$, $C_{db}$ etc. They are parallel $R$ and $C$ to
ground; they don't make the inductance.

The gate node is connected to ground through $R_S$
and to $V_x$ through $C_{gs}$. KCL at gate:

$$\frac{V_g}{R_S}+ (V_g-V_x)sC_{gs}=0$$

i.e.

$$\frac{V_g}{V_x}= \frac{R_S sC_{gs}}{1+R_S sC_{gs}}$$

$C_{gs}+R_S$ is a high-pass from output to gate.
For $\omega R_S C_{gs}\ll 1$,

$$V_g \approx V_x\, R_S sC_{gs}$$

The output variation is differentiated and fed
back to the gate.

Now KCL at the source. In small signal the
transistor branch carries $g_mV_{gs}$ from drain,
ac ground, to source, i.e. into the $V_x$ node,
$C_{gs}$ carries $(V_x-V_g)sC_{gs}$ out of the node
to the gate. With test current $I_x$ entering the
node:

$$I_x = (V_x-V_g)(g_m+sC_{gs})$$

$$V_x-V_g = V_x\frac{1}{1+R_S sC_{gs}}$$

so

$$Z_{out}= \frac{V_x}{I_x}= \frac{1+R_S sC_{gs}}{g_m+sC_{gs}}$$

For $sC_{gs}\ll g_m$, i.e. $\omega\ll g_m/C_{gs}=\omega_T$,

$$Z_{out}\approx \frac{1+R_S C_{gs}s}{g_m}
 =\frac1{g_m}+s\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m}$$

That is a resistor $1/g_m$ in series with an inductor

$$L \approx \frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m}$$

Physically, this is bootstrapping. A rise in $V_{out}$
couples through $C_{gs}$ to the gate. The coupling
current $\approx C_{gs}dV_{out}/dt$ must flow in $R_S$,
so it develops

$$V_g \approx R_S C_{gs}\frac{dV_{out}}{dt}$$

The gate rises, following the source. Hence the
effective $V_{gs}=V_g-V_{out}$ is smaller in magnitude
than $-V_{out}$. The transistor supplies less signal
opposing current. For a given $V_x$ you get less
$I_x$ as frequency rises. Rising $|Z|$ with frequency
is inductive.

In phasors: with $V_x$ as reference, the normal
resistive current $g_mV_x$ is in phase with $V_x$.
$V_g\approx j\omega R_SC_{gs}V_x$ leads by $90^{\circ}$.
Converted by $g_m$ and subtracted, $I_x\approx
g_mV_x-g_mV_g$ acquires a $-90^{\circ}$ quadrature
lagging component. Current lagging voltage is
inductive.

If $R_S=0$, $V_g=0$ always, $C_{gs}$ is just a
capacitive load to ground, no zero $1+R_S C_{gs}s$,
no $L$. The $R_S$ lets the fed-through voltage
build up. The $L$ is an active simulated inductance,
resonating with load capacitance to give peaking.

However, it omits the condition RS > 1/gm for inductive behavior and its low-frequency expansion drops a first-order denominator term, incorrectly implying any nonzero RS produces a positive inductance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a current in - voltage out amplifier
with shunt-shunt feedback. The feedback is positive.

$M_{1}$ is the forward common source:

gate $X$, drain $V_{out}$, $R_{D1}$ load.

$M_{2}$ is the feedback device:

it senses $V_{out}$ at its gate and returns a
current to node $X$ from its drain.

Sampling output voltage, mixing input current:
voltage-sampling, current-mixing, i.e. shunt-shunt.

Both stages are inverting, the loop is non-inverting.

### D.C.

$M_{1}$ gate draws no current, $M_{2}$ gate draws
no current, so

$$ I_{D2}=I_{in} $$
$$ V_{out}=V_{GS2} $$
$$ I_{D1}= \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} $$
$$ V_{X}=V_{GS1} $$

i.e.

$$I_{in}= \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}(V_{out}-V_{TH})^{2}
(1+\lambda_{n}V_{X})$$

$$\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}=
\frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}(V_{X}-V_{TH})^{2}
(1+\lambda_{n}V_{out})$$

$V_{SB}=0$ for both devices. For saturation

$$V_{X}\ge V_{out}-V_{TH2}\,,\quad V_{out}\ge V_{X}-V_{TH1}$$

### Small signal

Put $g_{m1},r_{o1}$ for $M_{1}$, $g_{m2},r_{o2}$
for $M_{2}$. Bodies to ground.

Node $X$ : $V_{x}$, node out : $V_{out}$.

$M_{1}$ : $g_{m1}V_{x}$ from $V_{out}$ to gnd in
parallel with $r_{o1}$ to gnd.

$M_{2}$ : $g_{m2}V_{out}$ from $V_{X}$ to gnd in
parallel with $r_{o2}$ to gnd.

$R_{D1}$ from $V_{out}$ to ac gnd.

KCL at $X$, $I_{in}$ injected:

$$ I_{in} = \frac{V_{x}}{r_{o2}} + g_{m2}V_{out} \tag{1}$$

KCL at output, no independent source:

$$ 0 = \frac{V_{out}}{R_{D1}} + \frac{V_{out}}{r_{o1}}
+ g_{m1}V_{x} \tag{2}$$

Hence the forward gain with loading

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{V_{x}} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})
= -A_{1} $$

Put in (1):

$$I_{in}=V_{x}\left[\frac1{r_{o2}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}
(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\right] $$

### Loop gain

Break the loop at the high impedance gate of $M_{1}$.
Inject $V_{t}$, follow around:

$$V_{out} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})V_{t}$$

$$V_{r}= -g_{m2}r_{o2}V_{out}$$

where $V_{r}$ is the returned voltage at $X$,
$I_{in}$ open. So

$$ L = \frac{V_{r}}{V_{t}} = +\,g_{m1}g_{m2}
(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2} >0 $$

Positive, i.e. positive feedback.

Indeed $V_{x}\uparrow \to V_{out}\downarrow \to$
less $M_{2}$ pull down $\to V_{x}\uparrow$.

Then (1)-(2) can be written

$$I_{in} = \frac{V_{x}}{r_{o2}}\,(1-L)$$

### Closed loop transimpedance

From (1)-(2)

$$ \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}} = \frac{r_{o2}}{1-L} $$

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})
\frac{r_{o2}}{1-L} $$

i.e.

$$ Z_{T}= \frac{-A_{1}r_{o2}}{1-L}
= \frac{L}{g_{m2}(L-1)} $$

Open loop, $g_{m2}=0$, $L=0$,
$Z_{T,open} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}$.
Closed loop is open loop divided by $1-L$.

This is $A/(1-L)$ for positive feedback.

### Terminal impedances

Input: already $V_{x}/I_{in}$ :

$$ R_{in} = \frac{r_{o2}}{1-L} $$

Output: set $I_{in}=0$, apply $V_{t}$ at output,
measure $I_{t}$.

$0 = V_{x}/r_{o2}+g_{m2}V_{t}$, so
$V_{x}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}V_{t}$.

$I_{t}=V_{t}/R_{D1}+V_{t}/r_{o1}+g_{m1}V_{x}$,
so

$$ I_{t}=V_{t}\left[\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}
-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right] $$

$$ R_{out} = \frac{R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}}{1-L} $$

Both open-loop resistances are divided by $1-L$.
Negative shunt feedback would divide by $1+L$.
Here positive feedback multiplies by $1/(1-L)$.

If $r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$:

$$L\approx g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}r_{o2}$$
$$Z_{T}\approx \frac{-g_{m1}R_{D1}r_{o2}}{1-L}$$
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{r_{o2}}{1-L}\,,\quad
R_{out}\approx \frac{R_{D1}}{1-L}$$

### Stability - amplifier vs latch

Characteristic equation is $1-L(s)=0$.
At low frequency $L>0$ real.

* $L<1$ : stable.

$$R_{in}>0,\;R_{out}>0,\;Z_{T}<0$$

magnitudes boosted over open loop by $1/(1-L)$.
This is a regenerative TIA. Poles satisfy,
neglecting feedthrough $C_{gd}$,

$$(1+s\tau_{x})(1+s\tau_{o})-L=0$$

with $\tau_{x}=r_{o2}C_{x}$,
$\tau_{o}=(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})C_{out}$.
$L\to 1^{-}$ pushes poles to lower frequency,
resistances increase, bandwidth shrinks.

* $L>1$ : $1-L<0$.

Small signal about the both-saturated bias:

$$R_{in}<0,\;R_{out}<0,\;Z_{T}>0$$

The bias is unstable, one closed-loop pole is in
RHP. The circuit regenerates away to a state where
one device is off or in triode, $g_{m}$ drops and
effective $L<1$.

In particular with $\lambda=0$, $r_{o}\to\infty$,
$L\to\infty$ :

$$V_{out}=I_{in}/g_{m2}$$
$$R_{in}= \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}} = -\frac1{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}$$

negative input resistance.

With normal intrinsic gains $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$,
$L=g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg1$
unless $R_{D1}$ is made very small. So as drawn the
both-saturated point is normally unstable.

Large signal $V_{out}=h(V_{out})$ with $h$ increasing
can have two stable intersections: low $I_{in}$ :
$M_{1}$ off, $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$, $M_{2}$ in
triode carrying $I_{in}$ with small $V_{X}$; high $I_{in}$ :
$M_{1}$ in triode pulling down, $M_{2}$ saturated,
$V_{out}\approx V_{GS2}$, $V_{X}$ large. The jump
up and down occur at different $I_{in}$. I.e. a
current-mode Schmitt trigger / latch.

In short: positive shunt-shunt feedback with loop
gain $g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}$.
Must be kept $<1$ for linear amplification, in
which case gain and terminal $R$ are enhanced by
$1/(1-L)$. $>1$ gives bistability and negative
small-signal resistances.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s gate connection to Vout, the positive-feedback loop through M1 and M2, and the resulting negative input resistance and instability/latching when loop gain exceeds one.

answer.text:
This is a current in - voltage out amplifier with
active shunt-shunt feed-back.

$ M_1 $ is the forward common source with

$$R_{D1}' = R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$$

gate = $X$, drain = $V_{out}$, source = gnd.

$ M_2 $ senses the output voltage at its gate
and returns a current to the input node at its drain,
source = gnd.

$$ V_{X,DC}=V_{GS1} \;,\; V_{out,DC}=V_{GS2} $$
$$ I_{D2,DC}=I_{B}\;,\; I_{D1,DC}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out,DC}}{R_{D1}} $$

$I_{in}=I_{B}+i_{in}$. Body is grounded, $V_{SB}=0$.
Assume saturation:

$$V_{DS1}=V_{out} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{X} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}$$

Small signal, $\lambda\ne 0$:

* $M_{1}$: $g_{m1}V_{x}$ from $V_{out}$ to gnd,
  $r_{o1}$ from $V_{out}$ to gnd.
* $M_{2}$: $g_{m2}V_{out}$ from $V_{x}$ to gnd,
  $r_{o2}$ from $V_{x}$ to gnd.
* $R_{D1}$ from $V_{out}$ to ac gnd.
* $i_{in}$ into $V_{x}$.

Node $V_{out}$:

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{V_{out}}{r_{o1}}+g_{m1}V_{x}=0 \tag{1}$$

i.e. the forward gain with $V_{x}$ as input

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{V_{x}} = -g_{m1}R_{D1}' $$

Node $X$:

$$ i_{in} = \frac{V_{x}}{r_{o2}} + g_{m2}V_{out} \tag{2}$$

Hence

$$V_{x} = -\frac{V_{out}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'} $$

$$i_{in}= V_{out}\left[g_{m2}-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}\right] $$

Put

$$L = g_{m1}R_{D1}'\,g_{m2}r_{o2} $$

Then the closed loop transimpedance is

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}} =\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{L}{L-1} $$

i.e.

$$ R_T = -\,\frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}{1-L} $$

Open loop, $g_{m2}=0$ but loading kept,
$i_{in}$ flows in $r_{o2}$:

$$R_{T0}= -g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}$$

so

$$R_T = \frac{R_{T0}}{1-L}$$

This is the classic formula for regenerative,
positive feed-back with loop gain $L$.

Indeed each stage is inverting:
$V_{x}\uparrow \to V_{out}\downarrow$ via $M_{1}$,
$V_{out}\downarrow \to I_{D2}\downarrow$ via $M_{2}$.
$I_{D2}$ is drawn out of the input node. Less
current drawn means, for fixed $i_{in}$, $V_{x}$
rises more. An increase in $V_{x}$ regenerates
itself. Phase around the loop is 0.

Formally voltage sampling, current mixing,
i.e. shunt-shunt, but with two inversions.

Stage gains with loading:

* $A_{1}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}'$, load is $R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$,
  next gate is open.
* $A_{2}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}$, load is $r_{o2}$,
  source is ideal $i_{in}$, next gate is open.

Loop gain:

$$ T = A_{1}A_{2}=+g_{m1}R_{D1}'g_{m2}r_{o2}=L $$

Input resistance: $R_{in}=V_{x}/i_{in}$

$$ R_{in}= \frac{-R_{T}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'} =\frac{r_{o2}}{1-L} $$

i.e. open loop $r_{o2}$ enhanced by $1/(1-L)$.

Output resistance: put $i_{in}=0$, drive
$V_{out}$ with $V_{test}$, current $I_{test}$.

$$0 = \frac{V_{x}}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}V_{test}$$
$$I_{test}= \frac{V_{test}}{R_{D1}'}+g_{m1}V_{x}$$

$$I_{test}=V_{test}\left[\frac1{R_{D1}'}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]$$

$$ R_{out}= \frac{R_{D1}'}{1-L} $$

i.e. open loop $R_{D1}'$ enhanced by $1/(1-L)$.

In contrast to negative feed-back TIA, $R_{in}$
and $R_{out}$ are increased.

Stability requires for positive feed-back

$$ L = g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}) < 1 $$

Then $R_{T}<0$, $R_{in}>0$, $R_{out}>0$.
As $L\to 1$, $|R_{T}|$, $R_{in}$, $R_{out}\to\infty$.

If $L>1$, $R_{in}$, $R_{out}$ go negative in small
signal, the high-gain bias with both in saturation
is metastable. The circuit is bistable, gain drops
by entering triode until $L<1$. In practice
$g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg 1$, so $L<1$ needs very small
$g_{m1}R_{D1}'$, i.e. a very low gain forward stage,
making stable bias very PVT sensitive.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s gate at Vout and the regenerative positive-feedback loop, derives the loop-gain-modified input resistance, and explains instability/bistability when the loop gain exceeds one.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a loop of two inverters.

$M_{1}$ is a common source with $R_{D1}$ load.
$M_{2}$ is a common source whose input is $V_{out}$ and
whose output is node $X$. $I_{in}$ is the
high impedance load of $M_{2}$.

Put for low frequency, in saturation,

$$M_{1}: g_{m1},\,r_{o1}\qquad M_{2}:g_{m2},\,r_{o2}$$

body effect neglected, sources grounded.
Let

$$R_{D1}' = R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1} = \frac{1}{G_{1}}$$
$$G_{1}= \frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}$$

DC, if both saturated:

$$I_{D2}=I_{IN}$$
$$I_{D1}= \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}$$

i.e. $V_{out}=V_{GS2}(I_{IN})$, $V_{X}=V_{GS1}(I_{D1})$.
This is the high gain point.

Small signal, $v_{x}$ at $X$, $v_{out}$ at output,
gates draw no current:

X-node: $I_{in}$ flows into $M_{2}$ drain:

$$i_{in} = g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{ds2}v_{x} \tag{1}$$

i.e. $M_{2}$ senses $v_{out}$ and returns a
current to the input. Voltage sampling, current
mixing, shunt-shunt.

Output node: current from $R_{D1}$ flows into
$M_{1}$ drain:

$$0 = g_{m1}v_{x} + \left(G_{1}\right)v_{out} \tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$v_{x} = -\frac{v_{out}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'} $$

$M_{1}$ inverts. Put in (1):

$$i_{in} = v_{out}\left[g_{m2}-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}\right]$$

Closed loop transresistance at the metastable
point:

$$ R_{M}=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}\,} $$

$$R_{M}= \frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}{L-1}$$

where

$$L = g_{m1}R_{D1}'\,g_{m2}r_{o2}$$

$L$ is the gain around the loop.

Indeed, break the loop at the gate of $M_{1}$,
$I_{in}$ AC open. $v_{test}\to$ gate $M_{1}$:

$$v_{out} = -g_{m1}R_{D1}'v_{test}$$
$$0 = g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{ds2}v_{r}$$
$$v_{r} = -g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{out}$$

$$\frac{v_{r}}{v_{test}} = +g_{m1}R_{D1}'g_{m2}r_{o2}=+L$$

Two inversions $=360^{\circ}$. This is
positive, shunt-shunt feedback.

Normally $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, $g_{m1}R_{D1}' >1$,
so

$$L\gg 1$$

For positive feedback the characteristic is $1-L=0$.
$L>1$ is unstable.

With $C_{X},C_{out}$ to ground at the two nodes,
ignoring feedthrough for illustration,

$$(C_{X}s+g_{ds2})v_{x}+g_{m2}v_{out}=i_{in}$$
$$g_{m1}v_{x}+(C_{out}s+G_{1})v_{out}=0$$

Determinant:

$$D(s)=(C_{X}s+g_{ds2})(C_{out}s+G_{1})-g_{m1}g_{m2}$$

$$D(s)=C_{X}C_{out}s^{2}+\cdots +g_{ds2}G_{1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}$$

$$D(0)=\frac{1-L}{r_{o2}R_{D1}'}$$

If $L>1$, $D(0)<0$ while $D(\infty)>0$.
There is a real positive-$s$ root. One RHP pole.
The high gain bias point is metastable. In general
any passive capacitive network leaves $D(0)$ the
same, so $L>1$ implies instability.

Closed loop impedances at that point reflect this.

Input: $R_{in}=v_{x}/i_{in}$:

$$R_{in}= -\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'}R_{M}$$

$$R_{in}= \frac{-r_{o2}}{L-1}$$

Output: apply $v_{t}$ at output, $i_{in}=0$ AC.
$0=g_{m2}v_{t}+v_{x}/r_{o2}$, $i_{t}=v_{t}/R_{D1}'+g_{m1}v_{x}$:

$$i_{t}=v_{t}\left[\frac1{R_{D1}'}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]$$

$$R_{out}= \frac{R_{D1}'}{1-L}$$

If $L\gg 1$:

$$\begin{aligned}
R_{M} &\approx \frac1{g_{m2}} \\
R_{in} &\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}'} \\
R_{out} &\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
\end{aligned}$$

Magnitudes are small as in shunt-shunt, but
negative because feedback is positive. With
$\lambda=0$, $L\to\infty$, $R_{M}\to 1/g_{m2}$,
$R_{in}\to -1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$, $R_{out}\to 0^{-}$.

In words: $+\Delta v_{x}\to -\Delta v_{out}$
via $M_{1}$ $\to$ decreased $M_{2}$ drain
current $\to$ less current sucked from $X$
$\to$ $v_{x}$ rises further. Positive feedback.

Hence the linear circuit cannot stay in
saturation with $L>1$. It is two back-to-back
inverters, i.e. a latch. The third, high-gain
solution is unstable. The stable solutions have
one device off or in triode, $g_{m}=0$ or low,
making $L<1$.

Varying $I_{IN}$, which is the tail current of
the $M_{2}$ inverter, moves its transfer
characteristic and flips the latch at two
different currents. The circuit is in large
signal a current-input Schmitt trigger / bistable,
with negative small-signal resistance in the
metastable region, not a stable linear
transimpedance amplifier unless sized for $L<1$,
in which case $R_{M}<0$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2 as a common-source device controlled by Vout, traces the positive-feedback loop, and derives the negative input resistance and instability/latching for loop gain above one. The conclusion matches the golden solution.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a 2-stage shunt-shunt transimpedance
amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate grounded for ac, source driven by $I_{in}$,
drain loaded by $R_{D1}$. Common-gate stage.
* $M_{2}$ : gate driven by $X$, source grounded,
drain loaded by $R_{D2}$. Common-source stage.
* $R_{F}$ from output voltage to input node feeds
back a current $i_{RF}$.

$i_{RF}$ is defined to flow from $V_{out}$ to the input:

$$i_{RF}= \frac{v_{out}-v_{A}}{R_{F}} $$

where $v_A$ is the ac voltage at the source of $M_1$.

Both devices are NMOS. Assume saturation.
$M_2$ has source to ground, no back gate.
$M_1$ has source $\ne$ ground, body to ground,
so $g_{mb1}\ne 0$ in general. Let $r_{o1},r_{o2}$
be the output resistances.

Voltage sampling at the output, current mixing
at the input: voltage-current, shunt-shunt,
transimpedance $V_{out}/I_{in}$.

Polarity: $I_{in}\uparrow \to v_A\uparrow \to
v_{gs1}\downarrow \to i_{d1}\downarrow \to
v_X\uparrow \to i_{d2}\uparrow \to v_{out}\downarrow$.
Increase of $I_{in}$ decreases $V_{out}$.
$i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_A)/R_F$ decreases,
opposing the increase of $I_{in}$. Negative feedback.

With large loop gain we expect

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}\approx -R_F $$

i.e. $I_{in}$ flows in $R_F$ to a virtual ground
at the input.

### Small signal equations

Put $V_{DD},V_b$ to ac ground.
$v_A$ = input node, $v_X$ = $M_1$ drain / $M_2$ gate,
$v_{out}$ = output.

$M_1$: $v_{gs1}= -v_A$, $v_{bs1}= -v_A$,
$v_{ds1}=v_X-v_A$

Drain current entering the drain:

$$i_{d1}=(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(-v_A)+\frac{v_X-v_A}{r_{o1}}$$

$M_2$: $v_{gs2}=v_X$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_X+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}$$

KCL $X$: no gate current,

$$\frac{v_X}{R_{D1}}+i_{d1}=0 \tag{1}$$

KCL $out$: open output,

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}-v_A}{R_F}=0 \tag{2}$$

KCL $A$: $I_{in}$ enters, $(v_A-v_{out})/R_F$
leaves to $V_{out}$, $-i_{d1}$ leaves into $M_1$
source:

$$-I_{in}+\frac{v_A-v_{out}}{R_F}-i_{d1}=0 \tag{3}$$

From (1):

$$v_X\left(\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)
 -v_A\left(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)=0$$

$$v_X = A_1 v_A \tag{4}$$

$$A_1=\frac{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+1/r_{o1}}{1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1}}$$

$A_1$ is the CG voltage gain $A$ to $X$.
If $r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$:

$$A_1\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})R_{D1}>0$$

Put (4) in (2):

$$g_{m2}A_1v_A+v_{out}G_o-\frac{v_A}{R_F}=0 \tag{5}$$

$$G_o=\frac1{R_{D2}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}+\frac1{R_F}$$

i.e. output conductance to ground.

(3) can be written:

$$I_{in}=v_A\left(\frac1{R_F}+g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+\frac1{r_{o1}}-\frac{A_1}{r_{o1}}\right)-\frac{v_{out}}{R_F}$$

But $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+1/r_{o1}=A_1(1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1})$,
so

$$I_{in}=v_AG_A-\frac{v_{out}}{R_F} \tag{6}$$

where

$$G_A=\frac1{R_F}+\frac{A_1}{R_{D1}}$$

i.e. input conductance to ground of the loaded
forward circuit.

(5)(6) give two equations for $v_A,v_{out}$.

Let

$$D = G_oG_A+\frac{g_{m2}A_1-1/R_F}{R_F}$$

Then

$$R_T=\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=-\frac{g_{m2}A_1-1/R_F}{D} $$

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_A}{I_{in}}=\frac{G_o}{D}$$

For $R_{out}$, set $I_{in}=0$, apply $V_t$ at
output. Then from (6) $0=v_AG_A-V_t/R_F$,
$v_X=A_1v_A$, and KCL at output gives test
current $I_t=V_tG_o+g_{m2}v_X-v_A/R_F$. Hence

$$R_{out}=\frac{G_A}{D}$$

So in compact form:

$$D=G_oG_A+\frac{g_{m2}A_1-1/R_F}{R_F}$$
$$R_T=-(g_{m2}A_1-1/R_F)/D,\quad R_{in}=G_o/D,\quad R_{out}=G_A/D$$

Check: $R_F\to\infty$ (no feedback):
$G_o\to 1/R_{D2}+1/r_{o2}$, $G_A\to A_1/R_{D1}$,
$D\to G_oA_1/R_{D1}$,
$R_T\to -g_{m2}R_{D1}/G_o=-g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}||r_{o2})$,
$R_{in}\to R_{D1}/A_1=(R_{D1}+r_{o1})/(1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1})$,
$R_{out}\to 1/G_o=R_{D2}||r_{o2}$.
This is the cascade CG + CS open gain, as expected.

### Feedback interpretation

$1/G_A$ is the loaded forward input resistance,
$R_{D1}||(A_1R_F)$, $\approx 1/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})||R_F$.
$1/G_o$ is the loaded forward output resistance,
$R_{D2}||r_{o2}||R_F$.

Write $D=G_oG_A(1+T)$ with

$$T=\frac{g_{m2}A_1-1/R_F}{R_FG_oG_A}\approx
\frac{g_{m2}A_1}{R_FG_oG_A}$$

Then

$$R_T=-R_F\frac{T}{1+T},\;
R_{in}=\frac{1}{G_A}\frac1{1+T},\;
R_{out}=\frac{1}{G_o}\frac1{1+T}$$

This is the classic shunt-shunt result with
$\beta=-1/R_F$ and forward gain $A$ such that
$T=A\beta$.

Approximate, $r_o\to\infty$, $g_{mb}=0$:

$$A_1\approx g_{m1}R_{D1},\;G_o\approx\frac1{R_{D2}}+\frac1{R_F},\;G_A\approx\frac1{R_F}+g_{m1}$$

$$T\approx \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_2}{1+g_{m1}R_F}$$

$R_2=R_{D2}||R_F$. If $g_{m1}R_F\gg1$,
$R_F\gg R_{D2}$:

$$T\approx \frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}$$

i.e. open transimpedance $g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}$
divided by $R_F$. The $g_{m1}$ cancels: the
CG transimpedance is $R_{D1}$ as long as
$1/g_{m1}$ is low.

Then

$$R_T\approx -R_F\frac{1}{1+1/T}\approx -R_F$$

more precisely:

$$R_T\approx -\frac{R_F}{1+\frac{R_F}{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}}$$

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_F}{1+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_2}\ll\frac1{g_{m1}}$$

$$R_{out}\approx \frac{R_2}{1+T}\ll R_{D2}$$

Feedback lowers the already low CG input
impedance by $1+T$ and lowers the output
impedance by $1+T$.

In words: first stage converts input current
to voltage $R_{D1}$, second provides $-g_{m2}R_{D2}$
voltage gain. $R_F$ closes a large inverting
loop to stabilize transimpedance to $-R_F$,
make input a virtual ground current-summer
and output a voltage source. Body effect on $M_1$
increases effective $g_m$, increasing $A_1$,
$T$, and lowering $R_{in}$. Finite $r_o$
reduces $A_1$ to $(g_m+g_{mb})(R_D||r_o)$
and raises open $R_{out}$ to $R_D||r_o$.

For frequency, the loop has high-impedance
poles at $X$ and at the output, plus a high
frequency pole at the low-impedance input.
It is essentially a two-pole feedback system;
with large $T$ and comparable $X$ and output
poles phase margin must be checked. Input
capacitance with $R_F$ is the usual TIA
stability concern.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a current to voltage converter,
a transimpedance amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate AC ground, source driven by $I_{in}$,
drain loaded by $R_{D1}$. Common-gate stage.
* $M_{2}$ : source grounded, gate driven by the drain
of $M_{1}$, drain loaded by $R_{D2}$. Common-source stage.
* $R_{F}$ from drain of $M_{2}$ to source of $M_{1}$.

$R_{F}$ senses the output voltage in parallel,
shunt sampling, and returns a current in parallel
to the input, shunt mixing. It is voltage-current,
shunt-shunt feedback.

Put $V_{in}$ = AC voltage at source of $M_{1}$,
$V_{X}$ = AC voltage at drain of $M_{1}$ / gate of $M_{2}$,
$V_{out}$ = AC output voltage.

$g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}$ for $M_{1}$, $g_{m2},r_{o2}$
for $M_{2}$, $M_{2}$ source grounded has no body effect.
Put $g_{m1}'=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$, $g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}$,
$g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$.

Polarity: $I_{in}\uparrow \to V_{in}\uparrow$.
CG is non-inverting: $V_{X}\uparrow$.
CS is inverting: $V_{out}\downarrow$.
Feedback current from input to output
$(V_{in}-V_{out})/R_{F}\uparrow$, i.e. it
steals more of $I_{in}$ from the forward path.
Negative feedback.

Two-port $Y$ of $R_{F}$:

$$Y_{11}=Y_{22}=1/R_{F},\quad Y_{12}=Y_{21}=-1/R_{F}$$

For shunt sampling, input loading is with
$V_{out}=0$. For shunt mixing, output loading
is with $V_{in}=0$.

Loaded open loop: forward CG+CS with $R_{F}$
to ground at input, $R_{F}$ to ground at
output. Feedback factor

$$I_{f}=Y_{21}V_{out},\quad \beta=-\frac{1}{R_{F}} $$

in the sense $V_{out}=A_{OL}(I_{in}+V_{out}/R_{F})$,
i.e.

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1-A_{OL}/R_{F}} $$

$A_{OL}<0$ is the loaded transimpedance.
Loop gain

$$T=-\frac{A_{OL}}{R_{F}}>0$$

and

$$Z_{T}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1+T}=-R_{F}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

Ideal $T\gg 1$: $Z_{T}\approx -R_{F}$.

Loaded forward gain. Looking into source of
CG with $R_{D1}$ at drain:

$$R_{in1}= \frac{r_{o1}+R_{D1}}{1+g_{m1}'r_{o1}}$$

$$\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}'}\;\;r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$$

With $V_{in}$ given,

$$V_{X}/V_{in}=A_{v1}=(g_{m1}'+g_{ds1})(r_{o1}\parallel R_{D1})$$

KCL at $X$: $V_{X}/R_{D1}+i_{d1}=0$,
$i_{d1}=-g_{m1}'V_{in}+g_{ds1}(V_{X}-V_{in})$.

CS stage loaded by $R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$:

$$V_{out}/V_{X}=A_{v2}=-g_{m2}(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

Input voltage from $I_{in}$:

$$V_{in}/I_{in}=R_{F}\parallel R_{in1}=R_{in,open}$$

Hence

$$A_{OL}=R_{in,open}\,A_{v1}\,A_{v2}$$

$$A_{OL}=-(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{v1}g_{m2}
(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

$$T=\frac{(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{v1}g_{m2}
(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})}{R_{F}}$$

Neglecting $r_{o}$, $g_{mb}$:

$$R_{in1}\approx 1/g_{m1},\;A_{v1}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}$$

$$A_{OL}\approx -\frac{R_{F}}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}
g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

$$T\approx \frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})}
{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}$$

$$Z_{T}\approx -R_{F}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

i.e.

$$Z_{T}\approx \frac{-g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})
\frac{R_{F}}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}}{1+T}$$

Closed loop input impedance is $V_{in}/I_{in}$
with feedback. Feedback theory for shunt mixing:

$$R_{in,closed}=\frac{R_{in,open}}{1+T}$$

$$R_{in,closed}=\frac{R_{F}\parallel R_{in1}}{1+T}$$

$\approx (R_{F}\parallel 1/g_{m1})/(1+T)$.
For large $T$ this is $\approx 0$, virtual ground.
Direct KCL gives $R_{in}=R_{F}/(1+g_{m1}'R_{F}+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{2})$
with $R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$.

Closed loop output impedance: set $I_{in}=0$,
drive output with $V_{t}$, measure $I_{t}$.

With $I_{in}=0$:

$$\frac{V_{t}-V_{in}}{R_{F}}=\frac{V_{in}}{R_{in1}}$$

$$V_{in}=V_{t}\frac{R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}$$

$$V_{X}=A_{v1}V_{in}$$

$$I_{t}=V_{t}/R_{D2}+g_{m2}V_{X}+g_{ds2}V_{t}
+(V_{t}-V_{in})/R_{F}$$

$$\frac{1}{R_{out}}=\frac{1}{R_{D2}}+g_{ds2}
+\frac{1+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{out}= \left[\frac{1}{r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}}
+\frac{1+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}\right]^{-1}$$

Neglecting $r_{o}$, $g_{mb}$:

$$\frac{1}{R_{out}}\approx \frac{1}{R_{D2}}
+\frac{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}$$

$$R_{out}\approx R_{D2}\parallel
\frac{R_{F}+1/g_{m1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}}$$

For $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$ and large $T$,
$R_{out}\approx R_{D2}/(1+T)$. Shunt
sampling lowers output impedance toward zero.

In summary, large forward gain makes it an
almost ideal transimpedance $-R_{F}$ with
small input impedance and small output
impedance. The loop has two high impedance
nodes $X$ and output, so stability and
bandwidth are set by poles at $R_{D1}$ and
$R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}$ with device and
load capacitances.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a transimpedance amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate grounded for ac, signal in the
source, signal out the drain $X$.
Common-gate with load $R_{D1}$.

* $M_{2}$ : source grounded, signal in the gate $X$,
signal out the drain $V_{out}$. Common-source with
load $R_{D2}$.

* $R_{F}$ from output to input.

Let small signal node voltages be $v_{in}$ at
the $I_{in}$ node, $v_{X}$, $v_{out}$.
Ignore body for the moment. Put

$$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}\;,\;r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$$
$$R_{D1}'=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\;,\;
  R_{D2}'=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$M_{1}$: $v_{gs1}=-v_{in}$,
$v_{ds1}=v_{X}-v_{in}$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

enters the drain, leaves the source.

$M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=v_{X}$,
$v_{ds2}=v_{out}$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{X}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

enters the drain.

### Feedback polarity and type

$R_{F}$ senses $v_{out}$, i.e. output voltage,
returns a current to the input node where it
sums with $I_{in}$. Shunt at output,
shunt at input : voltage-current,
shunt-shunt feedback.

Check sign: let $v_{out}\uparrow$.
Current $(v_{out}-v_{in})/R_{F}$ into
the input node $\uparrow$, $v_{in}\uparrow$.

$v_{in}\uparrow \to v_{gs1}\downarrow \to
i_{d1}\downarrow \to$ drop in $R_{D1}\downarrow
\to v_{X}\uparrow \to i_{d2}\uparrow \to
v_{out}\downarrow$.

The rise is opposed. Negative feedback.

For large loop gain the input is a virtual ground
and all of $I_{in}$ flows in $R_{F}$:

$$v_{out}\approx -I_{in}R_{F}$$

i.e. an inverting transimpedance $-R_{F}$.

### Small signal equations

KCL X, no gate current:

$$\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}+i_{d1}=0 \tag{2}$$

KCL input:

$$I_{in}+i_{d1}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0 \tag{1}$$

KCL output:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+
\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0 \tag{3}$$

From (2):

$$\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}(-v_{in})
+g_{ds1}(v_{X}-v_{in})=0$$

$$v_{X}=v_{in}\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}
{1/R_{D1}+g_{ds1}} =A_{1}v_{in}$$

$$A_{1}=(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})R_{D1}'\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}'$$

Positive CG gain.

Also $i_{d1}=-v_{X}/R_{D1}=-G_{1}v_{in}$ where

$$G_{1}=\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}
 =\frac{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}$$

$1/G_{1}$ is the input resistance into the
CG source with drain load:

$$R_{in1}=1/G_{1}= \frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}
{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

Then (1) becomes

$$I_{in}=v_{in}\left(G_{1}+\frac1{R_{F}}\right)
-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{F}} \tag{1'}$$

(3) becomes

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_{D2}'}+\frac1{R_{F}}\right)
+v_{in}\left(g_{m2}A_{1}-\frac1{R_{F}}\right)=0
\tag{3'}$$

i.e. with loading the $v_{in}\to v_{out}$ gain is

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{1/R_{D2}'+1/R_{F}}$$

$\approx -g_{m2}A_{1}(R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$.
The $1/R_{F}$ is direct feedthrough.

Solving (1')(3'):

$$R_{T}=\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}
 =-\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{(G_{1}+1/R_{F})(1/R_{D2}'+1/R_{F})
 +(g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F})/R_{F}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{T}=\frac{1-g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$$=-R_{F}\frac{1-1/g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}}
{1+G_{1}/g_{m2}A_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})
/g_{m2}A_{1}R_{D2}'}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$,
$A_{1}=g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $G_{1}=g_{m1}$,
$R_{D2}'=R_{D2}$:

$$R_{T}\approx
\frac{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}}
{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}+g_{m1}+(1+g_{m1}R_{F})/R_{D2}}$$

If $g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}\gg1$ and denominator
dominated by $g_{m2}A_{1}$,

$$R_{T}\approx -R_{F}$$

Check $R_{F}\to\infty$ : open loop transimpedance

$$R_{T,open}=-g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}'$$

indeed $v_{in}=I_{in}/G_{1}$,
$v_{X}=A_{1}v_{in}=R_{D1}I_{in}$,
$v_{out}=-g_{m2}R_{D2}'v_{X}$.

In two-port terms, voltage sampling, current
mixing loads the A-circuit with $R_{F}$ to
ground at input for $v_{out}=0$ and $R_{F}$
to ground at output for $v_{in}=0$.
Open loop with loading:

$$A_{OL}=\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}\Big|_{load}
 =-A_{1}g_{m2}(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})
 (R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$$

Loop gain, neglecting feedthrough,

$$T=\frac{|A_{OL}|}{R_{F}}
 \approx g_{m2}A_{1}(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})
 \frac{R_{D2}'}{R_{D2}'+R_{F}}$$

More exactly

$$T=\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{(G_{1}+1/R_{F})(1+R_{F}/R_{D2}')}$$

so that $R_{T}=-R_{F}T/(1+T)$.

Input resistance $v_{in}/I_{in}$ from (1')(3'):

$$R_{in}=\frac{1+R_{F}/R_{D2}'}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$\to 1/G_{1}=R_{in1}$ for $R_{F}\to\infty$.
For large $T$,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}$$

where $|A_{v}|\approx g_{m2}A_{1}
(R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$. Feedback lowers
the already low CG $1/g_{m1}$ by $1+T$.

Output resistance: set $I_{in}=0$ open,
apply $v_{x}$ at output, measure $i_{x}$.
Then $-G_{1}v_{in}+(v_{x}-v_{in})/R_{F}=0$,
$v_{in}=v_{x}/(1+G_{1}R_{F})$,
$v_{X}=A_{1}v_{in}$,

$$i_{x}=v_{x}/R_{D2}'+g_{m2}v_{X}+G_{1}v_{in}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}
 =\frac{1+G_{1}R_{F}}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$\to R_{D2}'$ for $R_{F}\to\infty$.
Feedback lowers it by $\approx 1+T$.

With body effect on $M_{1}$, whose body is
substrate ground, replace $g_{m1}$ by
$g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_{1}$ and $G_{1}$.

DC bias is through $R_{F}$: $I_{RD1}=I_{D1}$,
$I_{RF}=I_{D1}+I_{in,DC}$ flows input$\to$output,
$I_{D2}=I_{RD2}+I_{RF}$. $V_{X}=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}$,
$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{RD2}R_{D2}$, $V_{in}-V_{out}
=I_{RF}R_{F}$. $V_{b}$ sets $V_{gs1}$ and $I_{D1}$,
$V_{X}$ sets $I_{D2}$. Proper sizing must keep
both in saturation despite DC drop in $R_{F}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as the common-source stage driven by X, and RF as feedback from Vout to the input, forming a negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier. The detailed small-signal analysis is not needed for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a shunt-shunt feedback transimpedance amplifier.
It is the active-load version of the regulated-cascode TIA.

* $M_{1}$: NMOS, common gate. Source is the input node $X$,
drain is the output node $Y=V_{out}$, gate ac ground $V_{b}$.
* $M_{2}$: PMOS, common source feedback. Source to $V_{DD}$ ac ground,
gate to $Y$, drain to $X$.
* $I_{1}$ from $V_{DD}$ to $Y$ : load / bias for $M_{1}$.
* $I_{2}$ from $X$ to ground : bias sink.
* $I_{in}$ into $X$ : signal current.

Put $V_{X}, V_{Y}$ for small signal at $X,Y$.
$M_{2}$ has its n-well to its source, no back-gate.
$M_{1}$ in a normal p-sub has back-gate to ground:

$$G_{m1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$$

Put $g_{mb1}=0$ if triple well. Put $g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}$,
$g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$. Current sources ideal first,
$R_{1},R_{2}\to\infty$.

### DC bias

$Y$ has only $I_{1}$ and $M_{1}$:

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}$$

$X$ : $M_{1}$ current flows $Y\to X$, $M_{2}$ current
flows $V_{DD}\to X$ :

$$I_{2}=I_{in,DC}+I_{D1}+I_{SD2}$$

Typically $I_{in,DC}=0$, so

$$I_{SD2}=I_{2}-I_{1}>0$$

i.e. $I_{2}>I_{1}$.

$$V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1}$$
for $I_{D1}=I_{1}$,
$$V_{Y}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}$$
for $I_{SD2}=I_{2}-I_{1}$.

Saturation:

$M_{1}$: $V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN1}$,
$$V_{Y}-V_{X} \ge V_{b}-V_{X}-V_{THN1}$$
$$V_{Y}\ge V_{b}-V_{THN1}$$
$V_{THN1}$ includes body $V_{SB}=V_{X}$.

$M_{2}$: $V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{THP2}|$,
$$V_{DD}-V_{X} \ge V_{DD}-V_{Y}-|V_{THP}|$$
$$V_{Y}\ge V_{X}-|V_{THP}|$$
easily satisfied, $V_{Y}$ is normally $>V_{X}$.

$I_{1}$ needs $V_{DD}-V_{Y}$ headroom, $I_{2}$ needs $V_{X}$
headroom.

### Small signal low frequency

Gate $M_{1}$ grounded, body grounded.

NMOS $M_{1}$, drain current into drain:
$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}(0-V_{x})+g_{mb1}(0-V_{x})+g_{ds1}(V_{y}-V_{x})$$
$$i_{d1}=-G_{m1}V_{x}+g_{ds1}(V_{y}-V_{x})$$

PMOS $M_{2}$, source to ac ground, source-to-drain current:
$v_{SG}=-V_{y}$, $v_{SD}=-V_{x}$,
$$i_{sd2}=g_{m2}(-V_{y})+g_{ds2}(-V_{x})$$

Node $Y$: $I_{1}$ open, gate open.
$$i_{d1}=0 \tag{1}$$
i.e.
$$-G_{m1}V_{x}+g_{ds1}(V_{y}-V_{x})=0$$
$$V_{y}=\frac{G_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}}V_{x}
\approx G_{m1}r_{o1}V_{x} \tag{2}$$
This is the CG gain from source to drain into $r_{o1}$,
non-inverting and large.

Node $X$: $I_{2}$ open, $i_{in}$ enters, $i_{d1}$ enters
from $M_{1}$ source, $i_{sd2}$ enters from $M_{2}$ drain:
$$i_{in}+i_{d1}+i_{sd2}=0 \tag{3}$$

With (1), $i_{d1}=0$:
$$i_{in}+g_{m2}(-V_{y})+g_{ds2}(-V_{x})=0$$
$$i_{in}=g_{m2}V_{y}+g_{ds2}V_{x} \tag{4}$$

Intuition: because the load at $Y$ is ac open, the ac
drain current of $M_{1}$ must be zero. All signal input
current must be supplied by the feedback device $M_{2}$.
$V_{y}$ must move by $i_{in}/g_{m2}$ to change $M_{2}$
current by $i_{in}$.

From (2)(4):

Transimpedance:

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{G_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}} $$

i.e. with $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$:

$$R_{T}=\frac{(G_{m1}r_{o1}+1)}{g_{m2}(G_{m1}r_{o1}+1)+1/r_{o2}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

Positive, non-inverting TIA.

Input resistance $V_{x}/i_{in}$:

$$R_{in}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})/g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}(G_{m1}r_{o1}+1)+1/r_{o2}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}G_{m1}r_{o1}}$$

Very low, virtual ground if $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.

Output resistance: put $i_{in}=0$, drive $Y$ with $v_{test}$,
measure $i_{test}$. $i_{test}=i_{d1}$,
$i_{d1}+i_{sd2}=0$ at $X$. Solving:

$$R_{out}=\frac{(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})+g_{ds2}}
{g_{m2}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}(G_{m1}r_{o1}+1)}
{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}(G_{m1}r_{o1}+1)}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}}$$

If $\lambda=0$, $r_{o}\to\infty$:
$$R_{T}=1/g_{m2},\quad R_{in}=0,\quad R_{out}=1/g_{m2}$$

Finite $R_{1}$ of $I_{1}$ shunts $r_{o1}$, finite $R_{2}$
of $I_{2}$ shunts the input. If $R_{1,2}\gg 1/g_{m}$
the above is essentially unchanged.

### Loop

$V_{x}\uparrow \to V_{y}\uparrow$ via $M_{1}$,
$V_{y}\uparrow \to$ $M_{2}$ current into $X$ $\downarrow$,
$\to V_{x}\downarrow$. Negative shunt-shunt feedback.

Breaking at $M_{2}$ gate, which draws no current,
with $i_{in}=0$:

$$L_{0}= -\frac{V_{r}}{V_{test}} = G_{m1}r_{o1}\,g_{m2}r_{o2}$$

huge. Closed loop is stabilized to $1/g_{m2}$.

### Frequency, stability

Let $C_{X}$ total at $X$, $C_{Y}$ total at $Y$.
Nodal:

$$V_{y}(sC_{Y}+g_{ds1})=V_{x}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})$$
$$i_{in}=V_{x}(sC_{X}+g_{ds2})+V_{y}(sC_{Y}+g_{m2})$$

Hence

$$Z_{T}(s)=\frac{G_{m1}+g_{ds1}}
{(sC_{X}+g_{ds2})(sC_{Y}+g_{ds1})+(sC_{Y}+g_{m2})(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})}$$

Denominator:

$$s^{2}C_{X}C_{Y}+s\big[C_{X}g_{ds1}+C_{Y}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})\big]$$
$$+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}+g_{m2}(G_{m1}+g_{ds1})=0$$

Second order with all positive coefficients, LHP,
ideally unconditionally stable. Approx:

$$\omega_{n}^{2}\approx \frac{g_{m2}G_{m1}}{C_{X}C_{Y}}$$

$$\zeta\approx\frac12\sqrt{\frac{C_{Y}}{C_{X}}}\sqrt{\frac{G_{m1}}{g_{m2}}}$$

Usually $C_{X}\gg C_{Y}$, input photodiode etc., so
$\zeta$ small, peaking. Increasing $C_{Y}$,
decreasing $G_{m1}/g_{m2}$ damps but lowers bandwidth.
This is the classic RGC tradeoff.

In short: low-$Z_{in}$ current-to-voltage converter
with gain $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, $R_{in}\approx 1/L_{0}/g_{m2}$,
$R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2}$. $M_{1}$ provides large loop
gain to create virtual ground; $M_{2}$ sets the
transimpedance. Low-frequency noise of $M_{1}$ largely
cancels because its drain is ac open; input-referred
noise is dominated by $M_{2}$, $I_{1}$, $I_{2}$.
