answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a current in - voltage out amplifier.
A transimpedance amplifier.

$M_{1}$ is NMOS, $M_{2}$ is PMOS.

* $M_{1}$ : gate ac ground, source = input node $X$,
  drain = output node $Y$. Common-gate forward path
  $X\to Y$.
* $M_{2}$ : source ac ground $V_{DD}$, gate = $Y$,
  drain = $X$. Common-source feedback path
  $Y\to X$.

Call the lower dc sink $I_{B}$. For ac $I_{1},I_{B}$
are open, $V_{b}$ is ground. Let

$$v_{x}= {\rm ac\; at\;} X \;\;,\;\; v_{y}=V_{out}$$

$M_{2}$ has n-well tied to source, no back gate.
$M_{1}$ has body to GND.

DC, in saturation:

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}$$
$$I_{D2}+I_{D1}=I_{B}+I_{in,DC}$$

i.e. $V_{GS1}$ is set by $I_{1}$, $V_{SG2}$ is set
by $I_{B}-I_{1}$. Then

$$V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1}$$
$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}$$

$M_{1}$ saturated: $V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN}$ :

$$V_{out}-V_{X} \ge V_{b}-V_{X}-V_{THN}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{THN}$$

$M_{2}$ saturated: $V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|$ :

$$V_{DD}-V_{X}\ge V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|$$
$$V_{X}\le V_{out}+|V_{THP}|$$

This is satisfied by proper $V_{b},I_{1},I_{B}$.

Small signal. Put $g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$.

$M_{1}$, $v_{gs1}=-v_{x}$, $v_{bs1}=-v_{x}$,
$v_{ds1}=v_{y}-v_{x}$, drain current entering drain:

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$
$$=-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{y}\tag{1}$$

It enters $Y$ and leaves into $X$.

$M_{2}$, define source-to-drain current $i_{sd2}$
entering $X$:

$$v_{sg2}=-v_{y},\;v_{sd2}=-v_{x}$$
$$i_{sd2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}$$
$$=-g_{m2}v_{y}-g_{ds2}v_{x}\tag{2}$$

Let $R_{1}$ be ac impedance from $Y$ to ground,
i.e. $I_{1}$ output impedance, $R_{2}$ from $X$
to ground, i.e. $I_{B}$ output impedance. Ideal:
$R_{1},R_{2}\to\infty$.

KCL $Y$:

$$\frac{v_{y}}{R_{1}}+i_{d1}=0 \tag{3}$$

KCL $X$:

$$I_{in}+i_{sd2}+i_{d1}=\frac{v_{x}}{R_{2}} \tag{4}$$

This is shunt-shunt negative feedback.
$v_{x}\uparrow \to$ $M_{1}$ current $\downarrow$
$\to$ $v_{y}\uparrow$ $\to$ $M_{2}$ $V_{SG}\downarrow$
$\to$ current into $X$ $\downarrow$ $\to$ $v_{x}\downarrow$.

First $\lambda=0$, no body, $R_{2}=\infty$ for intuition:

From (3): $v_{y}/R_{1}-g_{m1}v_{x}=0$,

$$ \frac{v_{y}}{v_{x}} = g_{m1}R_{1} $$

common-gate gain. From (4):

$$I_{in}-g_{m2}v_{y}-g_{m1}v_{x}=0$$

$$I_{in}=g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{m2}v_{y}=g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{1})v_{x}$$

Hence

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{x}}{I_{in}}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{1})}$$

$$R_{m}=\frac{v_{y}}{I_{in}}=\frac{R_{1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{1}}$$

If loop gain $T=g_{m2}R_{1}\gg 1$,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}},\;\;
R_{m}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

Indeed breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{2}$,
$v_{t}$ on $M_{2}$ gate, $I_{in}=0$:

$$-g_{m2}v_{t}-g_{m1}v_{x}=0,\;v_{y}=g_{m1}R_{1}v_{x}$$

$$ \frac{v_{y}}{v_{t}}=-g_{m2}R_{1} $$

so return loop gain is

$$T = g_{m2}R_{1}$$

CG without feedback has $R_{in}\approx 1/g_{m1}$.
Feedback divides it by $1+T$.

For output resistance put $I_{in}=0$, drive $Y$
by $v_{test}$, measure $i_{test}$.

$$0=g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{m2}v_{y}$$
$$i_{test}=v_{y}/R_{1}-g_{m1}v_{x}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{1/R_{1}+g_{m2}}=R_{1}||\frac1{g_{m2}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}}$$

So to first order transimpedance = output impedance.

Full expression with $r_{o}$, body, $R_{1},R_{2}$.
Put $G_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$,
$R_{1}'=1/(g_{ds1}+1/R_{1})=R_{1}||r_{o1}$.

From (1)(3):

$$v_{y}=G_{1}R_{1}'\,v_{x}\tag{5}$$

This is $1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})R_{1}'$ CG gain.
Put in (4):

$$I_{in}=v_{x}\left[\frac1{R_{2}}+g_{ds2}+G_{1}\right]
+v_{y}(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})$$

i.e.

$$R_{in}= \frac{1}{\frac1{R_{2}}+g_{ds2}+G_{1}+(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})G_{1}R_{1}'}$$

$$R_{m}= \frac{G_{1}R_{1}'}{\frac1{R_{2}}+g_{ds2}+G_{1}+(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})G_{1}R_{1}'}$$

For $R_{out}$, with $I_{in}=0$:

$$R_{out}= \frac{1}{\frac1{R_{1}}+g_{ds1}+\dfrac{G_{1}(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})}{\frac1{R_{2}}+g_{ds2}+G_{1}}}$$

With ideal sources $R_{1},R_{2}\to\infty$:

$$R_{in0}= \frac{1}{g_{ds2}+g_{m2}G_{1}r_{o1}}$$

$$R_{m0}= \frac{G_{1}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}+g_{m2}G_{1}}$$

$$R_{out0}= \frac{G_{1}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}+g_{m2}G_{1}}$$

where $G_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$.

If $(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}\gg1$, $g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg1$:

$$R_{in0}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}}$$

$$R_{m0}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}}$$

$$R_{out0}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}}$$

$g_{mb1}$ just adds to $g_{m1}$. Without body,
replace $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ by $g_{m1}$.

Intuition with $R_{1}=\infty$: at $Y$ the only ac
branch is $M_{1}$ drain, so $i_{d1}=0$.
Hence all signal $I_{in}$ must flow in $M_{2}$:
$I_{in}+i_{sd2}=0$. But $i_{sd2}\approx -g_{m2}v_{y}$,
so $v_{y}\approx I_{in}/g_{m2}$. $M_{1}$ carries
no signal current, it acts as a huge CG voltage
amplifier $v_{y}/v_{x}\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}$
to drive $M_{2}$ from a tiny $v_{x}$.

Hence very low $R_{in}$, moderate $R_{out}\approx
1/g_{m2}$, positive $R_{m}\approx 1/g_{m2}$.

Poles: $C_{X}$ at $X$ sees $R_{in}$ tiny $\to$
non-dominant very high frequency pole.
$C_{Y}$ at $Y$ sees $\approx R_{1}'||1/g_{m2}$
$\to$ dominant pole. The loop is normally stable
if the two poles are well separated. The bridging
$C_{gd2}$ between $X$ and $Y$ with large positive
gain gives negative Miller capacitance, to be
checked at very high frequency.

In use this is a low-input-impedance TIA / active-
feedback common-gate stage. Linear range is limited
by $M_{2}$, which carries essentially the full
signal current: need $|I_{in}|\ll I_{D2}$ for
$g_{m2}$ constant.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate NMOS, M2 as the PMOS feedback device, and the feedback path to the input node. It gives the correct low input resistance and the approximate transimpedance and output resistance of 1/gm2.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is a shunt-shunt, current in - voltage out
amplifier. $I_{in}$ is the signal.

* $M_{1}$ is NMOS. $V_{b}$ DC, source $=$ input,
drain $=$ output. Common-gate forward amplifier.
* $M_{2}$ is PMOS. Source to $V_{DD}$ AC ground,
gate $=$ output, drain $=$ input.
Common-source feedback voltage to current.
* $I_{1}$ is the active load of $M_{1}$.
* The lower source, call it $I_{B}$, is the DC
sink at the input.

$M_{2}$ n-well is strapped to $V_{DD}$, no backgate.
$M_{1}$ p-sub is to GND, backgate $g_{mb1}$ exists.

Assume saturation.

DC, ignoring $ \lambda $ for the moment, $I_{in}=I_{in,DC}+i_{in}$:

Output KCL: gate draws no current,
$$ I_{D1}=I_{1} $$
Input KCL:
$$ I_{in,DC}+I_{D1}+I_{SD2}-I_{B}=0 $$
$$ I_{SD2}=I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in,DC} $$

$$ I_{D1}=\tfrac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}(V_{b}-V_{X}-V_{THN})^{2} $$
$$ V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1} $$
$$ I_{SD2}=\tfrac12\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|)^{2} $$
$$ V_{out}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2} $$

To first order $V_{X}$ is fixed by $I_{1}$ and $V_{b}$,
$V_{out}$ is fixed by $I_{SD2}$, i.e. by $I_{2}-I_{1}-I_{in}$:
$$ V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|-\sqrt{\frac{2(I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in})}
{\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}}} $$
Non-linear, non-inverting transimpedance. $dV_{out}/dI_{in}>0$.

Saturation needs

$$ M_{1}: V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN}\;\Rightarrow\;V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{THN} $$
$$ M_{2}: V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|\;\Rightarrow\;V_{out}\ge V_{X}-|V_{THP}| $$
easily met.

Small signal. Put $v_{x}$ at input, $v_{out}$ at output.
$I_{1},I_{B}$ AC open, $V_{b},V_{DD}$ AC ground.
$v_{gs1}=-v_{x}$, $v_{bs1}=-v_{x}$, $v_{ds1}=v_{out}-v_{x}$,
$v_{gs2}=v_{out}$, $v_{ds2}=v_{x}$.

NMOS convention into-drain:

$$ i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1} $$
$$ =-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{out} $$
$$ i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}=g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{ds2}v_{x} $$

Body current 0, so source into-current $i_{s1}=-i_{d1}$.

Output node: only $M_{1}$ drain and $M_{2}$ gate:
$$ i_{d1}=0\;\;AC \tag{1} $$
i.e.
$$ -(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{out}=0 $$
$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{x}}=\frac{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}}
\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1} $$
the CG gain with ideal load.

Input node: $i_{in}$ in, $i_{s1}$ out to $M_{1}$,
$i_{d2}$ out to $M_{2}$:
$$ -i_{in}+i_{s1}+i_{d2}=0 $$
$$ i_{in}=-i_{d1}+i_{d2} \tag{2} $$

With (1), $i_{d1}=0$, $i_{s1}=0$:
$$ i_{in}=i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{ds2}v_{x} $$

Let $G_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$. Then
$v_{x}=v_{out}g_{ds1}/G_{1}$ and

$$ i_{in}=v_{out}\left[g_{m2}+\frac{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}{G_{1}}\right] $$

Transimpedance:

$$ R_{T}=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{G_{1}}{g_{m2}G_{1}+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}+\dfrac{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}{G_{1}}} $$

$$ \approx \frac1{g_{m2}} $$

Positive, non-inverting. In the ideal $r_{o}\to\infty$ limit,
$v_{x}\to 0$, virtual ground, $i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}$.

Input resistance $R_{in}=v_{x}/i_{in}$:

$$ R_{in}=R_{T}\frac{g_{ds1}}{G_{1}}
= \frac{g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}G_{1}+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}} $$

$$ \approx \frac{1}{(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}\,g_{m2}} $$

i.e. the $1/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})$ of a CG divided
by loop gain.

Output resistance: put $v_{test}$ at output,
$i_{in}=0$, measure $i_{test}$.
$i_{test}=i_{d1}$, $0=-i_{d1}+i_{d2}$,
$$ R_{out}=\frac{G_{1}+g_{ds2}}{g_{m2}G_{1}+g_{ds1}g_{ds2}} $$

$$ \approx \frac1{g_{m2}} $$

This is feedback. Open loop forward transimpedance
with $M_{2}$ off is $A\approx r_{o1}'$, $r_{o1}'=r_{o1}\parallel R_{1}$,
non-inverting. Feedback $i_{f}$ returned to input by $M_{2}$
is $\approx -g_{m2}v_{out}$, so $\beta\approx -g_{m2}$.
Loop gain

$$ T=-A\beta\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}'\gg 1 $$

Closed loop $R_{T}=A/(1+T)\approx 1/g_{m2}$,
$R_{in}=R_{in,open}/(1+T)$,
$R_{out}=R_{out,open}/(1+T)$.

In $s$-domain $T(s)$ has the high-$Z$ output pole
$\omega_{out}=1/R_{out,open}C_{out}$ and the CG
input pole $\omega_{in}\approx(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})/C_{in}$.
Unity loop frequency $\approx g_{m2}/C_{out}$.
Stability needs $g_{m2}/C_{out}<(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})/C_{in}$,
normally satisfied unless $C_{in}$ is very large.

In short: low-$Z$ non-inverting TIA with
gain $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, $R_{in}\approx 0$,
$R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2}$, bandwidth $\approx g_{m2}/C_{L}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate NMOS input device and M2 as the PMOS feedback device, describes the feedback path to the input node, and derives very low input resistance with transimpedance and output resistance approximately 1/gm2.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No. It just gets slower.

There is no stable logical state. With an odd
number of inversions around the loop you cannot
satisfy $V_{2}=\overline{V_{1}}$, $V_{3}=\overline{V_{2}}$,
$V_{1}=\overline{V_{3}}$ in the static digital sense.
In large signal the signal must keep propagating
around, inverting each time. A larger $C_{L}$
just means a larger stage delay, i.e. a longer
period.

That can be seen small-signal. Bias each inverter
at its trip point, for start-up. Let $g_{m}$ be its
transconductance and $R$ its small-signal output
resistance driving $C_{L}$ :

$$ A(s) = \frac{-g_{m}R}{1+sR C_{L}} = \frac{-A_{0}}{1+s\tau} $$

with $A_{0}=g_{m}R$, $\tau = RC_{L}$.
Around the 3-stage loop,

$$ L(s) = A(s)^{3} = \left[\frac{-A_{0}}{1+s\tau}\right]^{3} $$

$L=1$ is the closed-loop pole. At DC $L=-A_{0}^{3}$,
i.e. $180^{\circ}$.

Put $s=j\omega$, $x=\omega\tau$. Per stage

$$ A(j\omega) = \frac{-A_{0}}{1+jx} $$

$$ \angle A = \pi - \tan^{-1}x $$

Total around loop:

$$ \angle L = 3\pi - 3\tan^{-1}x $$

For oscillation we need in total $2\pi$, i.e. $0$
mod $2\pi$, i.e. an extra $180^{\circ}$ from the
three poles:

$$ 3\pi -3\tan^{-1}x = 2\pi \;{\rm mod}\;2\pi $$

$$ 3\tan^{-1}x = \pi $$

$$ \tan^{-1}x = 60^{\circ} $$

i.e.

$$ x = \sqrt{3} $$

$$ \omega_{osc} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\tau} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{R C_{L}} $$

That is the frequency where the phases add up
for regeneration. At that frequency,

$$ |L| = \left[\frac{A_{0}}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\right]^{3}
      = \left[\frac{A_{0}}{\sqrt{1+3}}\right]^{3}
      = \left(\frac{A_{0}}{2}\right)^{3} $$

Start-up requires $|L|\ge 1$, i.e.

$$ A_{0} \ge 2 $$

$C_{L}$ has dropped out. Increasing $C_{L}$ pushes
the $180^{\circ}$-frequency down as $1/C_{L}$, but
the attenuation of the three low-pass poles at
that frequency stays exactly the same, $1/2$ per
stage.

Hence once $g_{m}R>2$ the metastable bias point
with all nodes at trip stays unstable, with
a complex pole pair in the RHP whose imaginary
part $\approx \sqrt{3}/RC_{L}\to 0$ as $C_{L}\to\infty$.
For any finite $C_{L}$, however large, the circuit
starts and then limits to a rail-to-rail ring
oscillation of period $\propto C_{L}$.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No. It gets slower, but it still starts up.

Put each inverter in its high-gain region with

$$A_v(s) = \frac{-g_m R_{out}}{1+sR_{out}C_L}
      = \frac{-A_0}{1+s/\omega_p}$$

$$\omega_p = \frac{1}{R_{out}C_L}$$

The loop gain of the 3 in a loop is

$$L(s)=\left[\frac{-A_0}{1+s/\omega_p}\right]^3$$

At DC, $L=-A_0^3$, i.e. $180^{\circ}$. The poles add
lag.

One stage at $s=j\omega$ has phase

$$\angle = 180^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}$$

3 stages modulo $360^{\circ}$:

$$\angle L = 180^{\circ}-3\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}$$

For Barkhausen, $\angle L = 0$ mod $360^{\circ}$.
We need $180^{\circ}$ extra from the 3 poles,
$60^{\circ}$ per pole:

$$3\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{osc}}{\omega_p}=180^{\circ}$$

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{osc}}{\omega_p}=60^{\circ}$$

$$\omega_{osc} = \sqrt{3}\,\omega_p = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{R_{out}C_L}$$

At that frequency the magnitude per stage is

$$\frac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+(\omega_{osc}/\omega_p)^2}}
 = \frac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+3}} = \frac{A_0}{2}$$

so

$$|L(j\omega_{osc})| = \left(\frac{A_0}{2}\right)^3
  = \frac{A_0^3}{8}$$

independent of $\omega_p$, i.e. independent of $C_L$.

If $A_0>2$ for start-up, $|L|>1$ at the $0^{\circ}$
frequency, and the DC metastable point where all
inverters are at $V_M$ is unstable.

Increasing $C_L$ just moves $\omega_p$ down, and
$\omega_{osc}$ moves down with it, as $1/C_L$.
The attenuation at crossover stays $1/2$ per stage.
In the time domain, the inverters just take longer
to charge the large $C_L$, so the period $\propto
C_L$, but there is still no stable digital DC state
for an odd ring.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that the ring continues oscillating at a lower frequency and supports it with a valid small-signal phase and gain analysis: the oscillation frequency scales as 1/CL while the loop-gain condition is independent of CL.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No. Making the $C_L$'s big only slows the
oscillator down. It does not kill it.

Put a realistic memoryless model on the inverter: infinite
input impedance, output current a function of input voltage
(and output voltage). E.g. in small signal

$$ v_{o} = -g_m \left(r_o \parallel \frac{1}{sC_L}\right) v_{i}
 = \frac{-g_m r_o}{1+s r_o C_L} v_{i} $$

Then for 3 identical stages in a loop the loop gain is

$$ L(s) = \left[\frac{-A_0}{1+s\tau}\right]^3 $$

where $A_0=g_m r_o$ and $\tau = r_o C_L$.

$L=1$ for pole:

$$(1+s\tau)^3 = (-A_0)^3$$

i.e.

$$1+s\tau = -A_0 \cdot \{1, e^{\pm j2\pi/3}\}$$

The first root is real stable. The complex pair is

$$ s = \frac{-1+A_0/2}{\tau} \pm j\frac{A_0\sqrt{3}}{2\tau} $$

It is in the right half plane iff

$$ A_0 > 2 $$

independent of $\tau$, i.e. independent of $C_L$.
That is the usual $60^{\circ}$ per stage:

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}=60^{\circ}$$

$$\omega_{0} =\sqrt{3}\,\omega_p = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{r_o C_L}$$

for the compressed large-signal gain of 2.

In other words, as $C_L$ grows the pole frequency
$\omega_p=1/r_oC_L$ falls, but the frequency where the
loop has $360^{\circ}$ of phase also falls in the same
proportion. At $\omega_0$:

$$\left|\frac{1}{j\omega_0 C_L}\right| = \frac{r_o}{\sqrt{3}}$$

stays comparable to $r_o$. Loop magnitude at the
phase crossover does not go to zero.

Large signal, this is even more general. With
$V_1,V_2,V_3$ the three node voltages,

$$ C_L \frac{dV_i}{dt} = G(V_{i-1},V_i) $$

where $G$ is the inverter's static $I$-$V$ characteristic.
$C_L$ is only a time-scale factor. Put $\tau = t/C_L$:

$$\frac{dV_i}{d\tau} = G(V_{i-1},V_i)$$

The phase portrait, equilibria, stability, existence
of a limit cycle are independent of $C_L>0$.

In particular $C_L$ is open at DC. It creates
no new DC equilibria. An odd ring has no stable
binary DC equilibrium. It must keep moving, except
for the analog metastable point where all $V_i=V_M$,
which is unstable when $A_0>2$.

What large $C_L$ does is:

* $\omega_{osc} \propto 1/C_L \to 0$
* growth rate $\sigma = (A_0/2-1)/r_oC_L \to 0^{+}$

i.e. the oscillation gets arbitrarily slow to start
and to run, but for any finite $C_L$ it starts.

Only in the strict mathematical limit $C=\infty$
does $dV/dt \to 0$ and the dynamics freeze.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that equal capacitors slow the ring without stopping oscillation. The small-signal analysis correctly shows that the oscillation condition is independent of capacitance and the frequency scales as 1/C_L; the additional time-scaling argument is also consistent.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
A 3 stage CMOS ring is to first order

$$f_{0}\approx \frac{1}{2N T_{d}}\qquad N=3$$

$T_{d}$ is the large signal delay of one inverter.
Model the inverter as an effective $R$ driving $C_{L}$,

$$ T_{d}\propto R C_{L} $$

$R$ is fixed by the transistor sizing. So

$$ f_{0} \propto \frac{1}{C_{L}} $$

Double the $C_{L}$: $f_{0}\to f_{0}/2$.

The dynamic power is

$$P \approx N C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0} \propto C_{L}f_{0}$$

so to first order

$$P = {\rm const}$$

with $C_{L}$.

For white-noise dominated operation the SSB phase
noise can be put in Leeson form

$${\cal L}(\Delta f) \propto \frac{1}{P}
\left(\frac{f_{0}}{\Delta f}\right)^{2}$$

at a given absolute offset $\Delta f$.
Indeed in Hajimiri-Lee language

$${\cal L}(\Delta f) \approx
\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^{2}}{2q_{max}^{2}}\,
\frac{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f}{ (2\pi\Delta f)^{2}}$$

$\overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f \approx 4kT\gamma g_{m}$ is
fixed by the transistors, $\Gamma_{rms}$ is fixed by
the normalized waveform shape, and

$$q_{max} \approx C_{tot}V_{DD} \propto C_{L}$$

is the maximum charge swing on the node.

Hence at fixed $\Delta f$

$${\cal L} \propto \frac{1}{q_{max}^{2}} \propto \frac{1}{C_{L}^{2}}
\propto \frac{f_{0}^{2}}{P}$$

Double $C_{L}$:

* $q_{max}\to 2q_{max}$
* $f_{0}\to f_{0}/2$
* $P\to P$

$${\cal L}\to \frac{1}{4}{\cal L}$$

i.e. about 6 dB lower phase noise at the same
absolute offset, in both $1/f^{2}$ and $1/f^{3}$
regions. The $1/f^{3}$ corner in absolute Hz is
essentially unchanged.

In other words the $20\log(f_{0}/\Delta f)$
is 6 dB smaller. Normalized to the carrier,
${\cal L}$ at $\Delta f/f_{0}=$const, and the
$P$-$f_{0}$ FOM, is unchanged.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly explains that doubling the capacitance roughly halves the oscillation frequency and gives a fourfold (about 6 dB) phase-noise reduction at a fixed absolute offset. It also correctly notes the unchanged result at a fixed relative offset.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
For first order, nothing changes in shape,
only in frequency scale.

Let the delay of one inverter be

$$t_d \approx R_{eff}C_L$$

so that for $N=3$

$$f_0 \approx \frac{1}{2Nt_d} \propto \frac{1}{C_L}$$

Double all the $C_L$'s, with the same inverters,
same $V_{DD}$:

* $f_0' = f_0/2$
* waveform vs. normalized time is the same,
  just played $2\times$ slower.

Dynamic power

$$P \approx N C_L V_{DD}^2 f_0$$

stays about the same, because $C_L f_0 = {\rm const}$.

Phase noise is, to first order,

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta f) \propto \frac{f_0^2}{P}\,
 \frac{1}{\Delta f^2} $$

white $1/f^2$ region, Leeson/Hajimiri-Lee.
In Hajimiri-Lee form at a fixed absolute $\Delta f$

$${\cal L}(\Delta f)\approx 
10\log \frac{\overline{i_n^2/\Delta f}\;\Gamma_{rms}^2}
{8\pi^{2}\Delta f^{2} q_{max}^{2}} $$

$\Gamma_{rms}$, the rms of the impulse-sensitivity
function, depends only on the normalized waveform,
so it does not change. $\overline{i_n^2/\Delta f}\approx
4kT\gamma \,\overline{g_m}$ averaged over phase
does not change.

What changes is the maximum charge swing

$$q_{max}= C_L V_{DD}$$

Double $C_L$ $\to$ double $q_{max}$.

Hence at the same absolute offset $\Delta f$:

$${\cal L}'/{\cal L} \approx \left(\frac{q_{max}}{q_{max}'}\right)^{2}
= \frac14 $$

i.e. about 6-dB lower phase noise power, both in
the $1/f^2$ and in the upconverted $1/f^3$ region.
This is just $20\log f_0'/f_0$.

In other words the FOM

$${\cal L}-20\log\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}+10\log P$$

is unchanged. At the same fractional offset
$\Delta f/f_0$, ${\cal L}$ is unchanged.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that doubling the capacitors halves the oscillation frequency and gives about 6 dB lower phase noise at a fixed absolute offset. The doubled charge swing provides a valid supporting argument; it also correctly notes that phase noise is unchanged at a fixed fractional offset.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
For the 3 stage loop to first order

$$f_{0}\approx \frac{1}{6t_{D}}$$

$t_{D}$ is the large signal delay of one inverter loaded
by $C_{L}$.

$$t_{D}\propto R_{on}C_{L}$$

for fixed inverter size. Put $C_{L}\to 2C_{L}$:

* $t_{D}\to 2t_{D}$
* $f_{0}\to f_{0}/2$

The waveform shape is essentially unchanged, just
stretched in time by $2\times$.

The average power, to first order dynamic plus
crow-bar,

$$P \approx N\,C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}+N\,E_{sc}f_{0}$$

$$E_{sc}\propto t_{trans}\propto C_{L}$$

so

$$P \propto N C_{L} \times \frac{1}{NC_{L}} = {\rm const}$$

Power stays essentially the same.

Phase noise: in Hajimiri-Lee terms

$${\cal L}(\Delta\omega)\propto
\frac{ \overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f}
{\Delta\omega^{2}\,q_{max}^{2}}$$

$\Gamma_{rms}$, waveform symmetry, cyclostationary
average of the inverter white noise $\overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f$
stay essentially the same, because the circuit
spends the same fraction of the period in
transition.

$$q_{max}=C_{L}V_{DD}$$

is the maximum charge swing on the capacitor.
Hence at a given absolute offset $\Delta\omega$:

$${\cal L} \propto \frac{1}{q_{max}^{2}}\propto \frac{1}{C_{L}^{2}}$$

In jitter terms, threshold crossing

$$\sigma_{t}^{2}\approx \frac{\overline{v_{n}^{2}}}{SR^{2}}$$

$$\overline{v_{n}^{2}}\approx \frac{kT}{C_{L}},\qquad
SR\propto \frac{1}{C_{L}}$$

$$\sigma_{t}^{2}\propto C_{L}$$

Period $T_{0}\propto C_{L}$, so

$${\cal L}(\Delta f)\propto f_{0}^{3}\sigma_{T}^{2}
\propto \frac{\sigma_{T}^{2}}{T_{0}^{3}}
\propto \frac{1}{C_{L}^{2}}$$

i.e. the familiar

$${\cal L}\propto \frac{kT}{P}\left(\frac{f_{0}}{\Delta f}\right)^{2}$$

with $P\approx$ const.

Doubling $C_{L}$ halves $f_{0}$, so for the same
$P$ and same absolute $\Delta f$,

$${\cal L}\to {\cal L}/4$$

about 6 dB lower phase noise, both in $1/f^{2}$
and $1/f^{3}$ regions.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly states that doubling the capacitors halves the oscillation frequency and lowers phase noise by about a factor of four (6 dB) at a fixed absolute offset, with a supporting delay argument.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
Yes. A large $C_L$ kills the loop.

Model each inverter in small signal at its high-gain
bias as $-g_mR$ with an output pole. Let $R$ be the
output resistance, $C_0$ the intrinsic capacitance
at each output. Then

$$ H_{2}(s)=H_{3}(s)=\frac{-A_0}{1+s\tau_0} , \qquad
H_1(s)=\frac{-A_0}{1+s\tau_1} $$

where $A_0=g_mR$, $\tau_0=RC_0$,
$\tau_1=R(C_0+C_L)$.

Close the 3 in a loop. Break the loop, the loop
transmission is

$$ L(s)=H_1H_2H_3 = \frac{-A_0^3}{(1+s\tau_1)(1+s\tau_0)^2} .$$

Natural frequencies satisfy $L=1$, i.e.

$$(1+s\tau_1)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0.$$

At DC $L$ is negative real: 3 inversions = net
inversion. This is negative feedback. To oscillate
it must get $180^\circ$ extra phase lag from the
poles to become positive feedback.

Indeed write $s=j\omega$:

$$\angle H_i = 180^\circ - \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_i .$$

$$\angle L = 3\times 180^\circ -\sum \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_i
\equiv 180^\circ-\sum \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_i \pmod{360^\circ}.$$

For $L=1$, $\angle L =0$, so we need

$$\tan^{-1}\omega_0\tau_1+2\tan^{-1}\omega_0\tau_0 = 180^\circ \tag{1}$$
$$|L|=\frac{A_0^3}{\sqrt{1+(\omega_0\tau_1)^2}
\left[1+(\omega_0\tau_0)^2\right]}\ge 1 \tag{2}$$

for some $\omega_0$. That is the Barkhausen
start-up condition. In particular the bias point must
be unstable.

If $\tau_1\gg \tau_0$, i.e. $C_L$ dominant, (1) is
essentially impossible with gain.

In fact the max phase from the dominant pole alone
is $90^\circ$. To get to $180^\circ$ you must go to
$\omega_0$ comparable to $1/\tau_0$, where the other
two poles contribute. Then $\omega_0\tau_1\gg 1$.

E.g. put $\tan^{-1}\omega_0\tau_1\approx 90^\circ$.
Then (1) needs $2\tan^{-1}\omega_0\tau_0\approx 90^\circ$,
i.e. $\omega_0\approx 1/\tau_0$. Then

$$|L|\approx \frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_0\tau_1)\times 2}
= \frac{A_0^3}{2}\frac{\tau_0}{\tau_1}
= \frac{A_0^3}{2}\frac{C_0}{C_0+C_L}\ll 1$$

for $C_L$ large. The dominant pole has rolled off
the gain below unity before the non-dominant poles
can give enough phase. More generally no $\omega$
satisfies (1) and (2) together once $C_L$ is large
enough.

In $s$-domain, $a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0$ with

$$\begin{aligned}
a_0 &=1+A_0^3\\
a_1 &=\tau_1+2\tau_0\\
a_2 &=2\tau_1\tau_0+\tau_0^2\\
a_3 &=\tau_1\tau_0^2
\end{aligned}$$

is stable iff $a_1a_2>a_0a_3$ by Routh-Hurwitz.
That is

$$(\tau_1+2\tau_0)(2\tau_1\tau_0+\tau_0^2)>
(1+A_0^3)\tau_1\tau_0^2,$$

which is satisfied for sufficiently large $\tau_1$.
The DC solution with all inverters at $\approx V_{th}$
becomes stable. This is just dominant-pole compensation
of a 3-stage negative-feedback amplifier.

Intuitively, $C_L\to\infty$ holds its node at AC
ground, $dV/dt=I/C_L\to 0$, breaking the AC loop.
Gain around the loop $\to 0$.

The odd number of inversions guarantees no $0/1$
digital equilibrium, but there is an analog
equilibrium with all gates linear. Normally it is
unstable and the circuit starts up to a limit cycle.
With a dominant pole it is stabilized, and perturbations
ring down to $V_{th}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that arbitrarily large loading on one node can stop oscillation, and explains the dominant-pole mechanism: the loaded node's lag causes excessive loop gain roll-off before the phase condition is met. The pole model and stability argument support the essential conclusion; its approximations do not change it.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
Yes. With finite-gain inverters the loop is stabilized.

Break the loop and model each inverter at its
switching point as an inverting low-pass,

$$ H_0(s) = \frac{-g_m R_0}{1+sR_0 C_0} $$

$C_0$ is the intrinsic load, $R_0$ the output
resistance, $-g_mR_0=-A_0$ the small signal gain.

Put $C_L$ on one node:

$$ H_L(s) = \frac{-A_0}{1+sR_0(C_0+C_L)} $$

The small signal loop gain of the 3 in a ring is

$$ L(s)=H_L(s)H_0^2(s)=
\frac{(-A_0)^3}{[1+s\tau_L][1+s\tau_0]^2}$$

where $\tau_0=R_0C_0$, $\tau_L=R_0(C_0+C_L)$.

At dc, $L_0=-A_0^3$. This is a negative feedback loop.
It oscillates only if the poles contribute an
extra $180^{\circ}$ lag at a frequency where
$|L|\ge 1$, i.e. Barkhausen $L(j\omega)=1$.

Let

$$\phi_L = \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_L,\qquad
  \phi_0 = \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0 .$$

$$ \angle H_L = 180^{\circ}-\phi_L,\;
   \angle H_0 = 180^{\circ}-\phi_0 $$

$$\angle L = 3\cdot 180^{\circ}-\phi_L-2\phi_0 .$$

Mod $360^{\circ}$, $\angle L=0$ requires

$$\phi_L+2\phi_0 = 180^{\circ} \tag{1}$$
$$\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_L+2\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0=\pi .$$

The magnitude is

$$|L| = \frac{A_0^3}
{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau_L)^2}\,[1+(\omega\tau_0)^2]} .
\tag{2}$$

For identical stages $\tau_L=\tau_0$ this gives
$\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0=60^{\circ}$, $\omega\tau_0=\sqrt3$,
$|L|=A_0^3/8$. $A_0>2$ oscillates.

Now let $C_L\to\infty$, $\tau_L\gg\tau_0$.
From (1), $\phi_L\approx 90^{\circ}$ for any
reasonable $\omega\gg 1/\tau_L$, so we need

$$2\phi_0\approx 90^{\circ},\quad \phi_0\approx 45^{\circ},$$

i.e.

$$\omega_{180}\approx \frac1{\tau_0} .$$

The $180^{\circ}$ frequency stays finite, determined
by the fast inverters. At that frequency from (2)

$$|L|\approx \frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_{180}\tau_L)\cdot 2}
 = \frac{A_0^3}{2\,\tau_L/\tau_0}\to 0
 \;\;{\rm as}\;\; \tau_L\to\infty .$$

In fact $C_L\to\infty$ is an ac short to ground.
The loop gain goes to zero at any finite frequency.
Phase $180^{\circ}$ is reached only where there is
no gain. Routh-Hurwitz on

$$(1+s\tau_L)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0$$

gives stability for

$$\frac{\tau_L}{\tau_0} > \frac{1+A_0^3}{2} .$$

So the linear equilibrium, all inverters biased
at $V_{th}$, becomes stable.

Physically, $V_1$ becomes very slow, $V_2,V_3$
follow quasi-statically. The two fast inverters
in cascade are a non-inverting high gain $+A_2A_3$.
Then

$$C_L \frac{dV_1}{dt} = I_1(V_3)=I_1(g(V_1))$$

with $dg/dV_1>0$, $dI_1/dV_3=-g_{m1}<0$.
This is first-order negative feedback:

$$\frac{d}{dV_1}\frac{dV_1}{dt}<0.$$

$V_1$ approaches the $I_{p}=I_{n}$ equilibrium
asymptotically, with no overshoot. Overshoot,
which requires the delay of inv2-inv3 to be
comparable to the $R_0C_L$ time, is what sustains
the normal ring limit cycle. For $C_L\to\infty$
the swing needed to switch inv2, $\sim I\,t_d/C_L$,
goes to zero. The circuit settles to a dc analog
value, not rail to rail.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly explains that a very large capacitor on one node creates a dominant pole, driving loop gain below unity at the required phase condition. The resulting slow-node, quasi-static settling explanation also agrees with the golden solution.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
Yes. With one stage heavily loaded the loop
becomes a stable negative feedback loop.

Model the inverter in the linear region around
its switching threshold by

$$ A(s) = \frac{-A_0}{1+s\tau}$$

$A_0 = g_mR_{out} >0$, $\tau = R_{out}C$.
Let $\tau_0$ be the intrinsic delay of the unloaded
inverter and $\tau_1$ the delay of the loaded
inverter,

$$p_0 = \frac1{\tau_0}\,,\quad p_1=\frac1{\tau_1}
 =\frac{1}{R_{out}(C_0+C_L)} .$$

Breaking the loop, the small signal loop gain is

$$ L(s) = \left(\frac{-A_0}{1+s/p_1}\right)
         \left(\frac{-A_0}{1+s/p_0}\right)^2
       = \frac{-A_0^{3}}{(1+s/p_1)(1+s/p_0)^2} .$$

At DC $L=-A_0^3$, i.e. $180^{\circ}$.
Oscillation start-up needs

$$L(j\omega)=1$$

i.e. $180^{\circ}$ more phase lag from the
three poles,

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{p_1}+2\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{p_0}=\pi \tag{1}$$

with

$$|L|=\frac{A_0^3}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/p_1)^2}\,
 \left[1+(\omega/p_0)^2\right]}\ge 1 .\tag{2}$$

(1) always has a solution $\omega_{180}$, since
the left side goes monotonically from 0 to $3\pi/2$.

Let $C_L\to\infty$, i.e. $p_1\to 0$.
For any finite $\omega>0$,
$\tan^{-1}(\omega/p_1)\to \pi/2$. Then (1) gives

$$\frac{\pi}{2}+2\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{180}}{p_0}\to \pi$$

i.e.

$$\omega_{180}\to p_0 .$$

The phase crossover stays finite. But then

$$|L(j\omega_{180})|\approx 
\frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_{180}/p_1)\cdot 2}\to 0$$

because $p_1\to 0$. In particular for large enough
$C_L$, $|L|<1$ at the $180^{\circ}$ frequency.
The Barkhausen condition fails.

In Routh-Hurwitz terms, $1-L(s)=0$ is

$$(1+s\tau_1)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0$$

i.e.

$$s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0$$

with $a_2=p_1+2p_0$, $a_1=2p_1p_0+p_0^2$,
$a_0=(1+A_0^3)p_1p_0^2$. Stability needs
$a_2a_1>a_0$, i.e.

$$2p_1^2+(4-A_0^3)p_0p_1+2p_0^2>0.$$

For $p_1=p_0$ and $A_0^3\gg 8$ this is $<0$:
unstable bias point, oscillation starts.
For $p_1\to 0$ this is $>0$: the bias point
becomes stable.

Physically, make $C_L$ dominant. The $C_L$ node
$V_1$ is slow, the other two inverters are
essentially instantaneous. Put $V_{in1}=h(V_1)$
where $h=f\circ f$ is the double inversion,
non-inverting, high gain around the threshold.
Then to first order

$$C_L\frac{dV_1}{dt}=I_P(V_{in1},V_1)-I_N(V_{in1},V_1)
\equiv I(V_1).$$

$I(V_1)>0$ for $V_1$ low, $<0$ for $V_1$ high,
strictly decreasing. There is one zero,
$V_1\approx V_{th}$, and

$$\frac{dV_1}{dt}$$

always pushes $V_1$ toward it. There is no overshoot.

In time domain: as soon as $V_1$ crosses $V_{th}$,
the fast inverters immediately flip the input of
the first inverter and reverse its output current,
before $V_1$ can swing to the rail. $V_1$ is
trapped at the analog threshold. The odd ring
has no digital stable state, but it has an analog
stable state with all inverters linear, i.e.
essentially single-dominant-pole negative
feedback.

answer.text:
It's a 3-stage CMOS ring. To first order nothing
happens to the waveforms except for the current and
capacitance level.

Let $C_1$ be the total capacitance on one output node,
$I_1$ the average charging/discharging current that
one inverter sees, $f_0$ the oscillation frequency.

$$ f_0 \approx \frac{1}{2N T_d} $$

$$T_d \approx \frac{C_1 V_{DD}}{I_1}$$

$C_1$ is

* gate $C_{ox}WL$ of the next stage
* drain junction + overlap of this stage

all $\propto W$ if interconnect is neglected.

$I_1$ is the MOS $I_D$ in switching, for the
same terminal voltages,

$$ I_1 \propto \frac{W}{L} $$

Double $W_{n},W_{p}$ :

* $C_1 \to 2C_1$
* $I_1 \to 2I_1$

Hence

$$T_d \to \frac{2C_1 V_{DD}}{2I_1}=T_d$$

Waveform shape, swing $\approx V_{DD}$, slew
$I_1/C_1$ and $f_0$ are essentially unchanged.

Dynamic power

$$ P = N f_0 C_1 V_{DD}^2 $$

goes to $2P$.

Put in Hajimiri-Lee form,

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta\omega) =
\frac{\overline{\Gamma_{rms}^2}}{q_{max}^2}\,
\frac{\bar S_i}{8(\Delta\omega)^2} $$

for white, and similarly with upconversion for $1/f$.

* $\Gamma(t)$, the impulse sensitivity function,
depends only on the normalized waveform. It is
unchanged.
* $q_{max}$, the maximum charge swing on the node,

$$q_{max} \approx C_1 V_{DD} \to 2q_{max}$$

* $\bar S_i$, the time averaged channel noise current:

thermal: $\;S_i = 4kT\gamma g_m$

$1/f$: $\;S_i = \frac{K}{WL C_{ox}f} g_m^2$

For the same $V_{GS}(t),V_{DS}(t)$ trajectory,
$g_m(t) \propto W$. So instantaneous and averaged

$$ \bar S_{i,th} \propto W \to 2\bar S_{i,th} $$
$$ \bar S_{i,1/f} \propto \frac{W^2}{W} = W \to 2\bar S_{i,1/f} $$

i.e. twice the noise power.

Hence

$${\cal L} \propto \frac{\bar S_i}{q_{max}^2}
 \propto \frac{W}{W^2} = \frac1W $$

Doubling $W$:

$${\cal L}_{new} = \frac{2}{4}{\cal L}_{old}
 = \frac12 {\cal L}_{old}$$

in power.

That is 6-dB reduction from $q_{max}^2$ minus 3-dB
increase from $S_i$, net:

*3 dB lower phase noise, both in the $1/f^2$ and
in the $1/f^3$ region.*

In essence $kT/C$ signal-to-noise is improved by
doubling $C$. You pay twice the power for it, so the
oscillator FoM is unchanged.

The frequency and doubled-power observations are also consistent.

for white noise, and with $\Gamma_{dc}^{2}$ for the

goes $\times 2$, i.e.

and for $1/f$,

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
Apply a small change $V_{x}$ to the common supply and
let $V_{o1},V_{o2},V_{o3}$ be the resulting changes at the
oscillator nodes. Put the circuit at the high gain
meta-stable point and linearize each inverter.

For one inverter let the input change be $V_{i}$,
the output change be $V_{o}$. NMOS: source ac ground.
PMOS: source $V_{x}$.

Small signal NMOS drain current into the drain:

$$i_{dn}=g_{mn}V_{i}+g_{dsn}V_{o}$$

leaving the output node.

Small signal PMOS source to drain current:

$$i_{sdp}=g_{mp}v_{sg}+g_{dsp}v_{sd}
 =g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})+g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o})$$

entering the output node. Bulk of PMOS is to $V_{x}$,
so $v_{sb}=0$.

KCL at the output, no other ac load,

$$i_{dn}-i_{sdp}=0$$

i.e.

$$g_{mn}V_{i}+g_{dsn}V_{o}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})
 +g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\\
g_{o}&=g_{dsn}+g_{dsp}\\
g_{n}&=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}\\
g_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}
\end{aligned}$$

Then for each inverter

$$g_{m}V_{i}+g_{o}V_{o}=g_{p}V_{x} \tag{1}$$
$$V_{o}= \frac{g_{p}}{g_{o}}V_{x}-\frac{g_{m}}{g_{o}}V_{i}.$$

For the 3-stage ring

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}V_{o3}+g_{o}V_{o1}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{o1}+g_{o}V_{o2}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{o2}+g_{o}V_{o3}&=g_{p}V_{x}
\end{aligned}$$

The excitation is common to all three identical stages.
The linear system is non-singular, so the solution is
symmetric:

$$V_{o1}=V_{o2}=V_{o3}=V_{o}.$$

Then from (1) with $V_{i}=V_{o}$,

$$(g_{m}+g_{o})V_{o}=g_{p}V_{x},$$

$$V_{o}=\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

In other words for supply variations each inverter
has $V_{i}=V_{o}$, i.e. is diode-connected.

The ac current entering the PMOS source, i.e. leaving
the $V_{x}$ node into one inverter, is $i_{sdp}$:

$$I_{1}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})+g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

Hence for the 3 inverters total current leaving $V_{x}$:

$$I_{x}= \sum_{k=1}^{3}\left[g_{p}V_{x}-g_{mp}V_{ik}
 -g_{dsp}V_{ok}\right].$$

With $V_{ik}=V_{ok}=V_{o}$,

$$I_{x}=3\left[g_{p}V_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})V_{o}\right]
 =3g_{p}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

$$V_{x}-V_{o}=V_{x}\left[1-\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}\right]
 =V_{x}\frac{g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}},$$

since $g_{m}+g_{o}-g_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}=g_{n}$.

Thus

$$I_{x}=3\frac{g_{p}g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

The low frequency impedance is three diode-connected
inverters in parallel:

$$R_{x}=\frac{g_{m}+g_{o}}{3\,g_{n}g_{p}}
 =\frac{1}{3}\frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{dsn}+g_{dsp}}
 {(g_{mn}+g_{dsn})(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})}.$$

With $g_{ds}\ll g_{m}$,

$$R_{x}\approx \frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}{3g_{mn}g_{mp}}
 =\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right).$$

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derivation is internally consistent for a static, linearized operating point, but it misses the dominant oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the load capacitances. The resulting gm-based resistance is the static analysis that the golden solution identifies as a major miss.

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
For one CMOS inverter let in small signal

* NMOS: $g_{mn},\,g_{dn}$ , source ac ground
* PMOS: $g_{mp},\,g_{dp}$ , source the common
$V_{DD}$ node, $n$-well to $V_{DD}$

Put a test source $V_{x}$ on the common $V_{DD}$
node. Let the three inverter input-output voltages be

$$ V_{a},V_{b},V_{c} $$

with

$$\begin{aligned}
1:&\; in=V_{a},\;out=V_{b}\\
2:&\; in=V_{b},\;out=V_{c}\\
3:&\; in=V_{c},\;out=V_{a}
\end{aligned}$$

For inverter $i$ with $in=V_{ini}$, $out=V_{outi}$,

NMOS drain current into drain:

$$ g_{mn}V_{ini}+g_{dn}V_{outi} $$

PMOS source to drain current:

$$ g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi}) $$

with $v_{sbp}=0$.  KCL at the output, neglecting
caps, gives

$$g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi})
 = g_{mn}V_{ini}+g_{dn}V_{outi}.$$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\\
g_{o}&=g_{dn}+g_{dp}\\
g_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{dp}\\
g_{n}&=g_{mn}+g_{dn}
\end{aligned}$$

Then

$$ g_{o}V_{outi}+g_{m}V_{ini}=g_{p}V_{x}. \tag{1}$$

Hence:

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}V_{a}+g_{o}V_{b}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{b}+g_{o}V_{c}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{o}V_{a}+g_{m}V_{c}&=g_{p}V_{x}
\end{aligned}\tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$\begin{bmatrix}
g_{m} & g_{o} & 0\\
0 & g_{m} & g_{o}\\
g_{o} & 0 & g_{m}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_{a}\\V_{b}\\V_{c}\end{bmatrix}
=g_{p}V_{x}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$$

$\det = g_{m}^{3}+g_{o}^{3}\ne 0$. The excitation
is common mode, the circuit is 3-fold symmetric.
Indeed

$$V_{a}=V_{b}=V_{c}=V$$

satisfies (2) with

$$(g_{m}+g_{o})V = g_{p}V_{x},$$

i.e.

$$V = \frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}. \tag{3}$$

By uniqueness this is the solution. For this
common mode excitation each inverter has in ac

$$V_{in}=V_{out},$$

i.e. it is diode connected.

The current drawn from $V_{x}$ by inverter $i$ is
the PMOS source current:

$$I_{si}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi})
 =g_{p}V_{x}-g_{mp}V_{ini}-g_{dp}V_{outi}.$$

Summing the three stages,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{x}&=\sum_{i}I_{si}\\
&=3g_{p}V_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{dp})(V_{a}+V_{b}+V_{c})\\
&=3g_{p}(V_{x}-V).
\end{aligned}$$

With (3),

$$I_{x}=3g_{p}\left(1-\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}\right)V_{x}.$$

But $g_{m}+g_{o}-g_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{dn}=g_{n}$. So

$$I_{x}=3\,\frac{g_{p}g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

The low frequency driving point admittance is
stable, the unstable complex poles are differential
and have zero sum, so are not excited. Hence

$$R_{x}=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=\frac{g_{m}+g_{o}}{3g_{p}g_{n}}.$$

i.e.

$$ R_{x}=\frac{1}{3}\,
\frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{dn}+g_{dp}}
{(g_{mn}+g_{dn})(g_{mp}+g_{dp})} $$

Each diode connected inverter is $\approx 1/g_{mn}+
1/g_{mp}$ from $V_{DD}$ to ground, three in parallel.
Neglecting $g_{d}$,

$$R_{x}\approx \frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}{3g_{mn}g_{mp}}
 =\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right).$$

In particular for $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, $R_{x}\approx 2/3g_{m}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derivation analyzes a static common-mode operating point and obtains a gm-based diode-connected resistance, but misses the dominant oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the node capacitances. The expected resistance is approximately 1/(3 f0 CL), not the static gm-based result.

answer.text:
By symmetry all of the stages respond identically to a
perturbation on the common $V_{DD}$.

Put a small signal $V_{x}$ on the common supply and let
$V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}$ be the small signal voltages at the
three inverter outputs, Fig. outputs 1,2,3. Let the $i$th
inverter have input $V_{prev}$ and output $V_{i}$.

For the NMOS, $V_{gs}=V_{prev}$, $V_{ds}=V_{i}$,
drain current, drain to source,

$$I_{n}=g_{mn}V_{prev}+\frac{V_{i}}{r_{on}} $$

For the PMOS, source is $V_{x}$, $V_{sg}=V_{x}-V_{prev}$,
$V_{sd}=V_{x}-V_{i}$, source to drain current, neglecting
body effect, the n-well moving with $V_{x}$,

$$I_{p}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{prev})+\frac{V_{x}-V_{i}}{r_{op}} $$

At the output node, at low frequencies, the gate of the
next stage draws no current,

$$I_{p}=I_{n}$$

i.e.

$$g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{prev})+\frac{V_{x}-V_{i}}{r_{op}}
 = g_{mn}V_{prev}+\frac{V_{i}}{r_{on}} $$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
G &=\frac1{r_{on}}+\frac1{r_{op}}=\frac1{R_{o}} \\
G_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp} \\
G_{n}&=g_{mn}+\frac1{r_{on}} \\
G_{p}&=g_{mp}+\frac1{r_{op}}
\end{aligned}$$

Then

$$V_{x}G_{p}-V_{prev}G_{m}-V_{i}G=0$$

$$V_{i}G+V_{prev}G_{m}=V_{x}G_{p}$$

For the 3 stage loop:

$$\begin{align*}
V_{1}G+V_{3}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}\\
V_{2}G+V_{1}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}\\
V_{3}G+V_{2}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}
\end{align*}$$

Hence $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V$ for the common mode drive.
Indeed summing,

$$(V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3})(G+G_{m})=3V_{x}G_{p}$$

Each inverter has, ac wise, gate shorted to drain:
$V_{in}=V_{out}$. It is a diode connected inverter between
$V_{x}$ and ground.

The current drawn from $V_{x}$ by stage $i$ is $I_{p,i}$,
$$I_{x}=\sum_{1}^{3}I_{p,i}$$

$$I_{p,i}=G_{p}(V_{x}-V_{i,m})$$

in the symmetric case $V_{i}=V$. Summing,

$$I_{x}=3V_{x}G_{p}-(V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3})G_{p}
 =G_{p}(3V_{x}-V_{sum})$$

With $V_{sum}=3V_{x}G_{p}/(G+G_{m})$,

$$I_{x}=3V_{x}G_{p}\left[1-\frac{G_{p}}{G+G_{m}}\right]$$

$$=3V_{x}G_{p}\frac{G+G_{m}-G_{p}}{G+G_{m}}$$

But $G+G_{m}-G_{p}=G_{n}$, so

$$I_{x}=3V_{x}\frac{G_{p}G_{n}}{G+G_{m}}$$

i.e. the impedance seen is

$$R_{X}=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=\frac{G+G_{m}}{3G_{p}G_{n}}$$

Since $G+G_{m}=G_{n}+G_{p}$,

$$R_{X}=\frac13\left(\frac1{G_{n}}+\frac1{G_{p}}\right)$$

$$R_{X}=\frac13\left[\frac{1}{g_{mn}+1/r_{on}}+\frac{1}{g_{mp}+1/r_{op}}\right]$$

the parallel of three identical diode-connected
inverters. With $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$,

$$R_{X}\approx \frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right)$$

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in the figure, somebody computes the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node as

```text
RX ~= (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)
```

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
Yes. The $1/g_m$ is a startup value.

For low frequency put a $v_x$ on the common
supply. For inverter $i$ let $v_{in,i},v_{out,i}$
be small signal. Neglecting $r_o$,

$$ i_{p,i} = g_{mp}(v_x-v_{in,i})+g_{dsp}(v_x-v_{out,i}) $$
$$ i_{n,i} = g_{mn}v_{in,i}+g_{dsn}v_{out,i} $$

$$i_{p,i}=(g_{o}+sC)v_{out,i}+g_m v_{in,i}\;\;{\rm with}\;\;
A=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}$$

$$(g_o+sC)v_{out,i}+g_m v_{in,i}=A v_x$$

For the 3 in a loop:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_1 &= [Av_x-g_mV_3]/(g_o+sC)\\
V_2 &= [Av_x-g_mV_1]/(g_o+sC)\\
V_3 &= [Av_x-g_mV_2]/(g_o+sC)
\end{aligned}$$

By symmetry $V_1=V_2=V_3$ for a common
$v_x$. I.e. incrementally

$$v_{in}=v_{out}$$

for every inverter. The gate moves with the drain.
That is the ``two diode connected devices in series''
for common mode:

NMOS diode $1/(g_{mn}+g_{dsn})$ from out to gnd
in series with PMOS diode $1/(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})$
from $V_{DD}$ to out.

Summing,

$$V_{sum}=3Av_x/(g_o+sC+g_m)$$

Supply current is sum of PMOS currents,

$$I_x =3Av_x-A V_{sum}$$

$$Z_x=\frac{v_x}{I_x}=\frac13\frac{g_m+g_o+sC}
{A\,(g_{mn}+g_{dsn}+sC)}$$

$$\approx \frac13\frac1{g_{mp}}+\frac1{g_{mn}}$$
at low $s$.

That linearizes at the metastable dc point,
all nodes at $V_{trip}$, both devices ON in
saturation with constant $g_m$. It is the
linear circuit before amplitude grows. It is what
a .ac gives.

Once the loop grows to steady large signal oscillation
that linearization is physically irrelevant.

* Nodes no longer move together. Large signal they
are $\approx 120^{\circ}$ apart at $f_0$.
Instantaneously $v_{in,i}\ne v_{out,i}$.
There is no diode connection.

* The devices no longer stay ON. Rail to rail,
each inverter is half the period NMOS OFF,
half the period PMOS OFF. There is ideally no
static path $V_{DD}$ to gnd. Instantaneous $g_m(t)$
is periodically zero, triode, saturation. It is
a periodically time varying small signal system,
with frequency translation, not an LTI $R_X$.

In the ideal switch limit with zero transition
time static current is zero, quasi-static

$$R_X \to \infty .$$

In practice current flows only during transitions.
The low frequency ``resistance'' is really

$$R_{X,av} = \frac{dV_{DD}}{dI_{av}}$$

where $I_{av}\approx N C V_{DD}f_0(V_{DD})$ is the
dynamic plus short-circuit charge per cycle.
It is set by how charge and frequency modulate
with $V_{DD}$, not by bias point $g_m$.
High tracks $V_{DD}$, low does not track, so
perturbation amplitude-modulates the waveform.
Effective $G_m$ is gain-compressed by Barkhausen
to unity loop gain, much smaller than startup
$g_m$.

So form is kept on average only if $g_m$ is
replaced by a describing / cycle-averaged
effective transconductance, which is much smaller.
$R_X$ grows dramatically.

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
Yes.

The $(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$ is an LTI
calculation around the metastable DC point,
with all inverters at threshold.

Put $v_x$ on the common supply and let $v_1,v_2,v_3$
be the small signal inverter outputs. Neglect caps
for the moment. With $A=g_{dn}+g_{dp}$,
$B=g_{mn}+g_{mp}$, $C=g_{mp}+g_{dp}$,

$$ A v_i + B v_{i-1} = C v_x \qquad i=1,2,3 \;\; {\rm cyclic} $$

i.e. $M{\bf v} = C v_x [1,1,1]^T$ with $M$
circulant. Its eigenvectors are the Fourier modes,
eigenvalues

$$\lambda_k = A + B e^{jk2\pi/3}\;\;,k=0,1,2 .$$

$k=0$ is the common mode $[1,1,1]$.
A common supply excites only $k=0$. At low
frequency with $|B/A|\gg 1$, $M$ is non-singular,
so

$$v_1=v_2=v_3=v .$$

Then for supply-induced signals $v_{in}=v_{out}$
for every inverter. The inverter looks, small-signal,
like gate-drain-shorted N in series with gate-drain-shorted P
between $v_x$ and ground:

$$I_{s} \approx (g_{mp}+g_{dp})(v_x-v)$$

with $v$ from KCL at the output. That gives

$$R_X =\frac{v_x}{3I_s}= \frac13
\frac{A+B}{(g_{mp}+g_{dp})(g_{mn}+g_{dn})}
\approx \frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right).$$

That whole argument collapses once the loop actually
oscillates.

An oscillator has no stable DC bias. The LTI poles
are in the RHP. The physical steady state is a large
signal limit cycle with the three node waveforms
nominally identical up to $T_0/3$, i.e. $120^{\circ}$
at $f_0$, swinging essentially rail to rail.

Then:

* There is no fixed $g_{mn},g_{mp}$. Each device goes
from off to saturation to triode over the cycle.
Small signal is linear periodically time varying,
not LTI. A tone at $\omega$ on $v_x$ generates
currents at $\omega \pm n\omega_0$.

* Instantaneously $v_{in}\ne v_{out}$. In fact for
most of the cycle an inverter is settled: one
device off, the other in triode, drawing essentially
zero DC current, i.e. open between VDD and GND.
Only the inverter in transition draws crowbar /
charging current. Time averaged $g_m$ is much
smaller than threshold $g_m$.

* Cyclic symmetry is now symmetry under
permutation + $T_0/3$ time shift. A common excitation
$e^{j\omega t}$ is invariant under $T_0/3$ shift
only for $\omega = k\cdot 3\omega_0$, in particular DC.
For general $\omega$ the three small signal responses
cannot be in phase. E.g. at $\omega_0$ a $T_0/3$
shift is $120^{\circ}$. So $v_1 \ne v_2 \ne v_3$,
$v_{in}\ne v_{out}$, no diode-connected.

In other words the inverters are not diode-connected
for the oscillation, nor in general for a perturbation
on top of the oscillation.

What survives is only the DC incremental form.
For a DC $\Delta V_{DD}$, symmetry still forces the
time-averaged waveforms to shift together by $\Delta V$.
Averaging KCL $\langle I_n\rangle =\langle I_p\rangle$
over a period,

$$\langle g_{mn}+g_{dn}\rangle\Delta V \approx
  \langle g_{mp}+g_{dp}\rangle(\Delta V_{DD}-\Delta V)$$

so

$$\frac{dV_{DD}}{dI_{avg}} \approx
\frac13\left[\frac1{\langle g_{mn}\rangle}+
\frac1{\langle g_{mp}\rangle}\right]$$

in form, but with cycle-averaged transconductances,
much smaller than the metastable bias $g_m$,
caps and frequency pushing ignored. Numerically it is
much larger, and for AC it becomes frequency dependent
with conversion. An .AC around the DC point does not
give the physical oscillating impedance. You need
PSS/PAC.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in the figure, somebody computes the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node as

```text
RX ~= (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)
```

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
Yes. The $(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$ is the
linear time-invariant impedance around the
metastable dc point. It is not what you physically
measure once the circuit has left that point and
is in large signal steady state.

Derivation of the LTI result assumes:

* all 3 inverters are biased identically, at the trip
point, in saturation, with constant $g_{m}$,
* the circuit is linearized there,
* a test $\Delta V_{DD}$ on the common supply
sees a circulant symmetric circuit.

Then by circular symmetry the forced response
must satisfy

$$\Delta V_{1}= \Delta V_{2}= \Delta V_{3}$$

Let $v_{i}$ be the small signal at output $i$.
For inverter $i$:

$$g_{mp}(v_{x}-v_{i-1})+g_{dp}(v_{x}-v_{i}) 
= g_{mn}v_{i-1}+g_{dn}v_{i}+sCv_{i}$$

with $v_{0}\equiv v_{3}$, $v_{x}$ the supply test
source. The symmetric vector $[v_{x},v_{x},v_{x}]$
excites only the $k=0$ eigenvector of the circulant,
$v_{1}=v_{2}=v_{3}=v$. Then for each inverter
in small signal

$$v_{in}=v_{i-1}=v=v_{i}=v_{out}.$$

Input can be virtually shorted to output. NMOS
looks diode connected, PMOS looks diode connected,
in series between supply and ground. At low
frequency $g_{m}\gg g_{d}$:

$$Z_{x}= \frac{A+B}{3C(A+B-C)}\approx
\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right)$$

with $A=g_{mn}+g_{mp}$, etc.

That is mathematics around the unstable
equilibrium. The oscillatory poles are in the
$k=1,2$ subspace, $B+A\exp(\pm j2\pi/3)=0$.
They have zero sum, $\sum v_{i}=0$, so they are
uncontrollable/unobservable from the common
supply in LTI theory. Math says $V_{x}$ to $I_{x}$
is stable even though the circuit itself is unstable.

Physically the circuit does not stay there.

Once in steady oscillation:

* There is no common dc bias. Large signal
$V_{1,0}(t),V_{2,0}(t),V_{3,0}(t)$ are essentially
rail-to-rail, $120^{\circ}$ apart:
$$V_{2,0}(t)=V_{1,0}(t-T/3),\;
V_{3,0}(t)=V_{1,0}(t-2T/3).$$
At any instant the three inverters are in different
states - high, low, in transition. Most of the time
one device is off, the other in triode. The path
$V_{DD}$ to ground is essentially open except
during transitions.

* $g_{mn},g_{mp}$ are not constants. They are
periodic functions of time, going from $\approx 0$
to peak, phase shifted from stage to stage:
$$g_{m2}(t)=g_{m1}(t-T/3),\;{\rm etc.}$$

The linearized circuit is linear periodically
time varying, not LTI circularly symmetric at
fixed $t$. Symmetry is permutation + $T/3$
time shift.

Hence a common perturbation $v_{x}(t)$ does not
produce $v_{1}(t)=v_{2}(t)=v_{3}(t)$. It produces
phase shifted perturbations,
$$v_{2}(t)=v_{1}(t-T/3),\;{\rm etc.}$$
In particular for inverter 1,
$$v_{in,p}(t)=v_{3,p}(t)\ne v_{1,p}(t)=v_{out,p}(t)$$
in general. You can no longer virtually short
input to output. The diode-connected equivalence
collapses instantaneously.

Consequences:

* ``Small signal resistance'' as an LTI number
no longer exists. A test tone at $\omega_{t}$
mixes with $\omega_{0}$ to $\omega_{t}\pm k\omega_{0}$.
You need a conversion matrix. A dc shift $\Delta V_{DD}$
changes amplitude, shape and, importantly, frequency,
i.e. unbounded phase accumulation, not just a common
dc shift.

* What you could call low frequency incremental
$\partial V_{DD}/\partial I_{avg}$, averaged over
many cycles, is set by dynamic and short-circuit
power, $I_{avg}\approx N C V_{DD}f_{0}(V_{DD})+
I_{sc}(V_{DD})$, not by $1/g_{m}$ at trip. Typically
it is much larger and mostly capacitive, with
periodic dips, and with fundamental $f_{0}$ cancellation
in supply current due to 3-phase sum $\approx 0$.

In short: the formula uses the trip-point $g_{m}$'s
and $v_{in}=v_{out}$. In oscillation there is no
trip-point bias, $g_{m}(t)\approx 0$ most of
the cycle, and $V_{in}\ne V_{out}$ even for
perturbations. An .ac around .op will give
$(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$, but a PSS / transient
with oscillation will not.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer correctly notes that oscillation invalidates the static small-signal model, but concludes the supply resistance is typically much larger because devices are off most of the cycle. The key result is that capacitive charging sets the resistance and it remains on the order of the MOS on-resistance, not much higher.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
This is a StrongARM latch.

With $CK=0$, $M_{7}$ is off and $S_{1}-S_{4}$ precharge
$P,Q,X,Y$ to $V_{DD}$. $M_{3}-M_{6}$ are off.

With $CK=1$, $S_{1}-S_{4}$ are off, $M_{7}$ is on.
$P,Q$ and then $X,Y$ discharge through $M_{1}$-$M_{7}$
and $M_{2}$-$M_{7}$.

As long as $X,Y$ are high, $M_{5},M_{6}$ are off.
The circuit is a dynamic integrator. Let

$$I_{D1,2}=I_{0}\pm \Delta I/2$$

$$ \Delta I \approx g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}$$

On $C_{X}\approx C_{Y}=C$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}(V_{X}-V_{Y}) \approx -\frac{I_{D1}-I_{D2}}{C}
= -\frac{g_{m1,2}}{C}\Delta V_{in}$$

The integration stops when the common mode of $X,Y$
has fallen by $|V_{THP}|$ and $M_{5}$ or $M_{6}$
turns on and regeneration begins. The common-mode
discharge is

$$V_{X,Y,CM}\approx V_{DD}-\frac{I_{0}}{C}t$$

so

$$t_{1}\approx \frac{C|V_{THP}|}{I_{0}}$$

is the available amplification time. The differential
built up at that time is

$$|V_{X}-V_{Y}|_{t_{1}}\approx \frac{g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}}{C}t_{1}
 = g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}\frac{|V_{THP}|}{I_{0}}$$

i.e. the pre-regeneration voltage gain is

$$A_{0}=\frac{|V_{X}-V_{Y}|}{\Delta V_{in}}\approx 
\frac{g_{m1,2}|V_{THP}|}{I_{0}}$$

$I_{0}$ is essentially half the $M_{7}$ current.
Larger $W_{7}$ gives larger tail current, faster
discharge.

$g_{m1,2}\propto \sqrt{I_{0}}$ but $t_{1}\propto 1/I_{0}$.
Net:

$$A_{0}\propto \frac{g_{m}}{I}\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{I_{0}}}
\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{W_{7}}}$$

The larger current leaves proportionally less time
to integrate than the increase in $g_{m}$. Initial
gain falls.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that initial gain decreases as M7 widens. The explanation is physically consistent: tail current increases, while input-pair transconductance grows only as the square root of current, so the available integration gain scales roughly as gm/I and falls.

answer.text:
This is the StrongARM latch. After $CK$ goes high
$X$ and $Y$ are discharged from $V_{DD}$ by $M_{1},M_{3}$
and $M_{2},M_{4}$.

Put $C_{X}\approx C_{Y}=C$. For a small $\Delta V_{in}$
the $M_{1}-M_{2}$ current difference is essentially constant
during the discharge,

$$I_{D1}-I_{D2}\approx g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}$$

so that the differential output integrates:

$$\Delta V_{XY}(t)=V_{X}-V_{Y}\approx \frac{1}{C}\int_{0}^{t}
(I_{D2}-I_{D1})dt \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}t}{C}\Delta V_{in} $$

Common mode falls as

$$V_{X,cm}(t) \approx V_{DD}-\frac{I_{tail}/2}{C}t $$

The ``amplification'' stops when $V_{X,cm}$ has fallen
enough, $\approx |V_{THP}|$, to turn on the $p$-latch
$M_{5}-M_{6}$. That is at

$$t_{int}\approx \frac{C|V_{THP}|}{I_{tail}/2}$$

Hence the differential voltage built up before
regeneration, normalized to the input, is

$$A_{v0}= \frac{\Delta V_{XY}(t_{int})}{\Delta V_{in}}
     \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}t_{int}}{C}
     \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}|V_{THP}|}{I_{tail}/2}$$

i.e. $g_{m}/I$ times the voltage swing.

A wider $M_{7}$ gives a larger $I_{tail}$ during
evaluation. $g_{m1,2}$ goes up only $\sim \sqrt{I_{tail}}$
in square law, $\sim$ const in velocity saturation,
whereas $t_{int}$ goes down $\sim 1/I_{tail}$ because
the $C_{X,Y}$ capacitors are discharged faster.

In square law,

$$A_{v0}\approx \frac{2|V_{THP}|g_{m1,2}}{I_{tail}}
\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{I_{tail}}}$$

So increasing $W_{7}$ shortens the integration time
more than it increases $g_{m}$, and the initial
integration gain falls.

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Delta V_{X,Y} \approx \frac{\Delta I}{C_{tot}} $$

regeneration, i.e. the initial voltage gain, is

$$ A_{v0} = \frac{\Delta V_{X,Y}(t_{p})}{\Delta V_{in}}

 \approx \frac{2|V_{THp}|g_{m1,2}}{I_{tail}} $$

larger $I_{tail}$.

$g_{m1,2}\propto \sqrt{I_{tail}}$ in strong inversion,
while $t_{p}\propto 1/I_{tail}$.

$$ A_{v0} \propto \frac{g_{m}}{I_{tail}} \propto

answers.question: In the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
The circuit is a StrongArm latch.

When CK=0, $S_{1-4}$ ON, $P,Q,X,Y$ are precharged to $V_{DD}$, $M_7$ is OFF.

When CK goes high, $M_7$ goes ON, $S_{1-4}$ go
OFF. $P$ and $Q$ discharge through $M_{1,2}$ with

$$ I_{1,2} \approx I_{CM} \pm \frac{g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}}{2} $$

When $P,Q$ have fallen by $\approx V_{THN}$, $M_{3,4}$
turn ON and $X,Y$ start to fall. When $X,Y$ have
fallen by $\approx |V_{THP}|$, $M_{5,6}$ turn ON and
regeneration takes over.

The differential developed on $X,Y$ up to that time is
the "initial" voltage for the latch:

$$ \Delta V_{0} = A_{v,init} \Delta V_{in} $$

$A_{v,init}$ is essentially an integrating gain:

$$ \Delta V_{0} \approx \frac{\Delta I \cdot T_{int}}{C} $$

Increasing $C_P,C_Q$ slows the fall of $P,Q$ and
hence the fall of $X,Y$. The common-mode discharge

$$\frac{dV_{X,CM}}{dt} \approx -\frac{I_{CM}}{C_X+C_P}$$

is reduced, so the time $T_{int}$ required for
$V_{X,CM}$ to fall from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$,
i.e. to turn $M_{5,6}$ ON, is prolonged.

The input pair and $M_{3,4}$ therefore have longer to
integrate the $\Delta I = g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}$ and to
positively feedback via the $M_{3,4}$ cross couple.
The developed differential $\Delta V_{0}$ is larger.

i.e. larger $C_P,C_Q$ gives larger initial amplification
gain, at the expense of speed.

answer.text:

* $CK=0$: $M_{7}$ off, $S_{1-4}$ on. $P,Q,X,Y$ are

$|V_{THP}|$. Up to that moment the circuit is a
dynamic integrator / NMOS amplifier. The differential

$$\Delta V_{XY0} = A_{0}\,\Delta V_{in}$$

is the ``initial'' voltage which the full CMOS
regeneration then amplifies to the rail.

In common mode $M_{3,4}$ are diode connected between
$X,Y$ and $P,Q$. First $P,Q$ must fall by $\approx V_{THN}$
to turn $M_{3,4}$ on:

$$I_{0}t_{0}\approx C_{P,Q}V_{THN}$$

Then $P$,$X$ and $Q$,$Y$ fall together. $X,Y$ must
fall by $\approx |V_{THP}|$ to turn $M_{5,6}$ on:

$$I_{0}t_{1}\approx (C_{P,Q}+C_{X,Y})|V_{THP}|$$

Total integration time before regeneration:

$$t_{reg}=t_{0}+t_{1}\approx
\frac{C_{P}V_{THN}+ (C_{P}+C_{X})|V_{THP}|}{I_{0}}$$

During $t_{reg}$ the input difference
$\Delta I = g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}$ is integrated,
and the cross coupled $M_{3,4}$ is allowed to
amplify. To first order the differential charge put
on the capacitors is $\Delta I\,t_{reg}$.

in proportion. $P,Q$ - and through $M_{3,4}$, $X,Y$ -
discharge more slowly, so the PMOS pair is kept off
longer. There is more time to integrate $\Delta I$
and more $g_{m3,4}/C$ time constants for the NMOS
pair to amplify before the PMOS regeneration starts.

Hence the differential voltage sampled on $X,Y$
when regeneration starts is larger. I.e. $A_{0}$
goes up, at the expense of a slower comparison.

answer.text:
This is a StrongARM latch.

differential amplifier. Strong regeneration starts
only when the $X,Y$ common mode has fallen by
$\approx |V_{thp}|$ to turn $M_{5,6}$ on.

Let at that moment $t=t_{1}$,

$$A_{0} = \frac{\Delta V_{X,Y}(t_{1})}{\Delta V_{in}}$$

be the ``initial'' voltage built up before the
CMOS latch takes over. That is what divides the
latch offset and noise.

For common mode $M_{3,4}$ are diode connected:
gate and drain both move with $V_{X,Y,cm}$.
Roughly $V_{P,cm}$ follows $V_{X,cm}$:

$$(C_{X}+C_{P})\frac{dV_{X,cm}}{dt}\approx -I_{D}$$

where $I_{D}\approx I_{tail}/2$. Hence the time
available for amplification, to get
$\Delta V_{X,cm}\approx |V_{thp}|$, is

$$t_{1}\approx \frac{(C_{X}+C_{P})|V_{thp}|}{I_{D}}$$

Increasing $C_{P,Q}$ directly prolongs the
amplification phase.

For differential mode $M_{3}$ gate sees $-v_{x}$
because it is connected to the opposite side $Y$,
and vice versa. Neglecting $g_{ds}$:

$$\begin{aligned}
C_{X}sv_{x} &= -i_{d3} \\
C_{P}sv_{p} &= i_{d3}-i_{d1}
\end{aligned}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{id}/2,\;\;
i_{d3}=g_{m3}(-v_{x}-v_{p})$$

i.e.

$$s\big[C_{P}C_{X}s+g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})\big]v_{x}
= -g_{m1}g_{m3}v_{id}/2$$

The cross coupled NMOS present positive feedback.
For common mode the effective cap is $C_{X}+C_{P}$,
for difference it is $C_{X}-C_{P}$.
In time domain for a step $\Delta V_{in}$,
once $at\gg 1$,

$$\Delta V_{X}(t) \approx \frac{g_{m1}t}{C_{X}-C_{P}}\Delta V_{in}$$

Put $t=t_{1}$:

$$A_{0}\approx \frac{g_{m1}t_{1}}{C_{X}-C_{P}}
\approx \frac{g_{m1}|V_{thp}|}{I_{D}}\,
\frac{C_{X}+C_{P}}{C_{X}-C_{P}}$$

Larger $C_{P,Q}$ gives longer $t_{1}$ and smaller
net differential capacitance. The differential
current $g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}$ has more time to
integrate to a larger $\Delta V_{X,Y}$ before

So the pre-regeneration gain goes up, at the
expense of a slower $t_{1}$.

reset switches.

$CK=0$: $M_7$ is off, $S_1-S_4$ are on. $P,Q,X,Y$

through the $M_3-M_1$ and $M_4-M_2$ paths.

$M_5,M_6$, the pmos cross-coupled pair, are initially
off:
$$V_{SG5}=V_{DD}-Y \approx 0\;, \;\; V_{SG6}=V_{DD}-X \approx 0$$

To start regeneration e.g. $X$ must fall by about
$|V_{THP}|$ to turn $M_6$ on and pull $Y$ back
to $V_{DD}$, and vice versa.

During this critical discharge time $M_5,M_6$
contribute essentially only capacitance to $X,Y$:

* drain capacitance of $M_{5}$ on $X$, of $M_{6}$ on $Y$
* gate capacitance of $M_{6}$ on $X$, of $M_{5}$ on $Y$
* overlap capacitances

The discharge current is set by $M_1-M_4$, essentially
independent of $M_5,M_6$. The time to get the
$|V_{THP}|$ drop needed for regeneration is

$$t_0 \approx \frac{C_{X,Y}\,|V_{THP}|}{I_{D1,2}}$$

Larger $W_5,W_6$ means larger $C_{X,Y}$, smaller
$dV/dt$, later turn-on of $M_5,M_6$.

Once regeneration starts the time constant is
of the form

$$\tau_{reg} \approx \frac{C_{X,Y}}{g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6}}$$

$C_{X,Y} \propto W_{5,6}$ while $g_{m5,6}\propto
\sqrt{W_{5,6}}$ in square-law, $\propto W_{5,6}$
at best in velocity saturation. The capacitance
grows faster than the transconductance. $\tau_{reg}$
therefore grows with $W_{5,6}$.

In other words $M_5,M_6$ load the nodes during
the whole discharge and only help after they turn
on. The net $CK$-to-output delay increases.

Larger $W_5,W_6$ also makes reset slower: more
capacitance to precharge to $V_{DD}$ through
$S_3,S_4$.

So stronger pmos latch does not mean faster latch.
For speed $M_5,M_6$ want to be small.

$P,Q,X,Y$ are precharged to $V_{DD}$. $M_{5,6}$ are off.

With gates at $Y,X\approx V_{DD}$, $M_{3,4}$ are on and

$V_{X,Y}$ falls by $|V_{THP}|$. Then $M_{5,6}$ turn
on and the $M_{3,4}$-$M_{5,6}$ cross coupled pair
regenerates.

interval. They contribute only load:

$C_{X}\approx C_{S3}+C_{D3}+C_{D5}+C_{G6}+C_{wire}$
$C_{Y}\approx C_{S4}+C_{D4}+C_{D6}+C_{G5}+C_{wire}$

almost proportionally, so $t_{0}$ goes up for the
same tail current. It takes longer to develop the
differential voltage.

the order

$C_{X,Y}$ grows $\propto W_{5,6}$ whereas $g_{m5,6}$
grows sub-linearly with $W_{5,6}$, and $M_{5,6}$
when on fight the n-pull down. The net $\tau_{reg}$
goes up. The reset time to precharge $X,Y$ also
goes up.

answer.text:
This is a StrongARM latch. $S_{1}-S_{4}$ are the
reset precharge switches.

* $CK=0$: $M_{7}$ off, $S_{1}-S_{4}$ on.
$P,Q,X,Y$ are precharged to $V_{DD}$. $M_{3}-M_{6}$
are off.

* $CK=1$: $S_{1}-S_{4}$ off, $M_{7}$ on. $P,Q$
are discharged by $M_{1},M_{2}$ at different rates.
$M_{3},M_{4}$ are on because $X,Y$ start at $V_{DD}$,
so $X,Y$ discharge with $P,Q$ through

```
X -> M3 -> P -> M1 -> M7
Y -> M4 -> Q -> M2 -> M7
```

$M_{5}$ and $M_{6}$ are the PMOS of the back-to-back
latch:

* $M_{5}$: source $V_{DD}$, drain $X$, gate $Y$
* $M_{6}$: source $V_{DD}$, drain $Y$, gate $X$

At the beginning of evaluation $V_{SG5}=V_{DD}-V_{Y}=0$,
$V_{SG6}=V_{DD}-V_{X}=0$. They stay off until

$$ V_{X,Y} < V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| $$

i.e. for a large fraction of the discharge time they
do nothing except load the nodes.

The capacitance on the regenerating nodes is roughly:

$$ C_{X} \approx C_{dS3}+C_{d5}+C_{g6}+C_{d3} $$
$$ C_{Y} \approx C_{dS4}+C_{d6}+C_{g5}+C_{d4} $$

Increasing $W_{5,6}$ increases $C_{d5,6}$ on its
own drain node and $C_{g5,6}$ on the opposite node.

1. Initial discharge time: The time to get $X,Y$
down by $|V_{THP}|$ to turn the PMOS on is

$$ t_{0} \approx \frac{C_{X,Y}\,\Delta V}{I_{D1,2}} $$

$I_{D1,2}$ is set by $M_{1,2},M_{7}$, not by
$M_{5,6}$. Larger $W_{5,6}$ just makes $C_{X,Y}$
larger, $t_{0}$ longer.

2. Regeneration: Once $M_{5,6}$ are on, the delay
is of the form

$$ t_{latch} \propto \frac{C_{X,Y}}{g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6}}\ln(\cdot) $$

$g_{m5,6}$ grows sublinearly with $W$ while $C_{X,Y}$
grows linearly. More important, while both $X$ and $Y$
are falling, both $M_{5}$ and $M_{6}$ are on pulling
up, fighting the NMOS pull-down through $M_{3,4}$.
Making the PMOS bigger makes that contention stronger
for the side that has to go to 0, and it has to be
overcome by the $M_{1}-M_{4}$ current difference.

In other words, during the critical high-gain discharge
the extra PMOS width is pure self-loading. The small
increase in $g_{m5,6}$ in regeneration does not make
up for the linear increase in $C$ and the larger
PMOS-NMOS fight.

It also makes reset slower: $S_{3},S_{4}$ must
precharge a larger $C_{X,Y}$ to $V_{DD}$.

So net clock-to-output delay goes up. For speed
$M_{5},M_{6}$ are kept small, just large enough to
reliably pull the high side back to $V_{DD}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M5/M6 as cross-coupled PMOS devices and notes that widening adds capacitance, but it wrongly concludes that this dominates from the outset. The initial speed improvement from stronger regeneration is the key result; added capacitance limits the benefit only at larger widths.

answer.text:
The 2 tristates form a dynamic master-slave toggle.

* $CK=1$: left tristate on,
$$X=\bar Z$$
right tristate off, $Y$ floating, $Z=\bar Y$ held.
* $CK=0$: left tristate off, $X$ floating,
$$Y=\bar X,\;\; Z=\bar Y$$

After a full cycle $Y \to \bar Y$. It is a $\div 2$.

Speed is the time to charge the dynamic nodes $X$
and $Y$ through the stack in the evaluate half cycle.

Take e.g. the left stack pulling $X$ high:

```
VDD - Rdp(Z) - Rcp(CKbar) - Cx - GND
            |
           Cint
```

$R_{dp}\propto 1/W_{data}$, $R_{cp}\propto 1/W_{ck}$ are
the on resistances of the data PMOS and the clocked
PMOS in series. $C_{x}$ is

$$ C_{x}=C_{g,next}+C_{d,ck}+C_{w} $$

i.e. gate load of the following data transistors,
drain capacitance of the clocked transistor that
touches $X$, wire. $C_{int}$ is the capacitance
of the internal node between the two series PMOS,

$$C_{int}\propto W_{data}+W_{ck}$$

Elmore approx:

$$t \approx R_{dp}(C_{int}+C_{x})+R_{cp}C_{x}$$

$$R_{cp}C_{x}= \frac{k}{W_{ck}}(C_{0}+cW_{ck})
 =\frac{kC_{0}}{W_{ck}}+kc$$

$C_{0}$ is the fixed part, $C_{g,next}+C_{w}$.
Similarly for pull-down through the data NMOS $M_{1}$
and the clocked NMOS.

Widening only $W_{ck}$:

* reduces $R_{cp}$, i.e. reduces the $kC_{0}/W_{ck}$ term.
* increases $C_{x}\propto W_{ck}$ and $C_{int}\propto
W_{ck}$ directly on the dynamic node.

The current is essentially limited by the data
transistor in series. Once $R_{cp}<R_{dp}$ further
reduction in $R_{cp}$ buys very little current,
whereas $R_{dp}C_{int}+R_{dp}C_{x}$ grows
$\propto W_{ck}$:

$$t \approx A\,W_{ck}+B/W_{ck}+{\rm const}$$

$$A=R_{data}(b+c),\;\; B=kC_{0}$$

$C_{0}$ is small - gates of minimum data devices
to keep the dynamic node light - and $R_{data}$ is
relatively large. The optimum is at very small
$W_{ck}$. In a balanced design you are already
past it. More $W_{ck}$ is more self-loading for
essentially the same drive current.

In addition:

* bigger $W_{ck}$ puts bigger $C_{db}$ on $X,Y$,
which must be charged/discharged every cycle.
* bigger $W_{ck}$ puts bigger gate load on $CK,\overline{CK}$,
slowing the clock edges for a given clock driver.
* the clocked devices touch $X,Y$ directly. Gate-drain
overlap $C_{ov}\propto W_{ck}$ injects

$$\Delta V\approx \frac{C_{ov}}{C_{ov}+C_{x}}V_{CK}$$

onto the floating node at turn-off. Larger $W_{ck}$
means larger feedthrough glitch, less held level,
less overdrive for the next stage.

Net: the evaluate delay at $X$ and $Y$ goes up,
the maximum toggle frequency goes down.

Keep clocked devices minimum for speed and clock power.
If more drive is needed, size the data devices.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes that widening lowers clocked-device on-resistance but adds node capacitance, yet concludes that widening degrades speed because the data devices limit the drive. The required result is that speed improves initially as clocked-device resistance falls, with added capacitance eventually limiting or reversing the benefit.

answer.text:
This is a dynamic divide by 2:

$$ Z \to {\rm Inv1}_{CK} \to X \to {\rm Inv2}_{\overline{CK}}
\to Y \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv3}} Z $$

Inv1 is on for $CK=1$, Inv2 is on for $CK=0$.
$X$ and $Y$ are dynamic nodes. The $f_{max}$ is
set by the time to charge/discharge $X$ through
Inv1 during the $CK=1$ half period and $Y$ through
Inv2 during the $CK=0$ half period.

E.g. for the left stack

```
VDD - data p - clock p - X - clock n - data n - GND
                CKbar         CK
```

and similarly on the right. The clocked devices
are the ones next to the output. Their drains tie
directly to $X,Y$.

$$ C_X = C_{g,next}+C_{d,clkp}+C_{d,clkn}+C_{ov} $$
$$ C_Y = C_{g,Inv3}+C_{d,clkp}+C_{d,clkn}+C_{ov} $$

To pull $X$ up current must flow through the
data-p in series with the clock-p. To pull $X$
down through the data-n, $M_1$, in series with
the clock-n. I.e. to first order

$$ \tau \approx (R_{data}+R_{clk})
       (C_{next}+C_{d,clk}) $$

Widening the clocked transistors:

* reduces $R_{clk}\propto 1/W_{clk}$,
* increases $C_{d,clk}\propto W_{clk}$ at the
output node, plus gate-overlap and clock load.

The data transistors are left unchanged. The
current soon becomes limited by $R_{data}$.
You do not get $\propto W_{clk}$ more current.

Moreover for a given transition only one of the
two clocked devices is even on. E.g. pull-up
is helped only by a wider clock-p. The wider
clock-n is off, it contributes only extra drain
capacitance to $X,Y$. You get half the $R$
benefit and full $C$ penalty.

In other words the outer, data, devices have
their drains on internal series nodes, not on
$X,Y$. Widening them reduces $R_{data}$ with
little increase in $C_X,C_Y$. Widening the
inner, clocked, devices puts the extra diffusion
capacitance directly on the dynamic output nodes
that have to be swung.

Net $CV/I$ goes up, the clock driver is also
loaded more, feedthrough to the floating $X,Y$
is increased. The loop delay increases, $f_{max}$
degrades.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the resistance reduction and added node capacitance, but concludes widening degrades speed. The expected trend is initial improvement from lower clocked-device resistance, with added capacitance limiting or eventually reversing the benefit.

answer.text:
The two 4-transistor gates are tri-state inverters.

* left: in $=Z$, out $=X$, transparent for $CK=1$
* middle: in $=X$, out $=Y$, transparent for $CK=0$

with $Z=\overline Y$. It is a master-slave toggle,
a divide-by-2. In one half period $X$ must be
charged/discharged to $\overline Z$ through the left
gate, in the next half period $Y$ must be charged/
discharged to $\overline X$ through the middle gate.

Consider one gate in the transparent mode, e.g.

$$V_{DD}-M_{p,in}-M_{p,CK}-X-M_{n,CK}-M_{n,in}-GND$$

The signal input sees $M_{p,in},M_{n,in}$, $M_{1}$.
The $CK$ devices are $ac$ ground common-gate
cascode switches in series with them.

To first order the large signal (dis)charge current
available at $X$, $Y$ is set by the input devices.
Making the cascode switch bigger lowers its triode
resistance a little and raises its saturation current
a little toward the limit imposed by the input device,
i.e. diminishing returns.

What it does proportionally is add capacitance to
the signal path:

* $C_{db}$ and $C_{gd,ov}$ of the $CK$ $p$ and $n$
  directly on $X$, $Y$,
* $C_{s}$ of the $CK$ devices plus $C_{d}$ of the
  input devices on the internal stack nodes $A,B$,
  which must be (dis)charged through the stack,
* $C_{g}$ on $CK,\overline{CK}$, i.e. more clock load.

In

$$t_{CK\to X,Y} \approx \frac{C_{X,Y}V_{DD}}{I_{stack}}$$

$C_{X,Y}$ grows $\propto W_{CK}$ while $I_{stack}$
saturates to the current of $M_{p,in},M_{1}$.
The Elmore delay

$$R_{in}(C_{int}+C_{L})+R_{CK}C_{L}$$

grows once $R_{CK}$ is no longer dominant.

Hence the transparent clocked-inverter delay
increases, the half-period needed to settle $X$
and $Y$ increases, the maximum clock rate falls.
Widening the switches is essentially more self-loading.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer recognizes the latch topology and a real capacitance penalty, but concludes that widening the clocked transistors degrades speed. The essential trend is that speed improves initially as their on-resistance falls, with added capacitance limiting or eventually reversing the benefit.

answer.text:
Yes. It is a dynamic divide by 2.

Put the two clocked stages as tri-state inverters.

Left:
VDD-P1-P2-X-N2-N1-GND
P2 = $\overline{CK}$, N2=$CK$, P1=N1=Z

so

* $CK=1$: P2,N2 on, $X = \bar Z$
* $CK=0$: P2,N2 off, $X$ held on its capacitance

Right:
VDD-P1-P2-Y-N2-N1-GND
P2 = $CK$, N2=$\overline{CK}$, P1=N1=X

so

* $CK=0$: P2,N2 on, $Y = \bar X$
* $CK=1$: P2,N2 off, $Y$ held on its capacitance

$Z = {\rm Inv3}(Y)=\bar Y$ always.

The loop is never closed statically. Alternately:

$CK=1$, master transparent, slave hold:
$$ X = \bar Z = Y_{prev} $$
$Y$ holds.

$CK=0$, master hold, slave transparent:
$$ Y = \bar X $$
$X$ holds, $Z=\bar Y$ follows.

Around the loop there are 3 inversions:
tri+tri+Inv3. It toggles.

In steady state at $f_{CK}$:

* $CK=1$: $X$ follows $Y$, $Y$ frozen
* $CK=0$: $Y = \bar X$, $X$ frozen

Hence $X$ can change only shortly after the rising
edge of $CK$, $Y$ can change only shortly after the
falling edge of $CK$. E.g. ideal:

```
CK  _|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_
X   ___|‾‾‾|___
Y   _|‾‾‾|___|‾
Z   ‾|___|‾‾‾|
```

$X$ falls on a rise, rises on the next rise, etc.
$Y$ rises on a fall, falls on the next fall, etc.

Both $X$ and $Y$ repeat every 2 $CK$ periods,
i.e. $f_{CK}/2$, with 50% duty - transitions are
rise-to-rise for $X$, fall-to-fall for $Y$ - and
the $X$-transition to $Y$-transition spacing is
one $CK$ half-period.

$$T_{out}=2T_{CK}$$
$$T_{X\to Y}=T_{CK}/2 = T_{out}/4$$

i.e. 90 deg at $f_{CK}/2$. $Z=\bar Y$ is the
complement.

Ideally $X$ vs $Y,Z$ are quadrature. In practice
the $T_{CK}/2$ spacing requires 50% duty $CK$
and matched tri-state delays.

answer.text:
Yes. It is a $\div 2$.

The left stack is a clocked inverter

* $PMOS$ input on top, $NMOS$ input at bottom $M_{1}$
* clock devices in the middle

```
VDD
 |
p - Z
p - CKbar
n - CK
n - Z    M1
 |
GND
 --> X
```

i.e. when $CK=1$, $\overline{CK}=0$ the middle
devices are on and

$$ X = \overline{Z} $$

when $CK=0$ the middle devices are off and $X$
is held dynamically.

The right stack is the same with opposite clock:

```
VDD
 |
p - X
p - CK
n - CKbar
n - X    M1
 |
GND
 --> Y
```

i.e. when $CK=0$ :

$$ Y = \overline{X} $$

when $CK=1$, $Y$ is held.

$$ Z = \overline{Y} $$ by $Inv_{3}$.

There are 3 inversions around the loop, net
inversion. Put in cascade:

* $CK=1$ : master transparent, slave hold
  $$ X = \bar Z\,, \; Y = hold $$
* $CK=0$ : master hold, slave transparent
  $$ X = hold\,, \; Y = \bar X $$

Let $R_{n}$ be rising edge, $F_{n}$ falling edge.
$Z=\bar Y$.

At $R_{n}$ :
$$ X_{n} = \bar Z_{n-1} = Y_{n-1} $$

At $F_{n}$ :
$$ Y_{n} = \bar X_{n} = \bar Y_{n-1} $$

So $Y$ toggles every $CK$ cycle. $X$ toggles
every $CK$ cycle. Frequency $= f_{CK}/2$.

Importantly $X$ changes shortly after $R$,
$Y$ changes shortly after $F$, by the
$CK$-to-$Q$ of the dynamic stage.

With $50\%$ duty $CK$, $R$ to $F$ is
$T_{CK}/2$. Output period is

$$T_{out}=2T_{CK}$$

so $R$-to-$F$ is $T_{out}/4$.

$X$ and $Y$ are both $f_{CK}/2$, $50\%$ duty
square waves offset by $T_{out}/4$, i.e.
$90^{\circ}$. $Y$ and $Z$ are complementary.

That is $I/Q$ in quadrature, up to
lead/lag ambiguity on start-up.
